name: colortwist
baseline: Intel IPP ippiColorTwist (and a plain C reference loop)
workload: Colour twist (3x4 matrix times RGB triple) on a 2048x2048 RGB48 and RGB24 bitmap, MB/s, repeated 100 times by test/testcolortwist.cpp, outputs compared against the C and IPP results.
claimed_speedup: RGB48 on i7-8700K, MSVC 19.27: IPP 1720.98 MB/s vs AVX 3291.02, AVX2 4297.74, AVX3 5175.55 MB/s (3.0x IPP for AVX3, derived from page data); RGB24: IPP 892.93 vs AVX3 2966.55 MB/s (3.3x, derived from page data). Ryzen 7 4700U, MSVC: RGB48 IPP 1836.64 vs AVX3 5572.38 MB/s (3.0x, derived from page data). i9-12900K, MSVC 19.31: RGB48 IPP 2203.86 vs AVX3 9091.08 MB/s (4.1x), RGB24 IPP 1116.93 vs AVX3 5441.54 MB/s (4.9x) (both derived from page data). Single-threaded on both sides.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.27.29112 and 19.31.31106.2, Intel icl 19.1.3.311, gcc 10.2.0 / 7.5.0 (no IPP rows for gcc). The README build steps use cmake --build . --config Release (CMake's default MSVC Release flags). /arch:AVX2 on colortwist_avx.cpp under MSVC, -mfma -mavx2 (AVX file) and -msse4.1 (SSE file) under GCC/Clang (lib/CMakeLists.txt). Static MSVC runtime (CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY MultiThreaded). IPP is linked statically from ippccmt.lib and ippcoremt.lib (test/CMakeLists.txt); the IPP version is not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-8700K @ 3.70GHz, AMD Ryzen 7 4700U, Intel Core m3-6Y30 and Intel Core i9-12900K for the IPP comparisons (Windows, MSVC/icl). Linux gcc, Raspberry Pi 3b/4, Snapdragon 7c, Apple M2 and OrangePi RV2 (RISC-V) rows compare only against the plain C version.
tradeoffs: Does one operation (colour matrix transform on RGB24/RGB48, plus RISC-V and NEON versions); not a general colour management engine; the IPP comparison is Windows-oriented and needs IPP to reproduce.
caveats: 1. IPP rows appear only in the Windows MSVC/icl tables. The IPP version is not stated: FindIPP.cmake searches the Parallel Studio and oneAPI install paths. 2. The harness never calls ippInit(). 3. IPP is linked from the default static libraries (ippccmt.lib, ippcoremt.lib); colortwist is also single-threaded, so the threading modes match. 4. Precision matches: the baseline is ippiColorTwist32f_16u_C3R / 32f_8u_C3R, IPP's float-matrix variant rather than a fixed-point path. colortwist computes in float with FMA, and the harness checks both outputs against the float C loop within 1 LSB. 5. The README's AVX, AVX2 and AVX3 rows predate the 2023-09-21 commit '(start to) remove older and slower implementations'. HEAD keeps one X64_AVX path, implemented by colorTwistRGB48_AVX3_Generic, so the AVX and AVX2 rows cannot be reproduced at HEAD. HEAD's RGB48 harness uses width 2049, not the README's 2048. 6. The README calls the project a finger exercise in SIMD optimization; 2 stars.

name: fast_image_resize
baseline: libvips 8.15.1 (single-threaded); also the Rust image 0.25.6 and resize 0.8.9 crates
workload: Single-threaded resize of a 4928x3279 image to 852x567 (RGB8, RGBA8 with alpha multiply/divide, L8) with Nearest, Box, Bilinear, Bicubic and Lanczos3 filters, criterion timings.
claimed_speedup: RGB8 Lanczos3: 13.52 ms (AVX2) vs libvips 17.31 ms, image 176.09 ms, resize 137.70 ms. RGB8 Bilinear: 3.55 ms vs libvips 5.58 ms. RGB8 Box: 2.65 ms vs libvips 61.51 ms. RGBA8 Lanczos3: 24.08 ms vs libvips 332.42 ms and resize 218.65 ms. Against libvips the Lanczos3 RGB8 lead is about 1.3x (derived from page data); the large margins are against the pure-Rust crates.
stars_or_usage: 463 stars, 42 forks; crates.io: 20,443,908 total downloads, 4,728,314 recent (crates.io API, 2026-10-03)
tradeoffs: Rust crate, not callable from C++ without writing a C shim (a Python binding cykooz.resizer exists). Supports u8/u16/f32 pixel types, SSE4.1, AVX2, NEON and WASM SIMD, and multithreading. Convolution (Box/Bilinear/Bicubic/Lanczos3) plus Nearest.
caveats: Rust crate, not C++ or C: it is outside the default C++ language filter for this category and would need an FFI wrapper for C++ use. It does not compare against ImageMagick or stb_image_resize, the category's named baselines; the closest incumbent measured is libvips 8.15.1, and the RGB8 lead over it is modest (Lanczos3 13.52 ms vs 17.31 ms, about 1.28x; Bilinear 3.55 ms vs 5.58 ms, about 1.57x; derived from page data). The large margins are against the pure-Rust image and resize crates. The harness does not make libvips do identical work: libvips Box uses vips_shrink instead of a box-filter convolution; the alpha rows run libvips premultiply/unpremultiply, which produce float images (the harness casts back to the band format), so libvips resamples RGBA/LA in float while fir works in integers, which accounts for much of the RGBA8 Lanczos3 gap (332.42 ms vs 24.08 ms); and each libvips iteration builds a new pipeline and copies the result out with image_write_to_memory, while fir writes into a preallocated image with a reused Resizer, an overhead that dominates the Nearest rows. libvips runs with concurrency 1 and its cache disabled. The benchmarks are the author's own, on the author's machine. The page header says fast_image_resize 6.0.1, which is not a published crates.io version (6.0.0 and 6.1.0 are); the page was last updated on 2026-07-21 with the 6.1.0 release. The README's copy of the RGB8 table comes from an older run (libvips Lanczos3 16.07 ms vs fir AVX2 13.26 ms). The ARM64 and WASM32 benchmark pages were not opened.

baseline: stb_image_resize2.h v2.18 (nothings/stb commit 904aa67, 2026-03-13; the vendored upstream/ copy's sha256 173e654634f6ccaad98f603e686ea212eec1fe8ea6d2a5e5e8056efa10ae3880 matches nothings/stb master), compiled -O2 -ffp-contract=off for the default x86-64 (SSE2) target

claimed_speedup: results/summary.csv (upstream at -O2/SSE2 vs the fork's runtime-dispatched library at -O3 with held-out PGO, 23 rows, min ns over repeats): geomean 1.3623x (upsample 1.3495x, downsample 1.3842x); per row 1.09-1.66x: uint8 1.29-1.60x, uint16 1.52-1.66x, float 1.12-1.42x, uint8 RGBA 1.32-1.35x, RGBA_PM 1.44-1.57x, sRGB 1.12-1.22x, half 1.09-1.11x. results/kernels.csv (the same library forced to its base vs AVX2 path): geomean 1.3491x over the non-half rows, half 1.00x. results/consumer.csv (load, resize, sRGB RGBA program vs stock -O2): geomean 1.230x (1.11-1.57x). The README's +32.8% without PGO has no committed CSV. The fork's own docs/MEASUREMENT.md says upstream compiled with -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 is byte-exact and +26-34% faster by itself, so these gains are upstream's AVX2 code path enabled at runtime, not a faster resampler.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; created 2026-09-29 with 5 commits, no GitHub release (CHANGELOG lists v1.0.0)
tradeoffs: Byte-identical output to upstream (README states a differential test of 8,284 cases on 3 dispatch paths). The resampler source is unchanged; the speedup comes from shipping a prebuilt static library with baseline and AVX2 variants chosen by CPUID at runtime, plus PGO. Header-only use gets only the baseline build. x86-64 gains only; aarch64 is a single scalar/NEON build. half output falls back to baseline.
caveats: A brand-new unofficial derivative of nothings/stb (not a GitHub fork object; 5 commits, all on 2026-09-29), not endorsed by the stb author, with no outside scrutiny. src/stb_image_resize2.h is byte-identical to upstream v2.18 (sha256 checked against nothings/stb master), and the fork adds only build glue: the same header compiled for SSE2 and for x86-64-v3 AVX2, a CPUID dispatch layer and PGO. All of the measured speedup therefore comes from build configuration, since the baseline is upstream at -O2 for the default SSE2 target. The fork's own docs/MEASUREMENT.md says upstream built with -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 is byte-exact and +26-34% faster on its own, and docs/REJECTED.md says PGO is neutral (0.9985x) on a monolithic build and only recovers the split library's layout (+32.8% to +38.0%). No head-to-head against an upstream x86-64-v3 build is published. The practical value is a portable x86-64 binary that uses upstream's AVX2 path at runtime; a project that can target x86-64-v3 gets the same speed from stock stb. Output is claimed byte-identical by harness/diff_lib.sh (8,284 checks on each of 3 dispatch paths), which is configured in CI (pass status not checked here); half-float output stays on the SSE2 path because of a signed-zero divergence. Timings come from a single WSL2 run on a hybrid P/E-core CPU, pinned to vCPU 3 with no PMU, min over repeats; the README calls per-row differences under about 3% noise. The fork documents upstream quirks it does not fix (an uninitialized read in the uint16 WRAP BOX upsample and some half filter paths; a UBSan false positive in the sRGB encoder).

name: tir (tiny image resize, in tinyexr)
baseline: stb_image_resize2 (successor of stb_image_resize, matched filter, float32 path); also tinyexr's own exr_resize_float
workload: Separable float32 resampling with a Mitchell (4-tap) filter on random data, 1-channel and 4-channel, shapes 960x640 to 1920x1280 (2x up), 1920x1280 to 960x640 (2x down) and 4096x2560 to 561x350 (7.3x down); output megapixels per second on one thread, about 0.3 s per measurement (tools/resize/tests/tir_bench.c).
claimed_speedup: README Performance tables (output MP/s of f32 pixels, one AVX2 core, Ryzen 9 3950X, Mitchell 4-tap), tir AVX2 / exr_v3 / stb2. 4-channel: 2x up 295 / 135 / 266; 2x down 78 / 30 / 73; 7.3x down 7.6 / 2.2 / 6.4. 1-channel: 2x up 1218 / 443 / 1279; 2x down 334 / 92 / 365; 7.3x down 27.3 / 8.2 / 25.4. Ratios vs stb2 (derived from page data): 4-channel 1.11x, 1.07x, 1.19x; 1-channel 0.95x (2x up), 0.92x (2x down, stb2 about 9% faster, more than the README's 'within ~5%'), 1.07x (7.3x down). Ratios vs tinyexr's own exr_resize_float (derived from page data): 2.2x to 3.6x. Author text: 'tir beats exr_resize_float 2-5x everywhere' and 'Against stb2 (matched filters) tir wins on every 4-channel case'; the triangle-filter rows the author also cites are not in the README table.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile target resize-bench: $(CC) -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -g (CFLAGS is not used by this recipe), no -march/-mavx/-mavx2/-mfma; the Makefile line 'CC ?= gcc' does not override GNU make's built-in default CC=cc, so the compiler is the system cc, name and version not stated in the README. tir's AVX2/FMA kernels are compiled with __attribute__((target(...))) in tools/resize/src/tir_kernels_x86.c and selected at runtime by CPUID (tir_cpu.c); stb_image_resize2.h picks SIMD at compile time (AVX/AVX2 only when __AVX__/__AVX2__ or STBIR_AVX/STBIR_AVX2 are defined), so under this recipe stb2 runs its SSE2 path. stb2 is enabled with make resize-bench STB=1 (-DTIR_BENCH_STB) after dropping the header into tools/resize/tests/.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (Zen 2), one AVX2 core
stars_or_usage: 836 stars (tinyexr repository; tir lives in tools/resize)
tradeoffs: Pure C11 with a header that is safe to include from C++. Internal float32 filtering with u8, u16, f16 and f32 pixel I/O; runtime SSE2, SSE4.1 and AVX2+FMA dispatch, NEON at compile time, SVE behind a runtime gate. One arena allocation, streaming push_row/pull_row API with O(support) memory, optional C11-threads band parallelism with output identical to serial. HDR-aware (antiring, no clamping), normal-map and height-map modes, premultiplied-alpha filtering. Filters: box, triangle, B-spline, Gaussian, Mitchell, Catmull-Rom, Lanczos-2/3. Not a standalone repository: the code sits under tools/resize in the tinyexr tree (no dependency on the EXR codec for the library itself).
caveats: The win over the named baseline is small and not like-for-like: the bench recipe builds stb_image_resize2 without -mavx/-mavx2/-mfma, so stb2 ran its SSE2 kernels while tir used runtime-dispatched AVX2+FMA; stb_image_resize2's own header says AVX is 10-40% faster and AVX2 about another 12%, which exceeds tir's 7-19% 4-channel lead, so tir may not beat an AVX2 build of stb2. On 1-channel Mitchell stb2 is faster in the two 2x cases (0.95x and 0.92x, derived from page data). The workload does matched work: Mitchell B=C=1/3 on both sides, clamp edges on both sides (tir default TIR_EDGE_CLAMP, stb STBIR_EDGE_CLAMP), straight alpha on tir and STBIR_4CHANNEL (no alpha weighting) on stb, f32 in and out, random data, one-shot calls that build coefficients each time; the bench does not compare outputs, and tir's SIMD kernels may reassociate sums within a small ULP budget. The Lanczos3 row compares against a 4-tap Catmull-Rom on the stb side and is excluded. The 2-5x figure is against tinyexr's own exr_resize_float, not an outside incumbent. Author-run on a single Zen 2 machine; the stb2 header version used is not recorded (gitignored, fetched on demand). tir is new (first commit 2026-07-02, last change to tools/resize 2026-07-05), developed with an AI co-author, version 0.x.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch '"faster than stb_image_resize" OR "faster than ImageMagick" OR "faster than libvips" image resize C++ library SIMD' (github.com only) surfaced syoyo/tinyexr; README section 'tir - tiny content-aware image resize' and tools/resize/README.md opened

tradeoffs: Small C99 library: only YUV420p <-> RGB24 (plus a few color-space matrices); aligned and unaligned SSE2 variants; no AVX2 or NEON. Author calls it an exercise in learning SSE intrinsics.
caveats: Author's own run on one laptop CPU (i7-5500U) with an old swscale 3.0.0 whose YUV420P to RGB24 path is MMX code; modern swscale has newer SIMD paths and would narrow the gap. Intel IPP 9.0.1 beat the SSE2 code on rgb2yuv (0.579-0.594 s vs 0.641-0.677 s) and was within 5% on yuv2rgb. The swscale contexts are created with flags 0 (default scaler) and the outputs of each method are written to separate files but never compared, so equivalence is not checked. The rgb2yuv gap (about 5.3x) is likely partly different work: swscale has no unscaled fast path for RGB24 input (its special case is BGR24), so the ffmpeg row probably ran the generic scaler with filtered chroma and higher-precision intermediates, while yuv2rgb uses 8-bit fixed-point coefficients and a plain 2x2 box average for chroma. The yuv2rgb direction (about 2x) is closer to like-for-like (both use one chroma sample per 2x2 block). Flags are the CMake Release preset (-O3 -DNDEBUG) plus -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -std=c99 from CMakeLists.txt; SSE2 is the x86-64 baseline so no -msse flag is needed. Single 4K image run 100 times (cache-warm). README numbers predate the Feb 2022 commits, which include a fix to the plain C (std) rgb2yuv path, not the SSE2 path.

name: epeg
baseline: ImageMagick convert -resize 150x150> (plain resize mode); ImageMagick's own -thumbnail mode with the jpeg:size hint is faster than epeg in the same table
workload: speedtest-resize (Go driver main.go and exec.go): for each of the first 10 JPEGs (5616x3744) in a folder, spawn the tool, load, scale to a 150x100 thumbnail and write a JPEG; the time includes process start-up. epeg runs as 'epeg -m 150' (libjpeg scale_denom 8 with JDCT_IFAST, no fancy upsampling and no block smoothing, i.e. a 702x468 decode, then nearest-neighbour point sampling in _epeg_scale, JPEG quality 85). ImageMagick_resize runs 'convert -resize 150x150>' (full-resolution decode plus ImageMagick's default convolution filter); ImageMagick_thumbnail runs 'convert -define jpeg:size=300x300 -thumbnail 150x150>' (DCT-domain downscale at decode, then a filtered resize).
claimed_speedup: speedtest-resize README, scenario run by contributor nono (3.4GHz Intel Core i7, Ubuntu 16.10, average over the first 10 JPEGs, one pass): epeg 0.079 s per file vs ImageMagick_resize ('convert -resize 150x150>') 0.568 s, 7.2x (derived from page data), but that ImageMagick command decodes the full 5616x3744 image and runs a convolution resize while epeg decodes at 1/8 scale in the DCT domain and point-samples. Against ImageMagick_thumbnail ('convert -define jpeg:size=300x300 -thumbnail 150x150>'), which uses the same libjpeg DCT-domain downscale, epeg is slower: 0.079 s vs 0.057 s (ImageMagick 1.39x faster, derived from page data). The vips binding (0.070 s) is also faster than epeg; vipsthumbnail (0.115 s) and GraphicsMagick_thumbnail (0.172 s) are slower.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated.
hardware: 3.4GHz Intel Core i7 (model not stated), Ubuntu 16.10; scenario run by GitHub user nono and added to the README. epeg and ImageMagick versions not stated.
license: MIT-enna (Enlightenment MIT variant: COPYING requires publicly documented acknowledgment when the source is not published; COPYING-PLAIN is a non-binding plain-English note). Not OSI-approved.
tradeoffs: JPEG only; reduces size by decoding only the DCT coefficients needed (libjpeg scaled decode), so quality is that of DCT-domain scaling rather than a Lanczos or bicubic resample; speedup is proportional to the pixel-count ratio between source and thumbnail.
caveats: Equivalent-work comparison fails: in the same speedtest-resize table ImageMagick's own thumbnail command ('convert -define jpeg:size=300x300 -thumbnail 150x150>'), which uses the same libjpeg DCT-domain downscale, takes 0.057 s per file against epeg's 0.079 s, and the vips binding takes 0.070 s. epeg only beats 'convert -resize 150x150>', which decodes the full 5616x3744 image and runs a convolution resize, while epeg decodes at 1/8 scale (JDCT_IFAST, no fancy upsampling) and then nearest-neighbour samples to 150x100, so it does much less work and gives a lower-quality thumbnail. The numbers are one pass over 10 files by a contributor (nono) on an unnamed Core i7 with process start-up included and no tool versions. The licence is the Enlightenment MIT variant (MIT-enna) with a public-acknowledgment clause, which is not OSI-approved. mattes/epeg is a maintained copy of Enlightenment's epeg, not a GitHub fork.

name: FFmpeg (libswscale and filters)
baseline: ImageMagick 7.1.1 (magick, convert)
workload: libvips vips-bench (ffmpeg.sh vs im7.sh/im.sh, driver benchmark.sh): the ffmpeg 7.1.1 CLI reads the 10000x10000 8-bit RGB image as a strip TIFF (x-strip.tif; benchmark.sh notes ffmpeg does not support tiled TIFF), crops 100 px per edge (crop filter), scales to 90 percent with the scale filter at libswscale's default SWS_BICUBIC (ffmpeg.sh passes no flags), runs a 3x3 sharpen (kernel sum 8, divided by 8) through the convolution filter, which accepts planar formats only, and writes a TIFF. ImageMagick 7.1.1 reads the tiled TIFF with crop-on-load, resizes 90 percent with -filter triangle and convolves the same 3x3 kernel; its script also runs vipsheader twice inside the timed command. Quickest real time of five runs, OMP_NUM_THREADS=16.
claimed_speedup: libvips wiki table (AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04, run 12 Aug 2025): ffmpeg 7.1.1 2.06 s and 1338.36 MB peak vs magick 7.1.1 4.41 s / 1500.52 MB and convert 7.1.1 4.44 s / 1499.29 MB, 2.1x faster (derived from page data); the page's 'times slower than libvips' column reads ffmpeg 3.61 vs magick 7.74.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (Ubuntu packages).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04 (run 12 Aug 2025 by the libvips maintainers)
license: LGPL-2.1-or-later (optional parts make the build GPL-2.0-or-later when configured with --enable-gpl, per LICENSE.md); libswscale and vf_convolution.c are LGPL
tradeoffs: The measured tool is the ffmpeg command line, not a lean resize library; peak memory 1338.36 MB. GitHub lists LGPL-2.1 with GPL-2.0 and GPL-3.0 options for some components.
caveats: One trivial I/O-dominated test (the wiki says it flatters libvips), so the 2.1x mostly reflects TIFF reading and writing and pipeline overhead rather than swscale itself. The pipelines are not identical: ffmpeg reads the strip TIFF (it does not support tiled TIFF) and resamples with libswscale's default bicubic filter (a wider kernel than ImageMagick's triangle), while ImageMagick reads the tiled TIFF with crop-on-load, resizes with -filter triangle, and its script runs vipsheader twice inside the timed command. vips-bench issue 8 (homm, 2017, about Pillow) notes that libvips uses 4-point bilinear interpolation while ImageMagick and GraphicsMagick use convolution resizing, so resampling differs per program. Distribution packages with no compiler or flags. Already recorded entries (zimg, yuv2rgb) use libswscale as their baseline rather than ImageMagick. FFmpeg becomes GPL-2.0-or-later when configured with --enable-gpl.

name: OpenCV
baseline: ImageMagick (6.9 via the Wand binding, single-threaded, in pillow-perf; magick and convert 7.1.1 in the libvips Speed-and-memory-use table)
workload: pillow-perf testsuite (run.py default 2560x1600 RGB; cv2_scale.py vs wand_scale.py, cv2_blur.py vs wand_blur.py): in-memory resampling and Gaussian blur, single-threaded, no file I/O; OpenCV downscales use INTER_AREA and upscales (2.14x) use INTER_LINEAR, INTER_CUBIC and INTER_LANCZOS4, while ImageMagick uses triangle, catrom and lanczos at every size; blur uses the same window (1 + 2*ceil(2.5r)) and sigma r. libvips wiki (vips-bench opencv.cc vs im7.sh): load a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 px per edge, resize to 90 percent (OpenCV's default INTER_LINEAR 4-point bilinear vs ImageMagick -filter triangle convolution), 3x3 sharpen, save.
claimed_speedup: pillow-perf i5-4430 (Core i5-4430, Ubuntu 18.04.3; both libraries single-threaded via cv2.setNumThreads(1) and MAGICK_THREAD_LIMIT=1; median of 5 runs, 3 for ImageMagick blur) on a 2560x1600 RGB image, like-for-like rows (derived from page data): 2.14x upscale to 5478x3424, OpenCV INTER_LINEAR 57.74 ms vs ImageMagick 6.9 triangle 1007.63 ms (17.5x) and INTER_CUBIC 115.25 ms vs Catmull-Rom 1256.13 ms (10.9x); Gaussian blur radius 1 px 69.39 vs 675.34 ms (9.7x), 10 px 445.67 vs 1768.07 ms (4.0x), 30 px 1399.39 vs 4090.08 ms (2.9x). The downscale rows the record called bicubic (320x200: 5.41 vs 89.20 ms; 2048x1280: 48.20 vs 222.93 ms) are OpenCV INTER_AREA supersampling (the raw i5-4430.txt labels them 'sup'; the JSON files them under 'bic') against ImageMagick Catmull-Rom convolution, so they are not like for like. libvips wiki (Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04): opencv 4.10 3.15 s vs magick 7.1.1 4.41 s and convert 7.1.1 4.44 s (1.4x, derived from page data). pillow-perf also shows OpenCV slower than ImageMagick at JPEG load (47.89 vs 27.38 ms) and save (56.70 vs 48.04 ms). The speedtest-resize opencv row (0.110 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s) uses go-opencv Resize with interpolation 0 (CV_INTER_NN, nearest neighbour) and is not comparable; ImageMagick_thumbnail (0.057 s) is faster there.

caveats: The pillow-perf downscale cells filed as bicubic for OpenCV (26x16, 320x200, 2048x1280) are INTER_AREA supersampling runs (cv2_scale.py; the raw i5-4430.txt labels them 'sup') compared against ImageMagick Catmull-Rom convolution; pillow-perf's own page says comparing OpenCV's bicubic with correct convolution implementations is meaningless and that supersampling is a different method, so those 16.5x and 4.6x ratios are not like for like. The like-for-like pillow-perf rows are the 2.14x upscale (INTER_LINEAR vs triangle; INTER_CUBIC with a=-0.75 vs Catmull-Rom, both 4x4 support) and the Gaussian blur (same window and sigma), all single-threaded. In the libvips pipeline OpenCV's default 4-point bilinear does slightly less filtering than ImageMagick's triangle convolution at 0.9 scale; the test is I/O dominated, the wiki says it flatters libvips, and OpenCV is listed among systems that do not thread automatically. stars_or_usage: 2.4k stars; VFX industry standard (Academy Software Foundation)
tradeoffs: Large dependency set; peak memory 2236.57 MB in this run, higher than ImageMagick (1500.52 MB) and libvips (94.28 MB).
caveats: The 1.3x margin is modest, and the test is trivial and I/O-dominated (the wiki says it flatters libvips). The wiki notes that oiiotool 'may not be the best way to test the library'. The run is by the libvips maintainer, a third party for OpenImageIO and ImageMagick. Both oiio and ImageMagick use triangle-filter convolution resizing, so the work is comparable, unlike libvips' affine bilinear (vips-bench issue 8, opened by the Pillow-SIMD author). oiio.sh has an unfixed bug, unchanged since 2014: it passes '--crop $widthx$height+100+100', and because widthx is an undefined shell variable this expands to '9800+100+100'. oiiotool 2.5.18's adjust_geometry parses that string as an origin offset (+9800+100) and keeps the 10000x10000 size, so oiio resizes and convolves a mostly black 10000x10000 frame instead of the 9800x9800 crop. That is about 4% more pixels, so the time is not flattered by doing less work, but the output is not the intended image. oiio also uses a gaussian kernel instead of the sharpen kernel (the cost is the same). Programs are distro builds with unstated flags, and 2.5.18 predates the current OpenImageIO 3.x line.

name: CompV
baseline: OpenCV (cv::resize bilinear; cvtColor CV_RGB2GRAY, CV_YUV2RGB_I420, CV_RGB2HSV)
workload: 10,000 iterations on a 1282x720 image: RGB24 to grayscale, YUV420P to RGB24, RGB24 to HSV (CV_RGB2GRAY, CV_YUV2RGB_I420, CV_RGB2HSV on the OpenCV side), and bilinear down-scaling to 1064x597. Per tests/image/scale.cxx (factor 0.83, COMPV_SUBTYPE_PIXELS_Y), scaling runs on an 8-bit grayscale image. CompV uses hand-written assembly, SSE/AVX and its own thread pool (8 threads on this machine).
claimed_speedup: From the result file (10k iterations, 1282x720): RGB24 to Gray 449 ms vs OpenCV 3086 ms ('680%, almost 7 times'); YUV420P to RGB24 968 vs 5919 ms ('611%, 6 times'); RGB24 to HSV 2137 vs 15709 ms ('735%, 7 times'); YUV420P to HSV 3045 vs 32920 ms ('almost 11 times'; OpenCV needs two calls). Bilinear scaling 1282x720 to 1064x597: 1474 ms (mt, avx2) vs OpenCV 4148 ms ('281%, almost 3 times'). CompV's mt plain C++ (2645 ms) also beats OpenCV, but its single-thread AVX2 (5435 ms) does not.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4790K @ 4.00GHz (8 CPUs), Apple iMac15,1 running Windows 8 Pro 64-bit
stars_or_usage: 212 stars, 46 forks; code used in the vendor's commercial SDKs
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 (copyleft, commercial use needs the vendor's licence); README says it is an R&D project with no documentation and is not intended for use by other companies; hand-written assembler and TBBMalloc/TCMalloc are part of the quoted results; large library with GPU back ends.
caveats: 1. Only evidence: a first-party result file, last edited April 2019, from an i7-4790K iMac running Windows 8. The OpenCV version, its build (IPP on or off, TBB, thread count) and the compilers and flags for both sides are not stated. The file only says 'full optiz' and notes OpenCV uses SSE2 and multithreading for scaling. 2. The CompV-side drivers are public (tests/image/chroma_conv.cxx, tests/image/scale.cxx; loop counts are set to 1 at HEAD) and check CompV's own MD5s; the OpenCV-side code is not in the repo. 3. No output comparison against OpenCV is published. 4. The HSV path uses an approximate SSSE3 reciprocal with its own MD5 set (dstMD5_rcp), so CompV HSV output can differ from an exact conversion. 5. CompV results use assembler plus TBBMalloc/TCMalloc. 6. Single-thread AVX2 bilinear (5435 ms) is slower than OpenCV's 4148 ms. Bicubic scaling and bicubic rotation rows are marked 'Shame!!' (no CompV result). 7. The 'Up to #50 times faster than OpenCV' claim is in the GitHub repo description, not the README. No row of the result file matches it: the largest ratio is about 28x (BruteForce matcher, 2840%), and the colour and scaling rows are about 3-11x. 8. The README says the project is undocumented and 'not intended to be used by other companies'; GPL-3.0.

name: DeltaCV
baseline: OpenCV (cv::cvtColor RGB2GRAY and RGB2HSV on CPU, and OpenCV chains for fused colour-space plus threshold operations)
workload: CPU: fused colour-space conversion plus threshold segmentation on a 1024x1280 image (ycrcbWithSeg, inRange, weightedGrayWithSeg, grayBRWithSeg), each producing an 8-bit mask, vs the OpenCV call chain (for example cvtColor then inRange). GPU: CUDA kernels on a 480x640 image vs CPU OpenCV. The GPU 'RGB2HSV' kernel (gpu/src/colorSpace.cu) does not output HSV: it masks the RGB input by an HSV range, unlike OpenCV's cvtColor RGB2HSV.
claimed_speedup: CPU, same machine (1024x1280, CPU not stated): fused ycrcbWithSeg 0.88-0.90 ms vs OpenCV cvtColor(RGB2YCrCb)+inRange 6.68-6.75 ms (7.4-7.6x); inRange 0.29-0.30 vs 1.06-1.18 ms (3.5-4.0x); weightedGrayWithSeg 3.39-4.33x; grayBRWithSeg 4.6-4.8x. GPU vs CPU, a different machine class (480x640, GTX 1070 kernel time vs OpenCV on i5 7500): RGB2GRAY 0.008-0.010 vs 0.340-0.360 ms. The README's speed-up cell says '3.4 - 45'; the timings imply 34-45x (derived from page data). The README's RGB2HSV row (0.150-0.200 vs 3.900-4.400 ms, 19.5-29.3x) compares different work and should not be cited as a speed-up.
compiler_and_flags: CPU part built with -mavx2 -march=haswell (compiler not stated)
hardware: GPU table: NVIDIA GTX 1070 8G versus OpenCV on Intel i5 7500; CPU SIMD table: CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Small collection of hand-written kernels rather than a full library; CPU kernels are fused operations (colour conversion plus segmentation) so they are not drop-in replacements for single OpenCV calls; GPU path needs CUDA and the transfer cost is not stated.
caveats: 1. GPU numbers compare a GTX 1070 against CPU OpenCV on an i5 7500, a different machine class; there is no OpenCV CUDA or NPP baseline. 2. GPU timings exclude host-device transfers: the leftover, commented-out timer in gpu/main.cpp starts after the cudaMemcpy upload and stops at cudaDeviceSynchronize. 3. The GPU RGB2HSV kernel does different work from OpenCV (an RGB mask, not an HSV image) and is buggy. The line '_h = (_h<0)*(_h + 360)' zeroes every non-negative hue. The +360 offset on the red branch forces hue positive. The V test uses the channel minimum instead of the maximum. Grey pixels divide by zero. 4. GPU RGB2GRAY uses low-precision 8-bit coefficients (76,150,30)>>8, and its own source comment gives 0.12 ms, not the README's 0.008-0.010 ms. 5. The CPU 'AVX2' functions use 128-bit SSE intrinsics. 6. ycrcbWithSeg returns bool without a return statement, and its tail loop compares a byte offset with a pixel count, so trailing pixels are never processed when the pixel count is not a multiple of 16 (the 1024x1280 benchmark size is unaffected). 7. The example programs carry no usable timing code; outputs are compared only by imshow. 8. The OpenCV version is not stated (a source comment cites opencv-4.0.1 coefficients). 9. Flags -O3 -mavx2 -march=haswell come from cpu/CMakeLists.txt; the compiler is not stated. 10. The SIMD table names no CPU model. 11. Last commit 2019-04-27.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/image-processing?l=c%2B%2B&q=high+performance (listing 'A high performance library for image processing'), then README read

The CPU examples carry no working timing code (cpu/examples/ycrcbWithSeg.cpp uses an undeclared loop variable and uninitialised timers; inRange.cpp has no timing at all), and the SIMD table names no CPU or compiler. The GPU table pits a GTX 1070, timing the kernel only, against OpenCV on an i5-7500 CPU.
verification.notes: Downgraded the claim, not the tier (stays C). The README's GPU RGB2HSV speed-up is invalid: the kernel masks RGB pixels instead of converting to HSV and zeroes the hue. GPU RGB2GRAY is kernel-only against a CPU OpenCV. The usable evidence is the same-machine CPU SIMD rows (3.4-7.6x for fused colour-space plus segmentation), which are first-party with no runnable timing code. Metadata (MIT, 128 stars, 12 forks, abandoned) checks out.

name: FastBoxBlur
baseline: OpenCV cv::blur (box filter)
workload: Box blur with reflect-101 style mirror padding (edge sample not repeated, like OpenCV's default BORDER_REFLECT_101) on 45 synthetic-size RGB 8-bit images from 1500x1000 to 11400x7600, box size 2*width-1, 1 and 2 passes; FastBoxBlur does horizontal sliding-sum passes, a blocked transpose, vertical passes as horizontal passes, and a transpose back (timings listed in py/performance.ipynb, plot in data/bench.png).
claimed_speedup: README Performance: 'designed to be a portable, easy, and faster replacement of cv::blur, using an i7-10750H, it's around 2x - 3x time faster'. The chart data (py/performance.ipynb, times in ms for 45 RGB 8-bit images from 1500x1000 to 11400x7600, box size 2*width-1): 1 pass cv::blur 20.2 to 1900.6 ms vs fastboxblur 15.9 to 650.8 ms; 2 passes cv::blur 39.3 to 3970.2 ms vs fastboxblur 23.6 to 1180.7 ms. Speedups (derived from page data): 1 pass 1.27x to 2.92x (median 2.62x), 2 passes 1.49x to 3.36x (median 2.90x), rising with image size.
compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile (the only build in the repo; the benchmark build is not stated): g++ fastboxblur.cpp -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17. The OpenCV side's version, compiler and build options are not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H
tradeoffs: Header-only (fast_box_blur.h), templated on pixel type and channel count, sliding-accumulator box blur plus cache-blocked transposition, N passes. Emulates mirrored border padding without extra memory, but the radius must stay below the image width. No SIMD (the README says SIMD could be faster); OpenMP in the demo build. Box blur only, and README says it is based on bfraboni/FastGaussianBlur.
caveats: Likely threads-versus-one-thread: fast_box_blur.h parallelises every horizontal pass and the transpose with '#pragma omp parallel for' and the Makefile builds with -fopenmp, so on the 6-core/12-thread i7-10750H FastBoxBlur probably ran on all hardware threads, while OpenCV 4.x's CPU cv::blur goes through boxFilter's single-threaded FilterEngine (no parallel_for_ in box_filter.dispatch.cpp or filter.dispatch.cpp) unless a HAL intercepts it; the 1.3-3.4x lead is smaller than the thread count, so per-core FastBoxBlur may not be faster. The cv::blur driver is not in the repo, so the OpenCV version, IPP/HAL build, setNumThreads value and exact cv::blur arguments cannot be checked. The kernel size 2*width-1 is extreme (thousands of pixels); OpenCV's FilterEngine pads each row by the kernel radius, so this size inflates OpenCV's border work, and typical small kernels were not measured. FastBoxBlur clamps the radius to dimension-1 per axis (r = min(r, w-1)), so on landscape images its vertical kernel is smaller than a cv::blur call given the same square ksize would use; whether the benchmark matched that is unknown. Integer accumulation with float normalisation and +0.5 rounding; output equivalence with cv::blur is not tested in the repo. Borderline for color-and-resampling (a convolution filter, not a resampler). MIT is stated only in the README; there is no LICENSE file. Last commit 2022-11-01; 5 stars.

The OpenMP-versus-single-threaded-OpenCV concern is strong enough that the orchestrator may want to note it as the main shortcoming.

name: FastOpenCV (fastcv kernels)
baseline: OpenCV 4.14.0 cv::resize (INTER_CUBIC, INTER_AREA), cv::transform and cv::pow, built from source by the repo's scripts with IPP disabled (WITH_IPP=OFF in every variant) and TBB threading at the default thread count; libfastcv is compiled against the linux-dispatch install, so the cv:: column is most likely that build, not a distribution build.
workload: bench/resize_cubic_bench.cpp: random 8UC1 and 8UC3 images, 1920x1080 down to 960x540 and 1280x720, 960x540 up to 1920x1080, and 1920x1080 to 640x480 (C3), cv::resize INTER_CUBIC versus fastcv::resizeCubic8u, 20 timed runs after 2 warm-ups, with maxDiff and non-zero-difference counts. bench/area_hist_bench.cpp: 1080p 8UC1 and 8UC3, INTER_AREA integer factors 2 and 4 versus fastcv::resizeAreaInt8u. bench/transform_bench.cpp: 1080p 32FC3 with a 4x4 affine matrix (so the output is 32FC4) versus fastcv::transform32f. bench/pow_bench.cpp: 1080p 32FC1 with values in [0.01, 10], exponents 1.7 and -0.3, versus fastcv::pow32f.
claimed_speedup: README table: resize INTER_CUBIC 3.4 -> 0.8 ms (4.1x, bit-exact), but the 3.4 ms OpenCV time is the first kernel-audit figure, which PLAN.md stage 5e says was taken with setNumThreads(0), a mode that slowed OpenCV+TBB about 4x; re-measured in default threading OpenCV takes 0.88 ms, and the author's own header (fastcv/include/fastcv/fastcv.hpp) and PLAN.md give fastcv::resizeCubic8u as 1.5-1.9x for downscaling (bit-exact) and 0.7-0.9x, i.e. slower than OpenCV, for upscaling. resize INTER_AREA integer factor x4: 18.7x (8UC1) and 3.5x (8UC3), maxDiff 1 on 0.2% of pixels; for x2 cv::resize is faster (README row: 0.92 -> 0.02-0.25 ms). transform 32FC3 with a 4x4 matrix: 7.9 ms (PLAN.md says 8.8 ms) -> 0.74 ms (10.7x, bit-exact). pow 32F with a general exponent (gamma): 19-22x, relative error about 1e-5, positive inputs only.
compiler_and_flags: g++ (version not stated); fastcv built with -O3 -march=native -fPIC against the repo's linux-dispatch OpenCV install (scripts/build-fastcv.sh). OpenCV 4.14.0 built by scripts/build-linux-opt.sh: Release, gcc/g++, LTO, TBB on, OpenMP off, WITH_IPP=OFF, LAPACK via OpenBLAS, CUDA 13.3; the dispatch variant uses an AVX2 baseline with AVX512_SKX dispatch and ENABLE_FASTMATH, while the stock variant keeps OpenCV's default CPU baseline and dispatch. Compile flags for the bench/*.cpp drivers are not given.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D (Zen 5, AVX-512 + VBMI, 32 threads), 128 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 4090; Arch Linux (CPU model named in PLAN.md stage 0)
tradeoffs: Drop-in kernels that need OpenCV headers plus an OpenCV build with the repo's patches for best results; -march=native build so the library is machine specific; requires AVX-512 VBMI for some kernels; Rust FFI crate included.
caveats: This is the author's own kernel library: the code in fastcv/src uses OpenCV universal intrinsics and AVX-512 intrinsics. It is not a wrapper over Qualcomm's proprietary FastCV SDK, nor OpenCV's Qualcomm FastCV HAL; only the name is shared. The headline resize INTER_CUBIC 4.1x compares a fastcv time against an OpenCV time taken with setNumThreads(0), a mode that PLAN.md stage 5e calls a trap that slowed OpenCV+TBB about 4x and then re-measured at 0.88 ms. The author's corrected figures are 1.5-1.9x for downscaling and 0.7-0.9x (slower) for upscaling, and the README was never updated. The resize kernel follows OpenCV's algorithm (bicubic A=-0.75, 11-bit fixed-point horizontal pass, float vertical pass, clamp-to-edge borders), so the bit-exact claim is plausible. resizeAreaInt8u handles only integer factors that divide the image size, on C1 and C3. It rounds ties up with a shift, while OpenCV's area-fast path rounds sum*(1/area) with cvRound, which explains the +/-1 differences. The README's 0.02-0.25 ms range does not match 0.92/18.7 = 0.05 ms (derived from page data). The transform benchmark uses a 4x4 matrix on 3 channels, so it produces a 4-channel output, which takes OpenCV's generic single-threaded scalar loop. fastcv's dcn=4 path is also scalar, so the 10.7x comes from running that loop on 32 threads; the SIMD 3x3 path is not what was benchmarked. pow32f uses exp2(p*log2(x)) polynomials with a mask for x <= 0 that is computed but never applied. Zero or negative inputs (black pixels in gamma) therefore produce garbage values instead of 0 or NaN, and there is no overflow or underflow clamping. The benchmark avoids this by using inputs in [0.01, 10]; it is also multi-threaded against cv::pow's scalar powf. Every OpenCV build in the repo disables IPP, so the results do not speak for IPPICV-enabled distribution builds. No result files for the 1080p numbers are checked in: bench/lena_fastcv.txt holds only an assertion crash in sortIdxRows32f, and only bench/lena_stock.txt has timings. The repo has 0 stars and no third-party reproduction, and resize is only a small part of a roughly 30-kernel library.

name: FastResize (fast_resize)
baseline: libvips 8.15 (vips CLI, parallel mode) and imageflow 2.0 (imageflow_tool)
workload: Batch resize of 1,000 images per format to 800 px width, JPEG quality 85 output, 2 runs averaged; JPG 1179x1409, PNG 2104x1160 RGBA, BMP 1045x1045, WebP 4275x2451.
claimed_speedup: JPG 2.10 s vs libvips 5.24 s vs imageflow 6.60 s; PNG 3.43 s vs 6.18 s vs 8.41 s; BMP 1.65 s vs libvips 4.72 s; WebP 14.03 s vs libvips 23.52 s vs imageflow 15.69 s. Page states up to 2.9x faster than libvips and 3.1x faster than imageflow; peak RAM PNG 138 MB vs libvips 439 MB.
tradeoffs: Batch-oriented resizer library and CLI with Ruby gem; its resampler is built on stb_image_resize2 (per the project description), so it is a pipeline and threading gain rather than a faster resampling kernel.
caveats: On the benchmarked Apple M2 (ARM) the default Mitchell filter is not what runs: src/resizer.cpp (unchanged since v1.0.0) routes any downscale with the Mitchell or triangle filter to the project's own NEON kernels in src/simd_resize.cpp, a plain 2-tap fixed-point bilinear for ratios under 3x (JPG 1179 to 800, PNG 2104 to 800, BMP 1045 to 800) and a box/area average above 3x (WEBP 4275 to 800); stb_image_resize2 is only the fallback (x86, upscaling, Catmull-Rom/box filters). So the measured path does less filtering than the requested Mitchell and than libvips' default kernel, and the 2-tap bilinear at 2.6x (PNG) aliases; the comparison is not quality-equivalent. Baseline libvips 8.15 was driven through the vips CLI ('parallel' row; how the parallelism and per-image processes were arranged is not stated) and imageflow 2.0 through imageflow_tool, so process start-up likely counts against the baselines. Benchmark commands and scripts are not published, one machine, two runs, no compiler or flags stated (CMakeLists.txt sets -O3, plus -march=native on x86). JPEG/PNG/WebP coding goes through libjpeg-turbo, libpng and libwebp, so much of the time is codec work. Repo is new (first commit 2025-12-03, latest 2026-01-07, 21 commits); 'fastest on the planet' is marketing language.

workload: ICC-profile image transforms (RGB to Lab, RGB to CMYK, CMYK to RGB, CMYK to CMYK, RGB soft-proof through CMYK, matrix-shaper RGB to RGB), 1 megapixel real photographs, GRACoL2006 and AdobeRGB1998 profiles, single thread, each measurement in its own process.

name: KLERP / KNERP
baseline: OpenCV resize (bilinear and nearest-neighbor interpolation)
workload: Grayscale (8-bit, single channel) image resize with bilinear (KLERP) and nearest-neighbor (KNERP) interpolation, up- and downscaling, AVX2 plus multithreading, matching OpenCV output.
claimed_speedup: README: 'exceeding OpenCV's implementation in speed by 25-100% while matching its output and capabilities in both interpolation modes'; 'the magnitude of the speed gain depends on whether you're downscaling or upscaling and by how much'. No per-case numbers are given.
compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile (not stated as the flags used for the OpenCV comparison): g++ -Ofast -std=gnu++14 -mavx2 -march=native -mfma -flto -funroll-all-loops -fpeel-loops -ftracer -ftree-vectorize, -lpthread
tradeoffs: Single header KLERP.h with no dependencies. Needs an AVX2 CPU, uses its own threads (links pthread), and handles grayscale images only (the README says it is meant for computer vision). A CUDA sibling (CUDALERP, CUDAFLERP) by the same author covers GPU use.
caveats: Only the percentage range appears in the README (and the identical header comment in KLERP.h and main.cpp). main.cpp is a KLERP-only timing loop (2000 warm-ups and 2000 runs, 2x2 image upscaled to 800x2000, multithreading=true) and never calls OpenCV, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo. CPU, OpenCV version and OpenCV build options (IPP, thread count) are not stated. KLERP spawns std::thread::hardware_concurrency() threads for outputs of 20000 pixels or more; OpenCV's resize is also parallelised with parallel_for_ by default, so threading is probably comparable, but this is not documented. Grayscale 8-bit only and AVX2 required; output is designed to match OpenCV's fixed-point bilinear ('silliness to match opencv's output' in KLERP.h). name: LibGaussianBlur (FFT Gaussian blur, from Blur_algorithms)
baseline: OpenCV cv::GaussianBlur
workload: True Gaussian blur of 3-channel 24-bit images with sigma = sqrt(image dimension), using pffft 1D separable FFT convolution in float32 tiles with reflect-101 padding, versus cv::GaussianBlur(image, image, Size(0,0), sigma) on 8-bit data. The notebook labels 46 sizes from 1500x1000 to 24000x14500; the commented-out loop in Source.cpp describes 45 sizes from 1500x1000 to 11400x7600. Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores.
claimed_speedup: Blur_algorithms README (repo archived 2024-12-26): 'how surprisingly fast is the 1D implementation in pffft compared to OpenCV that is the standard market reference', with linear versus exponential growth as size rises. py/performance.ipynb cell 0 holds hard-coded arrays in ms (pffft vs cv::GaussianBlur): 2000x1300 11.52 vs 107.43; 6500x4000 114.97 vs 1604.24; 12000x7300 433.94 vs 6317.43; 24000x14500 1728.56 vs 33509.56; at 1500x1000 OpenCV was faster, 24.97 vs 32.05. Derived from page data: pffft takes 9.0x (2500x1600) to 20.0x (23000x13900) less time at 45 of 46 sizes, and 0.78x at 1500x1000.
hardware: Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores, 16 MB cache setting for PocketFFT
stars_or_usage: 5 stars (LibGaussianBlur); 4 stars on archived Blur_algorithms; published on PyPI as gaussianblur 1.1.2 (2025-03-29)
tradeoffs: C++20 library using FFT tiles and pffft (a bundled FFT library); pads images to FFT-friendly sizes, so more memory than direct convolution; Python wheels, WebAssembly and mobile builds provided. The FFT approach pays off only for large sigma; small kernels are the OpenCV regime.
caveats: The numbers live in the archived predecessor Blur_algorithms (no LICENSE file), not in LibGaussianBlur. LibGaussianBlur's src/gaussianblur.cpp keeps the same pffft ordered-transform tile convolution (pffft_sorted_optimized_convolution) but has never been benchmarked against OpenCV in its own repo. Each size was timed once (std::chrono printf in Source.cpp, no repetitions or warm-up). The pffft time at 1500x1000 (32 ms) is higher than at 2000x1300 (11.5 ms), which points to a cold-start cost in the first run. The size axis cannot be matched to the code. The commented-out benchmark loop in Source.cpp covers 45 sizes in 225x150 steps up to 11400x7600, calls cv::Size(y, x) so each image is 1000 wide by 1500 tall, and sets sigma = sqrt(x). The notebook labels 46 sizes in 500x300 steps up to 24000x14500, and the README says 45 images up to 11400x7600. The repo states no compiler, flags, OpenCV version or OpenCV build (IPP, NEON, threading backend). The FFT path is multi-threaded through hybrid_loop (OpenMP or std::thread, chosen by build macros), and nothing records which was used or how many threads OpenCV ran. The two sides compute different things. The FFT side convolves in float32, truncates the kernel at radius sigma*sqrt(2 ln 255) - 1 and clamps it to the largest image dimension. OpenCV runs its own direct separable 8-bit convolution with its own kernel-size rule. No accuracy comparison against OpenCV output is published. sigma = sqrt(width) gives kernels of hundreds of taps, the worst case for direct convolution. The result does not transfer to small sigma, and OpenCV won at the smallest size. A Gaussian blur is a filter, not resampling or colour conversion, so the fit to this category is borderline. The last commit is an automated coverage-badge update.

The pipelines are not bit-identical: vips.c runs the 8-bit image through vips_reduce (linear kernel) and an integer-precision convolution, while im.sh/im7.sh use ImageMagick's '-filter triangle -resize 90x90%' and '-convolve' at ImageMagick's default 16-bit quantum depth; outputs are not compared. compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt: -std=c++11 -march=native -O3 -fPIC -DNDEBUG -pthread (static libstdc++ on Linux); compiler and version not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7 (Skylake), Ubuntu 14.04; OpenCV 3.2+ (master a85b4b5), Pillow 4.0.0, skimage 0.12.3, Python 2.7.3

The measured code does different work from the Pillow and skimage baselines: (1) Lycon's resize is OpenCV's resize code and runs multi-threaded through its pthreads parallel_for_ (src/lycon/util/defs.h HAVE_PTHREADS_PF; transform/resize/invoker.h), while Pillow 4.0 resizes on one thread; (2) for the exact 2x downsample used, Lycon (like OpenCV) turns INTER_LINEAR into the fast 2x2 area average (invoker.h line 207, hence Downsample Bilinear 0.0258 s = Downsample Area 0.0258 s), and its bicubic/Lanczos use fixed 4x4/8x8 taps without antialiasing, while Pillow's BILINEAR/BICUBIC/LANCZOS convolve with support widened by the reduction factor, so the 51x/13.7x/7.2x downsample ratios compare different filters; (3) the PIL timings include Image.fromarray and np.asarray copies of a ~400 MB image; (4) skimage.transform.resize returns float64. Against OpenCV, which does the same work, resize is at parity (1x) and only JPEG read/write is faster (1.3-1.5x, likely a libjpeg build difference). tradeoffs: Python-only API (not callable from C++ without embedding CPython); single-threaded; Lanczos resize is convolution-based with proper anti-aliasing.
caveats: The benchmark repository belongs to the python-pillow organisation and was written by the Pillow-SIMD authors (first-party, hence tier C); the compiler is not recorded. The ImageMagick baseline is the old 6.9.7-4 (Ubuntu 18.04 package, version given in docs/src/data/index.js), forced to one thread, and every Wand case clones the source image inside the timed region. Not all operations do the same work: Pillow's Gaussian blur is a three-pass extended-box approximation whose cost does not depend on the radius, while ImageMagick runs a true Gaussian (MagickBlurImage with radius 2.5r and sigma r), so the 3.6x to 21.9x blur ratios compare different algorithms; ImageMagick's grayscale conversion (setting the image type) need not match Pillow's L formula. Resizing (Lanczos/lanczos, Bilinear/triangle) and the 3D LUT (Color3DLUT against a Hald CLUT of the same 4^3, 16^3 and 36^3 sizes) are equivalent operations. Pillow-SIMD 7.0 AVX2 is about 4 to 7 times faster than plain Pillow at resizing in the same files (derived from page data). The libvips Speed-and-memory-use table includes only Pillow-SIMD, not plain Pillow.

name: RGB2Y
baseline: OpenCV cv::cvtColor (CV_BGR2GRAY)
workload: RGB (BGR) image to 8-bit grayscale conversion with OpenCV's default weights; main.cpp runs 50 warmups and 100 timed runs against cv::cvtColor and prints microseconds.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Roughly 3x faster than OpenCV's implementation with AVX2, or 2x faster than OpenCV's implementation if using SSE only'; repo description: '2-4x faster than OpenCV'. No measured timings are published. The current RGB2Y.h has only an AVX2 path: the NO_AVX_PLEASE switch the README mentions is not referenced anywhere in the code, so the SSE figure has no code behind it in the current version.
compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile: g++ -Ofast -std=gnu++17 -fomit-frame-pointer -mavx2 -march=native -mfma -flto -funroll-all-loops -fpeel-loops -ftracer -ftree-vectorize (no compiler version; no published run).
tradeoffs: Header-only (RGB2Y.h), AVX2 or SSE only, no NEON; single operation (RGB to gray) with equal or OpenCV-default weights; the author says SSE is about 50% slower than AVX2.
caveats: Claim is a README ratio with no CPU or measured timings; the harness (main.cpp: 50 warmups, 100 timed runs, both sides multithreaded) is public but its output is not published. Output is not bit-identical to the baseline: RGB2Y rounds each weighted channel term separately (_mm256_mulhrs_epi16 in Q15, then saturating adds), while OpenCV's 8-bit BGR2GRAY rounds the weighted sum once, so some pixels can differ by one grey level; main.cpp checks RGB2Y only against its own scalar reference (RGB2Y_ref, which uses the same per-term rounding), never against cv::cvtColor's output. Each 10-pixel block loads 31 bytes, so the final block of the last row reads at least 1 byte past the end of an unpadded input buffer (main.cpp's synthetic-image path pads by 128 bytes). AVX2 only in the current code; uses the MSVC keyword __forceinline (GCC/Clang portability not checked). The harness uses the OpenCV 3-era CV_BGR2GRAY constant, so it needs changes to build against OpenCV 4, and modern OpenCV may be closer. Code last updated 29 Sep 2018; last commit 23 Mar 2021 only added the MIT LICENSE file.

name: Smolscale
baseline: libswscale (FFmpeg), Pixman, stb_image_resize, GDK-Pixbuf, SDL_gfx and Skia (as wired into the project's own benchmark harness)
workload: Proportional scaling sweep (test.c run_benchmark_proportional) of a random 32-bit RGBA canvas from 0.01x up to 2x of the input size, so both downscaling and upscaling. The bench.sh defaults use 200 steps and 5 repetitions on 1920x1080 and 3840x2160 inputs (0.01-2x) and 7680x4320 (0.01-1x). TESTS_AVAILABLE adds sets such as 16383x16383 at 0.0001-0.1x. Each library runs its own filter: libswscale uses SWS_FAST_BILINEAR (scale <= 2) or SWS_AREA; Pixman uses separable box convolution (beyond 2x reduction) or bilinear; GDK-Pixbuf uses GDK_INTERP_BILINEAR; stb_image_resize uses a box filter in linear colorspace with premultiplied alpha.
claimed_speedup: No ratio against any baseline was seen. The repo (README, bench.sh, plot.sh, gnuplot/) ships no results. Snippets only, from the author's blog post 'Battle of the Bilerps: Image Scaling on the CPU' (2019-07-08; hpjansson.org is blocked here). One snippet says that on 8 threads Smolscale scaled a 16383x16383 image to a much smaller one in roughly 50 ms, about 5.3 gigapixels/s or ~21 GB/s of input. Another says the benchmarks ran on an i7-4770K (Haswell) at 3.5 GHz with a 2000x2000 RGBA input, with Smolscale MT averaging about 50 ms per frame. The per-library comparison plots in the post were not seen.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc. Smolscale is built with -Wall -Wextra -g -O2 -DSMOL_WITH_AVX2, and smolscale-avx2.c additionally with -mavx2 (runtime dispatch). test.c is built at -O2, and Skia at -O3 when enabled. The baseline libraries (libswscale, Pixman, GDK-Pixbuf, SDL_gfx) are system packages found through pkg-config, so their build flags are the distro's.
hardware: i7-4770K (Haswell) at 3.5 GHz according to a search snippet of the blocked blog post; not stated in the repo
stars_or_usage: 39 stars; vendored into hpjansson/chafa (5.3k stars) as chafa/internal/smolscale
tradeoffs: Three files (smolscale.c, .h, -private.h) plus an optional AVX2 file; copyable into a project. Handles 4-channel 32 bpp packed data (RGBA, ARGB, BGRA) and 3-channel data, premultiplied or unassociated alpha, host-byte-order agnostic, maximum 65535x65535. Quality goal is 'reasonable' (no aliasing), not Lanczos-class. Row-batch and one-shot APIs, easily parallelised. Dual licence: BSD 4-clause (advertising clause) or LGPLv3; closed-source use needs credit or an LGPL library split.
caveats: The evidence is snippet-only. The comparison numbers are in a blog post that could not be opened (egress blocked), so the speedup against each baseline is unconfirmed and the tier is capped at C. The public harness ships no results. Threading is asymmetric: 'Smolscale MT' (test.c scale_do_smol_threaded) runs a GThreadPool with g_get_num_processors() threads, while libswscale, Pixman, stb and GDK-Pixbuf are called single-threaded. The libraries also do different work, since each uses its own filter (fast bilinear or area, box convolution, bilinear, box in linear light), so quality differs. The README said at the time that the AVX2 file was 'mostly just a straight copy of the generic code'. The benchmark compares 2019-era library versions. The standalone repo's last commit is 2023-04-12, but the code is still developed inside Chafa (chafa/internal/smolscale, commits up to 2026-09-25), which is the maintained copy. The license is LGPLv3 or BSD 4-clause at the user's choice (COPYING). BSD-4-Clause is not OSI-approved, but the LGPLv3 option is.

name: sparkyuv
baseline: libyuv
workload: Google Benchmark timings (one conversion per iteration; the YCbCr paths are single-threaded, threading is only used by FastGaussian) of 8-bit and 10-bit YCbCr 4:4:4/4:2:2/4:2:0 to RGBA decode, RGBA8 to YCbCr 4:2:0/4:2:2 encode, NV12/NV21 to RGBA decode, and RGBA premultiply/unpremultiply, sparkyuv vs libyuv (I444/I422/I420ToABGR, I410/I210/I010ToARGBMatrix, NV12/NV21 conversions, ARGBAttenuate/ARGBUnattenuate) on one JPEG test image (filirovska.jpeg, not in the repo, dimensions not stated) expanded to opaque RGBA; libyuv is linked from a prebuilt libyuv.a of unstated version and build flags.
claimed_speedup: Valid like-for-like rows (README, Apple M3 Pro, ns per call, derived from page data): 8-bit decode 4:2:2 346,422 vs libyuv 458,754 (1.32x); 4:2:0 347,903 vs 458,823 (1.32x); 4:4:4 332,122 vs 365,939 (1.10x); NV21 and NV12 tie. Invalid rows: the 10-bit decodes (1.92-2.12x) pass element counts as byte strides so sparkyuv reads half-size planes and writes a different output depth; unpremultiply 1.54x is NEON vs libyuv's C fallback. Slower than libyuv: RGBA8 to YCbCr420 (libyuv 2.0x faster), RGBA8 to YCbCr422 (1.37x), premultiply (1.21x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the published run; the repository CMakeLists.txt builds C++20, adds -O3 to Release builds on non-MSVC compilers and uses Highway static dispatch on Apple (HWY_COMPILE_ONLY_STATIC). Compiler and libyuv build flags unknown.
hardware: Apple M3 Pro (12 cores; Google Benchmark header shows 24 MHz nominal clock)
tradeoffs: Supports many YUV matrices (YCgCo, YIQ, YDbDr, constant-luminance), 8/10/12-bit, 22 SIMD targets. Chroma-subsampled encode uses a fixed bilinear downscale that cannot be turned off.
caveats: Mixed result: the README says 8-bit decode is 'very close to libyuv', faster only on arm64 NEON and 'should be considered same' elsewhere, and libyuv is faster at 8-bit YCbCr encode (2.0x at 4:2:0, 1.37x at 4:2:2) and premultiply. The 10-bit wins compare different outputs (sparkyuv 10-bit RGBA in 16-bit storage vs libyuv 8-bit ARGB). Only arm64 numbers; no x86 results. Test image is not in the repo and its size is not stated; premultiply/unpremultiply run on fully opaque pixels from an RGB JPEG. libyuv comes from a prebuilt libyuv.a of unknown version and flags. Repo archived by owner 10 Feb 2025; last commit 14 Jul 2024. Licence files: LICENSE.md (Apache-2.0) and LICENSE-BSD.md (BSD-3-Clause, same author); source headers cite Apache-2.0. [retier] Headline 10-bit wins are a harness bug (element counts passed as byte strides) and compare different output depths; the valid wins are 8-bit decodes at 1.10-1.32x on NEON only. No tests (CI runs ctest with none defined), no libyuv equality check; the NV12 and NV21 libyuv calls are swapped, the libyuv 4:2:2 decode is fed 4:2:0 chroma, and J422 full range is compared against TV range. The 8-bit 4:2:0 SIMD encoder has a vertical chroma averaging bug (src/YCbCr420-inl.h). Depends on the author's Highway fork (awxkee/highway, widen_mul). libyuv is a prebuilt libyuv.a of unknown version and flags; arm64 numbers only; repo archived by its owner.

name: yuvutils-rs
baseline: libyuv built from source by the yuv-sys 0.3.x crate (livekit/rust-sdks, required as 0.3.7 in app/Cargo.toml); libyuv commit not stated
workload: 8-bit RGB/RGBA to YUV 4:2:0/4:2:2/4:4:4 and YUV to RGB/RGBA on a 1997x1331 image, plus 10-bit and rotation benchmarks, criterion timings.
claimed_speedup: Valid like-for-like rows (README, derived from page data; libyuv 1886 via yuv-sys 0.3.7, tables from Nov 2024 to Jan 2025): NV12 to RGBA 377.59 vs 621.11 us on NEON (1.64x), 917.52 vs 979.96 us on AVX2 (1.07x), 736.21 vs 800.85 us on AVX-512 (1.09x); YUV 4:2:0 to RGB 346.13 vs 675.72 us NEON (1.95x), 923.83 us vs 1.42 ms AVX2 (1.54x), 614.19 us vs 1.16 ms AVX-512 (1.89x); YUV 4:2:0 to RGBA 396.58 vs 710.88 us NEON (1.79x), 942.92 us vs 1.03 ms AVX2 (1.09x), 733.88 vs 870.64 us AVX-512 (1.19x). The RGB to YUV 4:2:0 encode rows (1.13-1.35x) come from benches commented out at HEAD; the Windows column and the NEON 10-bit rows compare SIMD against libyuv C fallbacks and are not valid.
tradeoffs: Pure Rust YUV conversion with approximate (fast_mode) and exact (professional_mode) paths; 8 to 16-bit depths; no C API stated, so not callable from C++ without a shim.
caveats: libyuv wins several rows: YUV 4:0:0 to RGBA on AVX2 (635.61 vs 651.88 us) and AVX-512 (525.56 vs 600.43 us), YUV 4:4:4 to RGBA on AVX2 (963.66 us vs 1.10 ms) and AVX-512 (803.62 vs 819.17 us), YUV 4:2:2 to RGBA on AVX2 (1.04 vs 1.10 ms), RGBA to YUV 4:2:0 and 4:2:2 on AVX-512, and 10-bit to RGBA8 on AVX2. The Windows AVX2 column has libyuv at 2.70-6.86 ms on the encode, RGB24-output and 10-bit rows but 525.90-579.24 us on 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4 to RGBA, consistent with a libyuv build (likely MSVC) missing some SIMD row paths (inference, not stated), so the 7-16x gaps on those rows should be ignored. The README rows do not say which YuvConversionMode (Fast, Balanced, Professional) was timed; Fast is documented as libyuv-level precision, Balanced as more precise and about 30% slower. The libyuv 4:2:2 encode row uses ABGRToJ422 (full range) against yuvutils limited range. SIMD and scalar yuvutils paths disagree by up to 2 levels on x86 (issue #144, open, opened 2026-10-02); bit-exactness against libyuv was not shown either way. [retier] Windows column invalid (cl.exe-built libyuv 1886 has SSSE3 only for I422/I444ToARGB; other rows run C); NEON 10-bit 2x is SIMD against C. name: zimg
baseline: FFmpeg 4.0.2 filters (README column label 'swscale 4.0.2'): the swscale scale filter for the Lanczos resize and the libavfilter colorspace filter for the BT.709 to BT.2020 conversion

claimed_speedup: Lanczos FHD->UHD resize: 7.7 ms vs 15.2 ms (Core i7-8565U), 10.8 ms vs 22.2 ms (Xeon Platinum 8176). BT.709 -> BT.2020 conversion: 8.3 ms vs 17.5 ms (i7-8565U), 11.5 ms vs 25.6 ms (Xeon 8176). About 2x on each row (derived from page data).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8565U and Intel Xeon Platinum 8176
tradeoffs: C++17 library covering scaling, colorspace conversion (Rec.709, Rec.2020, SMPTE-C, BT.2020 constant luminance) and depth conversion with dithering; designed to be thread-safe with allocation and I/O separated from processing. The README says it is optimized for Intel architecture. Not a colour management system (no drastic gamut reduction). Autotools is the supported build system.
caveats: README numbers only, added in commit 'Add performance information to README.md' on 22 Sep 2018 with z.lib 2.8 and FFmpeg 4.0.2, so they are about eight years old and swscale has been reworked since. zimg ships its own timing tools (src/testapp resizeapp.cpp and colorspaceapp.cpp take a --times benchmark-cycles option), but the README gives no command lines, compiler, flags, thread count or frame content for either side. name: libyuv
baseline: FFmpeg libswscale
workload: YUV/RGB format conversion and scaling (ARGB, I420, NV12 and others) in video and imaging pipelines.
claimed_speedup: libheif issue #1215 (a user report, no hardware stated): YUV420 HEVC multi-tile decode to interleaved RGB took 42 ms with the ffmpeg decoder plugin plus libheif's own yuv2rgb conversion vs 30 ms with the same decoder plugin plus libyuv for the conversion, about 1.4x for the whole step (derived from page data); since the decoder is the same, the 12 ms difference comes from the conversion (derived from page data). Against libswscale, search snippets only (ffmpeg-devel threads, blocked here): about 4.19 s for libswscale vs 0.93 s for libyuv (about 4-5x) scaling a 1088x1920 BGR24 frame to 480x854 YUV420P 500 times on a MacBook Pro (2016), and about 10x on an Apple M1 for unscaled RGBA to YUV420P, still about 5x after FFmpeg's aarch64 NEON optimizations.
stars_or_usage: 930 stars and 302 forks on this unofficial GitHub mirror (its description says to submit issues and PRs upstream); upstream is chromium.googlesource.com/libyuv/libyuv, and README.chromium marks it shipped and security-critical in Chromium.
tradeoffs: Optimized for SSSE3/AVX2 on x86, Neon/SVE2/SME on Arm, MSA on MIPS and RVV on RISC-V; conversion, scaling, rotation. Official upstream is chromium.googlesource.com/libyuv/libyuv; the GitHub repo is an unofficial mirror (issues and PRs go upstream).
caveats: The libswscale comparison rests on search snippets of ffmpeg-devel threads ('Why not integrate libyuv as a scale filter' and the June 2024 'swscale modernization proposal'), which this sandbox cannot open (ffmpeg.org pipermail, narkive, mail-archive and patchwork are blocked), so the numbers, hardware and swscale settings are unverified. In the same threads FFmpeg developers replied that libswscale defaults to a higher-quality scaler, that comparable speed is reachable by tuning its flags, and that libyuv does no dithering or advanced filtering, so the gap partly reflects quality settings; the snippet numbers may also predate later swscale work. The libheif numbers compare against libheif's own converter, not libswscale, are whole-step times, and state no hardware, compiler or code. No public benchmark code comparing libyuv with libswscale was found; libyuv's unittests benchmark only its SIMD paths against its own C code. The incumbent role is better documented by sparkyuv, yuvutils-rs and xxYUV, which benchmark against libyuv and beat it only on some paths. This GitHub repo is an unofficial mirror; upstream is Chromium's libyuv on googlesource. BSD-3-Clause with a separate Google PATENTS grant.

name: libutf
baseline: ICU 78.3 (ICU4C: ubrk grapheme break iterator, unorm2 NFC, ucol DUCET collation)
workload: Microbenchmarks on tiny fixed string sets, timed as totals with CLOCK_MONOTONIC: grapheme counting over 8 short strings x 200,000 iterations (bench_grapheme.c; ICU ubrk UBRK_CHARACTER iterator reused via ubrk_setText); NFC normalization of 10 short strings x 100,000 (bench_nfc.c; ICU unorm2_normalize into UTF-16); NFC quick-check of 9 already-NFC strings x 500,000 (bench_nfc_quickcheck.c; ICU u_strFromUTF8 plus unorm2_isNormalized); three-level comparison of 12 string pairs x 100,000 (bench_collate.c; ICU ucol_strcoll with ucol_open(""), i.e. CLDR root collation). The 'UTF-8 input' scenario times ICU including u_strFromUTF8 conversion; the 'core-to-core' scenario feeds ICU pre-converted UTF-16.
claimed_speedup: README table (M5 Max, ICU 78.3), UTF-8 input with ICU paying u_strFromUTF8 conversion: NFC 28 ms vs 59 ms (2.1x), NFC quick-check 62 ms vs 237 ms (3.8x), collation 31 ms vs 40 ms (1.3x), grapheme segmentation 237 ms vs 337 ms (1.4x). Core-to-core (ICU on pre-converted UTF-16): NFC 28 ms vs 39 ms (libutf 1.4x), grapheme 237 ms vs 277 ms (libutf 1.2x), collation 31 ms vs 22 ms (ICU 1.4x faster). No core-to-core figure exists for quick-check. Numbers predate later correctness fixes to the grapheme, NFC and collation code.
compiler_and_flags: Build lines in the bench/*.c headers: gcc -O2 -I../include ... -L.. -lutf -lm $(pkg-config --cflags --libs icu-uc [icu-i18n]); Makefile CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -std=c11 -g. Compiler version not stated (on macOS 'gcc' is normally an alias for Apple clang); ICU 78.3 origin and build flags not stated.
hardware: MacBook Pro, Apple M5 Max (stated in README)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (new repo, first visible commit 2026-03-24); code extracted from TinyMUX, in production there since 2008
tradeoffs: Pure C11, no malloc, no dependencies, 702 KB static library versus about 42 MB for ICU static libraries (README). Works directly on UTF-8 with compressed DFAs, so its advantage is largest when the application holds UTF-8 and ICU has to convert to UTF-16. Covers only grapheme segmentation, NFC, collation (DUCET), classification and case/width tables; no word, sentence or line-break segmentation, no bidi, no locale-tailored collation, no shaping. Unicode 16.0.
caveats: First-party microbenchmark on 8 to 12 short hand-written strings repeated 100,000 to 500,000 times, so it measures per-call overhead, not bulk throughput; README reports totals only and no raw result files are checked in. The README numbers were refreshed on 2026-07-30, before correctness fixes to grapheme segmentation (GB4 after CR, GB11 single ZWJ, GB12/13 adjacent regional indicators, 2026-09-29), NFC (D115 blocked composition, 2026-08-01) and collation (NFC tiebreak buffer sizing, 2026-09-04); they have not been re-measured. Grapheme segmentation is not equivalent work: src/grapheme.c implements Unicode 16.0 rules GB3-GB13 without GB9c (Indic conjunct breaks, in UAX #29 since Unicode 15.1), so on the benchmark's Devanagari string it returns a different cluster count from ICU, which follows Unicode 17 in ICU 78.x; there is no GraphemeBreakTest conformance test in tests/ (only test_color_ops.c, test_nfc_icu.c, test_collate_icu.c). Unicode versions differ for all modules (libutf 16.0, ICU 78 is 17.0). The 'UTF-8 input' headline ratios charge ICU for u_strFromUTF8 even though ICU offers native UTF-8 paths that the benchmark does not use (ucol_strcollUTF8, UText via utext_openUTF8 with ubrk_setUText, C++ Normalizer2::normalizeUTF8 and isNormalizedUTF8); core-to-core the gaps shrink to 1.2x to 1.4x and ICU wins collation by 1.4x. ICU's collator is CLDR root collation (ucol_open("")), not raw DUCET. Compiler version and ICU 78.3 build configuration are not stated. NFC and collation are differentially tested against ICU (50 NFC cases plus a 100,000-input fuzz, 33 collation comparisons). Category fit: Unicode segmentation, normalization and collation (ICU baseline), not font shaping; HarfBuzz and FreeType do not apply.

name: unicode-segmenter
baseline: Intl.Segmenter (the built-in JavaScript grapheme segmenter, ICU in V8/JavaScriptCore/SpiderMonkey); also graphemer, grapheme-splitter, @formatjs/intl-segmenter and a WebAssembly build of Rust unicode-segmentation
workload: Grapheme cluster segmentation (UAX #29) of six corpora (Lorem ipsum ASCII, emojis, Hindi, 'demonic' combining characters, tweet text, code snippet), per-iteration time in Node.js, Bun, Deno and browsers.
claimed_speedup: README: '1.3~2.5x faster than built-in Intl.Segmenter', '3.5~8x faster than WASM binding of the Rust unicode-segmentation' and '5~48x faster than other JavaScript libraries' in Node.js/Bun/Deno. Record 20260727, Apple M4 Pro, node 26.5.0: ASCII 2.65 us vs Intl.Segmenter 5.30 us (2x), emojis 829.70 ns vs 2.24 us (2.7x), Hindi 2.75 vs 5.44 us (1.98x), demonic characters 457.21 ns vs 1.05 us (2.3x), tweet text 4.12 vs 8.53 us (2.07x), code snippet 9.99 vs 18.97 us (1.9x). Same machine, bun 1.3.14: 1.41x (Hindi) to 2.04x (ASCII) faster than Intl.Segmenter. Record 20251213, Intel Core Ultra 7 258V, node 25.2.1 x64-linux: ASCII 3.71 vs 8.07 us (2.17x), other corpora 2.13x to 3.05x. In Firefox 154.0b1 (20260727, same Mac) it is 1.49x to 1.97x SLOWER than Intl.Segmenter on every corpus.
compiler_and_flags: JavaScript, no compiler: `yarn perf:grapheme` runs `node --expose-gc benchmark/grapheme/perf.js` (mitata ^1.0.34, gc('inner') per bench); each record header states the runtime, e.g. 'node 26.5.0 (arm64-darwin)', 'bun 1.3.14 (arm64-darwin)', 'node 25.2.1 (x64-linux)'. Browser runs use the Vite page (perf:grapheme:browser) and report cpu/runtime as null.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (~4.43 GHz), macOS 26.5, for the 20260727 Node/Bun/browser runs; Intel Core Ultra 7 258V (~4.65 GHz), Linux, for the 20251213 runs; 48 archived record files from 2024-09-02 to 2026-07-27 (Node, Bun, Chrome, Firefox, Safari; no Deno record) in benchmark/grapheme/_records.
stars_or_usage: 112 stars, 4 forks, 324 commits; npm latest 0.17.3 (registry.npmjs.org); listed as an e18e recommendation in the README
tradeoffs: Grapheme segmentation only (a few KB; 2,321 bytes min+gzip for the count/split API); keeps lookup tables in typed arrays (about 217 kB JS heap plus 19 kB ArrayBuffers retained, versus 86 kB for Intl.Segmenter). Unicode 17.0.0 data bundled, whereas Intl.Segmenter's Unicode version depends on the host. Works where Intl.Segmenter is missing (Hermes, QuickJS, old browsers). JavaScript only, not usable from C++.
caveats: JavaScript library, not C or C++: outside the default C++ language filter, and it cannot be called from C++ without embedding a JavaScript engine. The baseline is Intl.Segmenter, the JavaScript engine's built-in segmenter: a recognisable incumbent inside JavaScript runtimes, but the timing includes the engine's JS-to-native iterator overhead per segment, so it does not show a win over ICU4C's BreakIterator, HarfBuzz or any C++ library. The other JavaScript libraries (graphemer, grapheme-splitter, @formatjs/intl-segmenter) are weak baselines, and the Rust unicode-segmentation baseline runs as a wasm-bindgen build. Browser results differ: in the 20260727 Firefox 154.0b1 record unicode-segmenter is 1.49x to 1.97x slower than Intl.Segmenter, as the README concedes. The README's Deno claim has no archived record, and its 1.3x lower bound was not found in the three records read (lowest seen: 1.41x in Bun 1.3.14). The 20251213 Node record's file name says nodejs_24.2.1 while its header says node 25.2.1. Numbers are first-party; the harness checks output equality with Intl.Segmenter before timing. Category: this is Unicode text segmentation (wave 3's unicode-utf8 category), not font shaping or layout. The Rust port fast-grapheme-segmenter is a separate entry.

name: Typst
baseline: pdfLaTeX (pdfTeX 1.40.24, TeX Live 2022) and LuaLaTeX (LuaHBTeX 1.15.0); the same shootout also ran WeasyPrint 68.1, Apache FOP 2.11 and speedata Publisher 5.3.18 Pro
workload: Mail-merge letters (logo, sender and recipient blocks, justified hyphenated 105 mm body text) built to PDF from XML, 1 page and 500 pages, timed end to end with hyperfine (--warmup 3 for 1 page; --warmup 1 --min-runs 3 for 500 pages). The 500-page input (generate_fakenames.py) is 500 identical copies of one record. Typst reads the XML natively (typst compile --input xml=...); pdflatex and lualatex are driven by a Python script that parses the XML, renders a Jinja2 template and runs one engine pass, and that Python start-up and rendering is inside the timing.
claimed_speedup: Repo README results, macBook Air M4 16 GB, Typst 0.14.2: 500 pages Typst 156.6 ms vs pdflatex 712.3 ms (4.55x), LuaLaTeX 2.356 s (15.04x), FOP 1.607 s (10.27x), speedata sp 4.354 s (27.80x), WeasyPrint 8.672 s (55.38x). 1 page: Typst 105.7 ms vs pdflatex 329.1 ms (3.1x, derived from page data), LuaLaTeX 518.6 ms (4.9x, derived from page data); speedata sp is fastest at 94.5 ms (1.12x faster than Typst).
compiler_and_flags: Not applicable (prebuilt tools); versions are listed in the README (Typst 0.14.2, pdfTeX 3.141592653-2.6-1.40.24, LuaHBTeX 1.15.0, hyperfine 1.17.0, Python 3.14.3).
hardware: MacBook Air M4 (Apple M4), 16 GB RAM, as stated in the README; run by pgundlach (speedata) in February 2026 (3 commits, 2026-02-10 and 2026-02-11).
tradeoffs: A different markup language and ecosystem from LaTeX (fewer packages, no TeX compatibility); incremental compilation and an instant-preview mode are the design goal. Rust, not usable as a C++ library (CLI or Rust crate).
caveats: Rust, not C or C++: outside the default C++ language filter. The baselines are document typesetting engines (pdfTeX 1.40.24 and LuaHBTeX 1.15.0 from TeX Live 2022, four years older than Typst 0.14.2), recognisable incumbents for TeX-style typesetting but not HarfBuzz, FreeType or ICU; Typst is a whole typesetting system, so this is a text-layout entry at most. The benchmark comes from speedata (pgundlach, 1-star repo, companion blog post on news.speedata.de that is blocked here; a search snippet says the author would not pick the fastest engine and that a mail merge is the 'hello world' of typesetting). The documents are not equivalent: Typst uses the system 'Helvetica', pdflatex the helvet package (URW Nimbus Sans, Type 1, T1 encoding) and LuaLaTeX TeX Gyre Heros via fontspec; LaTeX sets the sender block in a minipage beside the recipient while Typst places it absolutely; the PDFs are not committed, so page counts could not be checked (each template forces one letter per page). The LaTeX and LuaLaTeX timings include the Python interpreter, Jinja2 import and template rendering; Typst parses the XML itself. The 500-page input is one record repeated 500 times, which favours Typst's memoised layout: 500 pages take 156.6 ms against 105.7 ms for 1 page, about 0.1 ms per extra page (derived from page data), and Typst's user time (241.3 ms) exceeds its wall time, so it used more than one core while pdflatex runs single-threaded. speedata Publisher is fastest at 1 page (94.5 ms, 1.12x faster than Typst). The Typst README claims fast incremental compilation and gives no LaTeX comparison. texlode/luatex-benchmark (MIT, accompanying the TUGboat 2026 paper 'Real-Time LuaTeX: Recompiling Large Documents in 1 ms') reports Typst 0.14 and later about 1.6-2.2x slower per incremental edit than 0.12/0.13 at 300 pages on x86 (no difference on Apple M4), and says the paper's Typst figures came from an earlier script and do not reproduce with bench.mjs (issue #1).
found_via: WebSearch 'typst compile time benchmark vs LaTeX faster layout performance numbers github' surfaced speedata/typesetting-benchmark and texlode/luatex-benchmark; raw README of both repos read; typst/typst page and commits page read

verification.tier_reason: speedata/typesetting-benchmark's README holds hyperfine output matching every claimed number, from public runners (benchmark.sh, run_typst.sh, run_latex.sh, run_lualatex.sh, mailmerge.typ, mailmerge_template*.tex, mailmerge_*latex.py) on a named machine (MacBook Air M4, 16 GB) with tool versions; it was run by pgundlach of speedata, a competing vendor whose own engine loses at 500 pages, so it is an independent measurement of Typst. Not A: binary builds are unstated, and the timed pipelines are not equivalent (the LaTeX timings include a Python 3.14 + Jinja2 wrapper, fonts differ, and the 500-page input is 500 identical records).
verification.notes: Numbers verified against the speedata README and its runner scripts; B kept as an independent but narrow, non-equivalent shootout. Language Rust is correct (language-filter mismatch). Category: Typst belongs under text layout/typesetting, not font shaping; pdflatex is a typesetting-engine incumbent, not a shaping library.

corrected_fields.workload: Mail-merge letters (logo, sender and recipient blocks, hyphenated 105 mm body text) built to PDF from XML data, 1 page and 500 pages, timed with hyperfine.
corrected_fields.hardware: macBook Air M4, 16 GB RAM
corrected_fields.caveats: The benchmark comes from speedata, the maker of a competing engine (speedata/typesetting-benchmark, 1 star), not from the Typst project; the repo has public templates and runner scripts, a named machine and versions, but a single trivial mail-merge workload and a TeX Live 2022 toolchain (pdfTeX 1.40.24), so it is a narrow shootout (tier B, not A, since TeX build flags are not known). Typst's 500-page time (156.6 ms) is barely above its 1-page time (105.7 ms), which suggests startup dominates and something about the template is cheap. The Typst README itself says 'fast compile times thanks to incremental compilation' and gives no LaTeX comparison. Independent caution: texlode/luatex-benchmark (MIT, TUGboat 2026 paper) reports that Typst 0.14 and later is 1.6x to 2.2x slower per incremental edit than 0.12/0.13 at 300 pages on x86 (no change on Apple M4), and its own paper claim of about 1 ms per paragraph in a live LuaTeX session is a different workload; the paper's Typst figures do not reproduce with the repo's script. Baselines are not HarfBuzz or FreeType, although Typst shapes text with a HarfBuzz port internally. Not on the known list.
