Speedups over go-runewidth (derived from page data): 1.64x mixed strings, 2.27x East Asian, 2.30x ASCII, 1.57x emoji, 3.31x East Asian runes, 1.04x ASCII runes (parity), 1.83x and 2.11x truncation.

The baselines are Go libraries; go-runewidth (about 720 stars, the de facto Go terminal-width library) is a recognisable incumbent within Go, but ICU, HarfBuzz and FreeType are not involved. Display width is a text-layout primitive, not shaping. No C++ implementation is involved.

name: fast-grapheme-segmenter
baseline: icu_segmenter 2.3.0 (ICU4X grapheme cluster segmenter) and unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 (the common Rust crate)
workload: UAX #29 extended grapheme cluster segmentation of about 300-byte samples in nine corpora (English, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, emoji, source code), three modes: counting clusters, collecting every cluster, collecting offsets; criterion.

name: fontdue
baseline: FreeType 2 (glyph rasterization, via freetype-rs); also rusttype 0.9.2 and ab_glyph 0.2.3 for rasterization, glyph_brush_layout 0.2.0 for layout
workload: Time to produce glyph metrics and bitmaps for the 37-character string 'Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow.' at 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and 200 px/em, for an Exo2 TrueType (glyf) font and the OpenType (CFF) version of it; separate layout benchmark of 100-1000 Roboto-Regular characters with word wrapping.
claimed_speedup: README says it 'currently has the lowest end to end latency for a font rasterizer' and gives plots only, no numbers. Reading the plotted lines (approximate, derived from page data): TrueType, fontdue about 15 us vs FreeType 2 about 45 us at 10 px/em (about 3x) and about 235 us vs about 545 us at 200 px/em (about 2.3x); OpenType/CFF, fontdue about 12 us vs FreeType about 135 us at 10 px/em (about 11x) and about 220 us vs about 625 us at 200 px/em (about 2.8x). Layout plot: fontdue about 24 us vs glyph_brush_layout about 139 us at 1000 characters (about 5.8x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Rust, no_std, pure-Rust rasterizer and naive layout only; no text shaping (author points to Cosmic Text for that), no hinting. Fonts are fully parsed into custom structures on load (slow, allocating load is an explicit non-goal to fix), so it wins on per-glyph latency, not load time. Not directly usable from C++ without writing an FFI layer.
caveats: Evidence is three plots in /images with no table, CPU model, rustc version, flags or FreeType version; the numbers in claimed_speedup are read off the charts (approximate; checked against the images). The plots were last updated on 2020-09-05 (commits 'Freetype bench' and 'More data and be more color blind friendly'), when fontdue was far older than today's 0.9.4, and they have not been regenerated since. Benchmark code is public (dev/benches/rasterize.rs and layout.rs, criterion 0.3; the FreeType case only builds with the freetype_benchmark feature, freetype-rs 0.26). The comparison is not apples-to-apples: (1) fontdue::Font::from_bytes, run outside the timed loop, parses and flattens every glyph outline up front, with FontSettings.scale set to the exact benchmarked size, so the timed fontdue loop only rasterizes cached geometry; (2) the FreeType loop calls set_char_size and then load_char with LoadFlag::RENDER for every character, so it parses each glyph (glyf or CFF charstrings), applies FreeType's default hinting and renders, while fontdue does not hint. The large CFF gap at small sizes (about 11x at 10 px/em) is consistent with charstring parsing and hinting landing only on the FreeType side. The layout benchmark compares with glyph_brush_layout 0.2.0 (a Rust library), not a C/C++ incumbent. fontdue began as a fork of font-rs and was rewritten; font-rs is a separate entry.

name: msdfgl
baseline: msdfgen (Chlumsky's CPU multi-channel signed distance field generator, single-threaded and OpenMP builds); incumbent for MSDF font atlas generation, not one of HarfBuzz or FreeType
workload: Generating an MSDF texture for ASCII characters 0-127 of the font DejaVu Sans at four scale factors (1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0), mean of 100 runs, OpenGL context creation and destruction time and shader compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: Chart numbers in README image (msdfgl vs msdfgen vs msdfgen with OpenMP): scale 1.0 0.0081 s vs 0.4890 s vs 0.1334 s; scale 2.0 0.0164 s vs 1.9390 s vs 0.5182 s; scale 4.0 0.0645 s vs 7.7407 s vs 1.9939 s; scale 8.0 0.2345 s vs 31.0000 s vs 8.0000 s (the two msdfgen values at 8.0 were extrapolated by the author). Ratios (derived from page data): about 60x, 118x, 120x and 132x faster than single-threaded msdfgen, and about 16x, 32x, 31x and 34x faster than OpenMP msdfgen.
hardware: Core i7 8550m (as written in README) with Intel UHD Graphics 620, Debian Linux
tradeoffs: GPU implementation written from scratch in C; needs an OpenGL 3.3 core or OpenGL ES 3.2 context. The algorithm was reworked to run in shaders: no cubic Bezier segments (so CFF/PostScript-flavoured OpenType outlines are not handled), constant memory, no pointers. Shader compilation takes about one second once. Output is a ready-to-use GPU atlas and index texture, so no upload step.
caveats: First-party benchmark with no benchmark code in the repo; compiler, flags and the msdfgen version (2019 era) are not stated. GPU versus CPU: the msdfgl timings run on the laptop's integrated Intel UHD Graphics 620 and the msdfgen timings on the same laptop's 4-core CPU (README writes 'Core i7 8550m'), so it is the same SoC rather than a discrete GPU, but the win comes from moving the per-pixel step to the GPU, not from a faster CPU algorithm, and it needs an OpenGL 3.3 or ES 3.2 context. msdfgen's timing excludes uploading the bitmaps to a texture while msdfgl's includes it (favors msdfgen); shader compilation (close to a second) and GL context creation are excluded. The scale 8.0 msdfgen values (8.0000 s and 31.0000 s) are extrapolated, not measured. msdfgl drops cubic segments (README TODO: needed for OpenType/CFF fonts) and lacks edge-coloring for teardrop contours with 1 or 2 segments; the test font DejaVu Sans is TrueType (quadratic only), so the benchmark avoids the missing paths. Output quality parity with msdfgen, including its error correction, is not evaluated. Baseline is msdfgen, not a listed incumbent (HarfBuzz, FreeType). Numbers read from bar labels in img/benchmarks.png.

Not a C/C++ incumbent such as HarfBuzz with FreeType or Pango.

When a whole document is handed to one parley Layout, parley is far slower (devanagari 10,000 lines: 78,782 ms vs cosmic-text 3,265 ms). massive PR 154 (merged 2026-09-15), docs/adr/0005-dual-shaping-engines-cosmic-text-and-parley.md (criterion, bundled JetBrains Mono 13 px, M-series Mac, warm cache): single ASCII cluster cosmic-text 1.8 us vs parley 2.1 us (cosmic-text ~16% faster); full mixed line parley 28 us vs cosmic-text 137 us (~4.8x); full-screen throughput parley ~2x; fallback stress parley ~2.7x; cold start with a fresh font database parley 61 us vs cosmic-text 36 ms (~600x in parley's favour, caused by cosmic-text's FontSystem construction).

caveats: Third-party measurements by two downstream projects (flui and massive), not by the Parley authors and not peer reviewed. Rust, so it does not match the catalog's default C++ language filter. Baseline cosmic-text is a recognisable Rust-ecosystem incumbent but not a C/C++ one (HarfBuzz with FreeType, Pango); the two libraries use different HarfRust versions (0.5.2 vs 0.12.0), so part of the gap may come from the newer shaper rather than Parley's own code. The flui harness lays out at unbounded width, so line wrapping is not exercised; it requests system fonts by generic family and did not check fallback quality (tofu glyphs would still count); glyph counts differ on emoji_zwj (-3.19%) and arabic_mixed (-0.25%). The flui PR, co-authored with an AI assistant, went through three correction rounds (a quadratic cost when the whole document is one parley Layout, 78,782 ms vs 3,265 ms on 10,000 Devanagari lines; a memory-retention asymmetry; mismatched font generics and a destruction boundary inside the timer); the earlier 30-38x memory figures are superseded. name: text-shaper
baseline: harfbuzzjs ^0.4.13 (HarfBuzz compiled to WebAssembly, called from JavaScript), not native HarfBuzz; opentype.js also compared; the rasterization rows compare with FreeType through the freetype2 (node-freetype2) Node native binding
workload: OpenType shaping of word to paragraph texts in Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar and CJK (Noto fonts and texts from the reference/rustybuzz submodule; Cyrillic, Greek and CJK use macOS's Arial Unicode.ttf), plus glyph path extraction, text to SVG and grayscale/LCD rasterization, timed under Bun with a batch timer (bench/utils.ts measure: shaping uses 10 warmup calls, then 3 timed batches of 100 calls).
claimed_speedup: README table vs harfbuzzjs: path extraction 16x, text to SVG 1.2-1.5x, Latin 1.5x, Arabic 1.2x, Hebrew 1.6x, Hindi 3.6x, Myanmar 10.5x, CJK 1.3-1.5x; vs opentype.js 4x to 86x; the README says it 'outperforms harfbuzzjs (WebAssembly) and opentype.js across all benchmarks'. The committed results file (docs/.vitepress/data/benchmarks.json, ops/s, M1 Pro, Bun 1.3.4) gives different ratios vs harfbuzzjs (derived from page data): English paragraph 1.48x, Russian/Ukrainian/Belarusian 1.18-1.26x, Greek 1.17x, Chinese/Japanese/Korean 1.26-1.31x, Hebrew 1.24x, Arabic 1.04x, Thai 1.58x, Khmer 2.25x, Hindi 3.25x, Myanmar 10.60x, glyph path extraction 50x, text to SVG 5.3-7.1x; with no features on mixed text text-shaper is slower (82,320 vs 90,800 ops/s, 0.91x). Only the Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and CJK rows (about 1.2-1.5x) do comparable work on both sides. The same file reports rasterization vs FreeType (freetype2 binding) of 1.50x at 12 px to 10.21x at 200 px (derived from page data), with the caveats below.
compiler_and_flags: Bun 1.3.4 runtime running the TypeScript sources via bun test ./bench/ (from benchmarks.json meta and package.json); no build flags apply
hardware: Apple M1 Pro MacBook Pro, 16 GB (meta block of docs/.vitepress/data/benchmarks.json, generated 2025-12-16, 1 run); the README table states no hardware
tradeoffs: Pure TypeScript (zero dependencies, runs in browsers and Bun/Node), so not usable from C++. Also does TrueType hinting and FreeType-style or libass-style rasterization. Young project (npm 0.1.x).
caveats: Baseline is harfbuzzjs, the WebAssembly build of HarfBuzz driven from JavaScript, not native HarfBuzz; each timed harfbuzzjs call creates a buffer, copies the text into WASM memory, guesses segment properties, shapes and destroys the buffer, while text-shaper reuses its buffers (shapeInto). Several headline rows time different work: (1) Path extraction: getGlyphPath caches paths per font and glyph in a WeakMap (src/render/path.ts), so after warmup the text-shaper side times a cache lookup while harfbuzzjs glyphToPath rebuilds an SVG path string on every call. (2) Complex scripts: bench/shaping.test.ts calls shapeInto without script or direction, and UnicodeBuffer.addStr never sets them (script defaults to 'Zyyy', direction LTR), so the cached shape plan enables only the default features (ccmp, locl, rlig, rclt, calt, liga, kern, mark, mkmk; src/shaper/shape-plan.ts) and no RTL reversal runs. Arabic joining forms and Indic/Myanmar/Khmer script features from the fonts are therefore not applied on the text-shaper side, while harfbuzzjs guesses script and direction and runs the full script shaper; the Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Khmer, Thai and Myanmar ratios compare unequal work, and the output is not checked against HarfBuzz. (3) Rasterization vs FreeType: rasterizeGlyph defaults to hinting off and reuses the cached glyph path (hinted runs reuse a hinted-glyph cache), while FreeType's loadGlyph({render: true}) loads, hints with default flags and renders every call through a Node native binding. The README table does not match the committed results file (e.g. path extraction 16x vs 50x; text to SVG 1.2-1.5x vs 5.3-7.1x; Arabic 1.2x vs 1.04x), so its source run is unknown; 'outperforms across all benchmarks' is contradicted by the no-features row (0.91x). The results file is a single run from 2025-12-16, while the bench code read here is the 2026-07 HEAD. Bench fonts and texts come from the reference/rustybuzz git submodule (harfbuzz/rustybuzz @ 51d99b8), so they are public; the Cyrillic, Greek and CJK cases need macOS's /System/Library/Fonts/Supplemental/Arial Unicode.ttf.

name: ugrapheme
baseline: ICU's character BreakIterator called through PyICU (the Python binding to ICU's C++ library), driven by a Python generator; also pyuegc, uniseg and grapheme (the other Python grapheme splitters)
workload: Splitting one short string of 15 extended grapheme clusters ('Hello', '!', spaces, two emoji ZWJ sequences with skin-tone modifiers and the Devanagari word अनुच्छेद) into a list of grapheme strings (UAX #29), timed with IPython %%timeit (mean of 7 runs of 100,000 or 1,000,000 loops).
claimed_speedup: README %%timeit means: ugrapheme grapheme_split 337 ns vs PyICU BreakIterator loop 2.84 us (8.4x, derived from page data; README says 8x); pyuegc EGC 8.19 us vs 337 ns (24x; the section heading says 25x); uniseg 14.6 us vs 340 ns (README says 45x; 43x derived from page data; wrong split of a Devanagari conjunct); grapheme 17.4 us vs 332 ns (52x; also wrong split).
stars_or_usage: 40 stars, 2 forks; PyPI ugrapheme 0.8 with wheels for CPython 3.8+
tradeoffs: Cython extension with sparse bitmap property tables (under 11 KB) and a small DFA; passes the Unicode 16.0 UAX #29 grapheme break tests; behaves like a Python str with grapheme indexing; needs a compiled wheel.
caveats: First-party IPython %%timeit sessions on a single 15-grapheme string; no CPU, OS, Python, Cython, PyICU or ICU version stated (a separate ASCII throughput remark cites only 'a fast 2024 laptop') and no benchmark script in the repo. The PyICU harness converts the input to icu.UnicodeString, calls nextBoundary() once per grapheme through the binding inside a Python generator and builds a Python str per slice, so the 8.4x gap mostly measures CPython and binding overhead on a tiny input, not ICU's C++ segmentation; there is no comparison against ICU from C or C++ or on long text. Unicode versions are not matched: ugrapheme passes the Unicode 16.0 GraphemeBreakTest, while the ICU and pyuegc versions used are not given; uniseg and grapheme produce wrong splits, so their ratios compare unequal output. CPython-only extension, not callable from C++. Belongs in Unicode segmentation (wave 3 unicode-utf8), not font shaping. Last commit and last release (0.8) on 2024-10-28.

name: uni-algo
baseline: ICU (word break and extended grapheme cluster break iteration over UTF-16 text)
workload: Count UAX #29 word-break and extended-grapheme-cluster boundaries in 50,000 UTF-16 strings. Each string is three copies of the CC BY-SA 1.0 attribution paragraph in English, Latvian, Russian, Bengali, Chinese, Japanese and Korean (perf/perf_segment_utf16.h fill_1). uni-algo una::views::grapheme/word::utf16 with std::distance is compared against an ICU BreakIterator (createCharacterInstance/createWordInstance, US locale) first()/next() loop. Each figure is the total steady_clock time in milliseconds for all 50,000 strings (lower is better), repeated five times.
claimed_speedup: MSVC 19.12 x64, first of five runs, total ms for 50,000 strings (unit from the harness's std::chrono milliseconds): word breaks 2355.47 (uni-algo) vs 11379.4 (ICU), 4.83x; grapheme breaks 2067.16 vs 5600.95, 2.71x. MSVC 19.12 x86: word breaks 2544.55 vs 13137.1, 5.16x; grapheme breaks 2239.48 vs 6766.44, 3.02x (ratios derived from page data; the five runs agree within about 1%). GCC 7.3 -O3 rows show uni-algo alone (word 1467.2 ms x64, grapheme 1035.15 ms x64) because ICU was not built under MinGW.

license: MIT OR Unlicense (LICENSE.md offers a 'Public Domain License' whose text is the Unlicense, or MIT)

The result file states no units (the harness prints std::chrono milliseconds), no CPU model, no ICU version and no compiler flags for MSVC, and ICU was measured only under MSVC 2017. The ICU path copies each string into an icu::UnicodeString inside the timed loop; that is negligible next to about 228 microseconds per string for ICU word breaks (derived from page data). The CI comparison runs on a shared GitHub Actions runner with -count=3 and -benchtime=100ms, and the workflow itself calls these results directional with 10-20% variance, which matters for the 1.1-1.4x rows (ZWJ, table header, combined). The work is not identical. go-runewidth v0.0.19 StringWidth runs full UAX #29 grapheme segmentation (clipperhouse/uax29/v2) on every string, ASCII included. uniwidth instead takes a SWAR ASCII path and a lightweight ZWJ/VS16/flag/skin-tone state machine without full segmentation. The Unicode tables differ too: 16.0 in uniwidth, 15.1.0 in go-runewidth (script/generate.go). Both treat East Asian Ambiguous as narrow by default outside CJK locales; go-runewidth picks the setting from RUNEWIDTH_EASTASIAN or the locale or console. The bench never checks that the libraries agree, and their outputs can differ on VS16 sequences (uniwidth forces any character followed by U+FE0F to width 2) and on clusters that only UAX #29 merges. go-runewidth's optional CreateLUT() lookup table is not enabled. The bench/README Windows table looks stale against the current code: it gives uniwidth ASCII long as 340 ns, against 64 ns in CI and ~50 ns in the CHANGELOG. The README headline '3-46x' overstates the low end, since non-ASCII StringWidth gains are 1.1-2.2x in CI. Display width is a text-layout primitive, not shaping. The baselines are Go libraries, not HarfBuzz, FreeType or ICU.

name: uwcwidth
baseline: jquast/wcwidth, the standard Python terminal-width package, which was pure Python when measured (most likely 0.2.13, the only wcwidth release between January 2024 and September 2025 per PyPI); cwcwidth, a Cython binding to the C library's wcwidth/wcswidth, was also measured; neither version is stated
workload: wcswidth of the 11-codepoint string 'コンニチハ, セカイ!' (full-width katakana plus ASCII) in IPython %%timeit, 7 runs of 10^6 or 10^7 loops; that one string is the whole benchmark.
claimed_speedup: README IPython %%timeit of wcswidth('コンニチハ, セカイ!') gives wcwidth 1.73 us ± 7.93 ns, cwcwidth 211 ns ± 3.63 ns and uwcwidth 41 ns ± 0.0363 ns per loop. That is about 42x vs wcwidth and 5.1x vs cwcwidth (derived from page data). The README heading says 'Performance: 40x faster than wcwidth'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the timing. The package is a Cython extension built with -O3 on non-MSVC compilers and with no extra flags under MSVC (setup.py). Python, wcwidth and cwcwidth versions are not stated.
tradeoffs: Cython wrapper over about 4 KB of bitmap lookup tables derived from musl libc; covers Unicode 16.0 emoji with VS15/VS16 and ZWJ; width only, no grapheme segmentation (use ugrapheme for that).
caveats: The 40x comes from one short string with no CPU, OS or Python version, and the numbers are first-party. Most of the 40x is the gap between a compiled Cython extension (uwcwidth.pyx, -O3) and the pure-Python wcwidth of 2024. The like-for-like compiled comparison is cwcwidth, which uwcwidth beats by about 5x. cwcwidth's widths come from the platform libc, so its Unicode coverage varies by system. The baseline has since moved: wcwidth is at 0.9.1 (2026), describes itself as a Python and C11 library and ships platform abi3 wheels, and that version was not measured, so the 40x should be treated as stale. Semantics differ slightly. uwcwidth uses Unicode 16.0 (draft) tables derived from musl's wcwidth, skips the codepoint after a ZWJ unconditionally and forces width 2 on VS16. It returns -1 for control characters, as wcwidth does. The tests do not compare outputs against wcwidth. Terminal cell width is a text-layout primitive rather than shaping, and the baseline is a Python package, not HarfBuzz, FreeType or ICU.

name: xxUTF
baseline: ICU4C (unorm2 NFD normalization on UTF-8 input; also compared for NFC, NFKD, NFKC and case folding per README)
workload: NFD normalization of UTF-8 text from eight real-text files in bin/common/inputs (Arabic, Chinese, Hebrew, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Latin, Russian; e.g. Latin.txt 86,940 bytes pure ASCII, Arabic.txt 81,685 bytes, Korean.txt 66,600 bytes). bin/benchmark/benchmark.zig feeds each file in 4096-byte chunks (trimmed to code-point boundaries), times each chunk with the awake clock and sums per pass, 1000 timed passes after 50 warm-up passes, and reports mean throughput in GiB/s labelled GB/s. The ICU side (IcuNormalizerUtf8) runs u_strFromUTF8, unorm2_normalize with the NFD instance and u_strToUTF8 per chunk into stack buffers; xxUTF works on UTF-8 directly. The README's link to /benchmarks/inputs is stale.
claimed_speedup: README claims 'the fastest open source implementations of the supported algorithms' and shows one bar chart, doc/neon_utf8_nfd.png (NFD on UTF-8, ARM NEON, GB/s). Values measured from bar pixel heights (derived from page data; 1 pixel = 0.049 GB/s on the 0-35 axis, so each value is +/-0.05 GB/s and the small ICU bars carry 10-20% uncertainty): Arabic 1.91 vs 0.54 GB/s (about 3.5x), Japanese 2.69 vs 0.78 (3.4x), Chinese 4.06 vs 1.03 (4.0x), Hindi 2.59 vs 0.68 (3.8x), Russian 2.44 vs 0.54 (4.5x), Hebrew 2.35 vs 0.64 (3.7x), Korean 0.78 vs 0.24 (3.2x), Latin 34.85 vs 0.34 (about 100x) for xxUTF vs ICU4C. Latin.txt is pure-ASCII lorem ipsum (already NFD), so the Latin bar measures an ASCII pass-through against ICU's UTF-8 to UTF-16 to UTF-8 round trip.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 build system: 'zig build bench' compiles the xxUTF C amalgamation with ReleaseFast (forced to ReleaseFast if the build mode is Debug), -Wall -Wextra ... -Werror and -DXXUTF_IMPLEMENTATION_NEON=1 on NEON targets (build.zig); ICU4C is linked dynamically as the system icu-uc library, version and build flags not stated.
hardware: Unnamed 'machine supporting ARM NEON'; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: C library distributed as a single-header amalgamation (callable from C++), no allocation, no libc dependency, UTF-8/UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE, NFD/NFC/NFKD/NFKC plus case folding, streaming helpers. Built for Unicode 17.0.0. README shows ARM NEON results and says not many instruction sets are supported yet (it claims to be fastest even in scalar mode). Build system is Zig 0.16.0. Input is assumed valid.
caveats: No numeric table or result file: values come from a PNG chart and are approximate (+/-0.05 GB/s per bar). CPU model, OS, ICU version and ICU build flags are not stated; the README only says 'a machine supporting ARM NEON' and asks users to match ICU's Unicode version to xxUTF's (Unicode 17.0.0). The chart was last regenerated in commit 4d1689f 'Improve ASCII normalization' (2026-06-26), and the next commit 5d54cc2 'Fix edge case bugs induced by previous commit' fixed the NEON UTF-8 ASCII fast path (missing '*out_length += 63' and 'last_ccc = 0' resets), so the chart was measured on code later fixed for correctness bugs (the fix adds a few scalar operations per block and probably changes speed little). The Latin bar (about 100x) is pure-ASCII already-normalized text and reflects a pass-through, not decomposition work; per-chunk timing of 4 KiB at about 35 GB/s is roughly 110 ns per timed interval (derived), so timer resolution affects that bar. ICU is charged for UTF-8 to UTF-16 and back conversion around unorm2_normalize; ICU's C++ Normalizer2::normalizeUTF8 was not tried. Unpublished ICU case-fold and UTF-16 benchmark variants are biased against ICU (ucasemap_open/close or ucnv_open/close inside every timed chunk, and ucnv transcoding of UTF-16 input). The work is equivalent in output: NFD is standard-defined, xxUTF case folding uses full folding (CaseFolding.txt C and F entries, Turkic and simple skipped) like ICU's U_FOLD_CASE_DEFAULT, and the AFL++ fuzzer (test/fuzz.c) checks every output against ICU4C. Alpha status per README with a security review pending; 15 stars. Category: Unicode text processing (normalization and case folding), wave 3's unicode-utf8 category with an ICU baseline, not font shaping or layout.

name: Pretext
baseline: Browser DOM text measurement (getBoundingClientRect, offsetHeight and the layout reflow they trigger)
workload: Measuring multiline text height and line breaks in the browser without DOM layout: prepare() once per text, then layout() as pure arithmetic over cached widths.
claimed_speedup: No Pretext-versus-DOM numbers in the repository. The current README says 'Fast, accurate' and that layout() is 'pure arithmetic. No DOM layout & reflow!'. Early README versions in the npm tarballs 0.0.0 to 0.0.4 (March-April 2026) gave first-party absolute timings with no DOM baseline: prepare() about 17-19 ms and layout() about 0.09-0.10 ms for a shared 500-text batch. Third-party blogs and landing pages (snippets only) call it '300-600x' or '500x faster' than DOM measurement; none of this is measured in the repo.
tradeoffs: Layout only: the browser still paints the text, and it reads font widths through canvas measureText, so correctness depends on the host font engine; no bidi levels or visual order; not a general CSS inline formatting engine; in a worker small emoji measure too wide in Chrome and Firefox on macOS. JavaScript, not usable from C++.
caveats: Tier D: no head-to-head DOM measurement table in README, RESEARCH.md, DEVELOPMENT.md, harness/README.md, pages/ or the early npm READMEs; the bun harness bench compares Pretext builds with each other. The baseline (browser DOM measurement via getBoundingClientRect/offsetHeight and the reflow they force) is the recognisable web-platform incumbent, but not a C/C++ library, and the project is TypeScript, so it does not match the catalog's default C++ language filter. The work differs from the baseline: prepare() still measures segments with the browser's Canvas text measurement, and layout() is arithmetic over cached widths, so a 'faster than DOM' figure compares a cached re-layout with a full style and layout pass. It measures and breaks lines; it does not shape glyphs, so HarfBuzz or FreeType are not comparable baselines. Included as a notable (50.7k stars) tier D entry.

name: fpng
baseline: libpng
workload: Lossless 24/32bpp PNG encode, and decode of fpng-produced PNGs, single-threaded, on the QOI benchmark suite (QOIR harness) and on 303 GPU-texture test images (fpng README).
claimed_speedup: README text: about 23x faster compression and 2.5-3x faster decompression than libpng (decompression only on fpng-compressed PNGs). QOIR benchmark: fpng encode 192.16 MPixels/s vs libpng 5.49 (about 35x, derived from page data) and decode 148.19 vs 56.18 (about 2.6x, derived from page data); output files about 1.29x larger than libpng (CmpRatio 0.3115 vs 0.2423, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc (Debian 10.2.1-6) 10.2.1; script/run_full_benchmarks.sh defaults to CFLAGS '-Wall -O3' and compiles each codec adapter with -march=native; fpng.cpp is vendored in qoir third_party/fpng and #included into adapter/png_fpng_adapter.cpp, so fpng itself is built with -Wall -O3 -march=native (without the -fno-strict-aliasing that fpng's README says it was tested with); libpng is Debian Bullseye's system package (build flags not stated) driven through its simplified API at default settings; fpng's own README benchmarks used MSVC 2019 (flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded; fpng README: Xeon E5-2690 3.00 GHz
tradeoffs: Encoder writes standards-conformant PNG readable by any decoder, but the fast decoder only accepts PNGs written by fpng (returns FPNG_DECODE_NOT_FPNG otherwise). 24/32bpp only. SIMD (SSE4.1 plus PCLMUL for CRC and Adler) is x86 only. Output about 29% larger than libpng. Single source file, no dependencies. README recommends Wuffs for decoding untrusted PNGs.
caveats: fpng's README tables compare against qoi, lodepng and stb_image only; its libpng claim (~23x encode, 2.5-3x decode on fpng-compressed PNGs) is a prose line from MSVC 2019 runs on a Xeon E5-2690. The A tier rests on nigeltao/qoir's public harness (Nov 2022, one i5-10210U, gcc 10.2.1, Debian Bullseye libpng at the simplified API's default zlib settings; faster libpng settings such as a lower zlib level were not tried). Trade-off: fpng's PNGs are about 29% larger than libpng's in that run (CmpRatio 0.3115 vs 0.2423, derived from page data). Output is standard PNG that any decoder reads, but fpng's fast decoder only accepts fpng-written files, and the harness has each codec decode its own encoder's output, so the 2.6x decode figure compares fpng decoding fpng files with libpng decoding libpng files; Wuffs decodes the original PNGs at 140.79 MP/s in the same run. The harness never checks decoded pixels against the source. SIMD paths are x86-only (SSE4.1/PCLMUL). The author recommends Wuffs for reading arbitrary PNGs; an Aug 2024 commit fixed an off-by-four-bytes chunk bounds check on malformed input, and the issue tracker has heap-buffer-overflow and macOS segfault reports. Unlicense public-domain dedication: no patent grant.

The speed-up comes from a third party's harness (nigeltao/qoir, Nov 2022), not from fpnge's README, which has no libpng comparison. Trade-off: fpnge's files are about 15% larger than libpng's in that run (CmpRatio 0.2798 vs 0.2423, derived from page data). Baseline is Debian Bullseye's libpng at the simplified API's default zlib settings with unstated distro build flags; faster libpng settings were not tried, and the 57x ratio is above the 50x level at which unstated baseline flags usually cap a tier. One laptop-class CPU (i5-10210U), gcc 10.2.1, and a 2022 fpnge snapshot; upstream has changed since (BGR input, custom chunks, a simpler predictor in 2025), so current speed may differ. SIMD code is x86-only (AVX2 or SSE4.1) and the author calls it a proof of concept. Robustness: issue #25 (FPNGEOutputAllocSize underestimate causing a heap overflow on a 1x64000 grayscale image, fixed 2023-05-22; qoir's vendored copy uses a generous 1024 + 2*bytes*channels*w*h estimate) and issue #31 (memory corruption on one 4-channel image, opened 2024-09-29, closed). The harness never checks the encoded output.

name: libspng
baseline: libpng 1.6.37 (Debian Bullseye)
workload: PNG decode speed in the Wuffs project's 'mimic' benchmarks on six test images from 19k (8bpp) to 4002k (24bpp) decoded bytes, libspng 0.7.3 vs libpng 1.6.37.
claimed_speedup: Wuffs blog appendix (third-party, MB/s of decoded output, libpng = 1.00x): libspng with checksum verification decodes 1.02x to 1.07x faster on the 19k, 40k, 77k and 4002k images (e.g. 4002k_24bpp 110 MB/s clang9 vs 104 MB/s) and 1.39x (clang9, 203 MB/s) / 1.33x (gcc10, 194 MB/s) on 552k_32bpp_verify_checksum vs libpng 146 MB/s; the blog's best ratio, 1.62x (236 MB/s, 552k_32bpp_ignore_checksum/clang9), compares checksum-skipping libspng against libpng, which cannot skip checksums. mango README (i7-11800H, 2560x1600 image): spng decode 37.7 ms vs libpng 57.3 ms (1.52x) and encode 215.9 ms vs 820.5 ms (3.8x); 4833x5875 image: decode 296.6 ms vs 379.5 ms (1.28x), encode 2424.7 ms vs 14051.3 ms (5.8x) (ratios derived from page data). libspng README: 'outperforms the reference implementation in common use cases' with a chart image only.
compiler_and_flags: clang 9 and gcc 10 with -O3 -DWUFFS_MIMIC (blog Reproduction section: gcc -O3 test/c/std/png.c -DWUFFS_MIMIC -lm -lpng -lz); libspng spng.c is #included into the harness translation unit; libpng is Debian Bullseye's packaged libpng16.so
hardware: Intel Core m3-6Y30 @ 0.90GHz (Skylake laptop, x86_64) for the Wuffs blog numbers; Intel Core i7-11800H for the mango README numbers
tradeoffs: Simpler API than libpng, not API-compatible; security focus (OSS-Fuzz); does not require zlib (optional miniz); encoder included; progressive read supported; animated PNG still planned. Same file format so output is interchangeable.
caveats: Decode gains over libpng are modest and image-dependent (1.02x to 1.07x on four of five Wuffs test images). Wuffs' mimiclib notes that libspng 0.6.2 did not verify Adler-32 (an inverted SPNG_CTX_IGNORE_ADLER32 check, fixed in commit 9c35dc3, Dec 2020) and never verifies the final IDAT chunk's CRC-32; the blog does not pin the libspng commit, so the small gains may partly reflect skipped verification. In mango's png_benchmark.cpp the spng decoder is set to SPNG_CRC_USE (CRC errors ignored) while libpng uses defaults, and the spng encoder uses compression level 3 with the Up filter only while libpng uses default settings, so spng's 3.8x to 5.8x encode lead comes with 14% to 21% larger files (3232 vs 2843 KB; 34083 vs 28180 KB). The same blog shows libpng with zlib-ng is 1.01x to 1.21x faster than stock libpng, which narrows the gap. Code activity: the only 2026 commits are a copyright-year update; the previous commit is from 2023-12-20.

RGB and RGBA 8-bit only. Reference implementation is deliberately not heavily optimised and loads the whole file into RAM; limited to 400 million pixels.
caveats: QOI is a different file format from PNG (readers need QOI support) and trades compression for speed: overall CmpRatio 0.2823 vs libpng 0.2423 (QOI output about 17% larger, derived from page data) and vs WebP lossless 0.1651; QOI compresses worse than libpng on every subset row of doc/full_benchmarks.txt (for example photo_wikipedia 0.6618 vs 0.5663, photo_kodak 0.5829 vs 0.5630). The libpng baseline (PNG/libpng row, 'Debian Bullseye's libpng' per the file's Notes) is the distro package driven through the simplified API: adapter/png_libpng_adapter.c calls png_image_write_to_memory with image.flags = 0, so PNG_IMAGE_FLAG_FAST is not set and libpng runs at its defaults (zlib default compression level, all-filters heuristic), i.e. its default compression level, not a speed-tuned setting. Timing in test/benchmarks.c: 5 repetitions per image with gettimeofday, single-threaded, allocation included; the harness does not compare decoded pixels with the source (no round-trip check). The WebP_Lossless row uses libpng for images with a dimension above 16383 px, and the WebP decode adapter adds a full-image memcpy. The vendored qoi.h differs from current upstream only by the April 2025 modulo-to-mask change (about 1.4% faster encoding) and stricter qoi_read/qoi_write file-I/O error checks, so the numbers still represent current code. The phoboslab/qoi README itself has no numbers: it says compression is 'usually worse than libPNG' while 'throughput is a lot higher' and links qoiformat.org/benchmark (egress-blocked, not opened); its first-party qoibench.c benchmarks stbi, libpng and QOI. The fpng README (richgel999/fpng) measured QOI at 83.90 and 138.18 MP/s against stb_image and lodepng, not libpng. WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark (CLIC2021, i7-12700H, Windows 10, Pillow PNG rather than libpng, times include process startup) lists QOI at 19.061 compress and 18.970 decompress time vs PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 and 33.677 (lower is better, unit not stated).

name: Zpng
baseline: libpng

claimed_speedup: QOIR benchmark: ZPNG_Lossless encode 126.21 MPixels/s and decode 256.32 vs libpng 5.49 and 56.18 (about 23x and 4.6x, derived from page data) with smaller output (CmpRatio 0.2182 vs 0.2423, about 10% smaller, derived). README: takes less than 6% of a PNG compressor's time and produces a file 66% of the size (one 13.9 MB photo). WangXuan95 CLIC2021 shootout: ZPNG 25.909 s compress and 24.083 s decompress, 1,755,786,378 bytes vs Pillow PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes.

tradeoffs: Custom non-PNG format that needs Zstd (bundled in the repo). C API plus command-line tool, about 500 lines. Works best on photographic images. Author calls it experimental and does not expect others to use it.
caveats: Zpng is its own format (custom header plus zstd), not PNG-compatible. Compression trade-off: overall CmpRatio 0.2182 vs libpng 0.2423 (smaller), and smaller than libpng on every subset row checked (for example photo_kodak 0.4776 vs 0.5630, screenshot_web 0.0584 vs 0.0757), but WebP lossless is smaller still (0.1651). The libpng baseline (PNG/libpng row, 'Debian Bullseye's libpng' per the file's Notes) is the distro package driven through the simplified API: adapter/png_libpng_adapter.c calls png_image_write_to_memory with image.flags = 0, so PNG_IMAGE_FLAG_FAST is not set and libpng runs at its defaults (zlib default compression level, all-filters heuristic), i.e. its default compression level, not a speed-tuned setting. Timing in test/benchmarks.c: 5 repetitions per image with gettimeofday, single-threaded, allocation included; the harness does not compare decoded pixels with the source (no round-trip check). The WebP_Lossless row uses libpng for images with a dimension above 16383 px, and the WebP decode adapter adds a full-image memcpy. The measured code is nigeltao/qoir's vendored third_party/zpng/zpng.cpp, identical to catid/Zpng HEAD except for an added noFilter flag (and a header bit) used only by the ZPNG_NofilLsl variant; the adapter copies the output buffer once more in both encode and decode, which slightly penalizes ZPNG. name: CharLS
baseline: WebP lossless via Pillow 10.1.0 (libwebp, quality=100, method 1 and 5), Pillow PNG plugin (zlib, not libpng) and Pillow JPEG 2000 plugin (OpenJPEG), all run in-process in Image-Compression-Benchmark; the CharLS README separately cites the original HP JPEG-LS code, JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000
workload: Lossless compression and decompression of 585 CLIC2021 RGB 24-bit images (4.1 GB), single-threaded, total time and total size, using the CharLS-based pillow-jpls 1.3.2 plugin.
claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark, CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB; times in seconds, measured with time.time() in RunBenchmark.py): JPEG-LS (CharLS via pillow-jpls) compress 72.237 / decompress 66.567, size 1931584595 bytes. Versus WebP lossless m1 (libwebp) 720.160 / 37.044, 1496478650 bytes: about 10.0x faster compression but 1.8x slower decompression and 29% larger output (derived from page data); versus WebP lossless m5 1112.134 / 49.442: 15.4x faster compression, 1.35x slower decompression (derived from page data). Versus Pillow PNG (optimize=False, zlib) 334.791 / 33.677: 4.6x faster compression, about 2x slower decompression, slightly smaller output. Versus Pillow JPEG2000 (OpenJPEG) 319.912 / 275.398: 4.4x and 4.1x faster (derived from page data). CharLS README: 'about twice as fast as the original HP code, and beats both JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000 by a factor 3' (cites imagecompression.info, not opened).
compiler_and_flags: Python 3.9, Pillow 10.1.0, pillow-jpls 1.3.2 wheel (links CharLS 2.4.2 statically via Conan per its conanfile.txt); wheel compiler and flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10
tradeoffs: JPEG-LS (ISO/IEC 14495-1) is a lossless/near-lossless codec with low complexity; decode is about twice as slow as Pillow's PNG decode in the cited suite. README notes Hewlett Packard patents on JPEG-LS (licensed free for conformant implementations; some may have expired). No SIMD: speed comes from templates and traits.
caveats: The page does compare against a listed baseline: Pillow's WebP plugin is libwebp. Against it CharLS wins only on encode (about 10x vs WebP lossless with quality=100, which is libwebp's maximum-effort lossless setting) and loses on decode (1.8x slower) and ratio (29% larger). Pillow's PNG codec uses zlib directly rather than libpng, and Pillow's JPEG 2000 plugin is OpenJPEG. All Pillow-based rows (PNG, WebP, JPEG 2000, JPEG-LS) run in-process through exec() with the same PNM read/write overhead, so they are comparable to each other, while EXE-based codecs include per-file process startup. JPEG-XL -e1 (43.0 s / 57.7 s, smaller files) and QOI/fNBLI beat JPEG-LS on the same table, so CharLS is not the fastest lossless codec here. The README's 'twice as fast as HP code' claim rests on an unopened, dated imagecompression.info page. The 'JPEG-LS-ext' row is a different codec (ImCvt) and is not counted.

name: HALIC (High Availability Lossless Image Compression)
language: unknown (binaries only; README says built with GCC and Clang)
baseline: libwebp lossless (Pillow 10.1.0, method 1) and PNG (Pillow 10.1.0, optimize=False)
workload: Total compress and decompress time and compressed size on CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB) and GDCC2020 (100 RGB images, 1.0 GB) in the Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout, all codecs single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: CLIC2021: HALIC 1,473,481,803 bytes, 22.187 s compress, 28.447 s decompress versus WebP lossless m1 1,496,478,650 bytes, 720.160 s, 37.044 s (about 32x faster compress, 1.3x faster decompress, 1.5% smaller, derived) and PNG optimize=False 2,003,016,524 bytes, 334.791 s, 33.677 s (about 15x compress, 1.18x decompress, 26% smaller, derived). GDCC2020: HALIC 4.780 s compress and 5.426 s decompress versus PNG optimize=False 152.321 s and 11.545 s (about 32x and 2.1x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: most codecs are prebuilt Windows .exe files in the benchmark's codec folder, WebP and PNG run through Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0; commands are listed in the README (PNG: Image.open('in.pnm').save('out.png', optimize=False))
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700H, 16 GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10; every codec single-threaded, SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Binary releases only (Windows and Linux executables), PPM and PNM input, ANS (FSE) entropy coder with independent blocks, multithreading only from version 0.7 on. Compression ratio is behind JPEG XL, EMMA and NBLI; the 'HALIC fast' variant trades size for speed and failed to decompress one gray test image (zone_plate.pnm) in the benchmark.
caveats: The repository holds only README, LICENSE (MIT) and .gitignore; the releases (0.6.0 to 0.7.2) carry only Windows AVX/AVX2 .exe and static Linux binaries plus GitHub's automatic archives of that README-only tree, the author's HALIC-Image-Converter (GPL-3.0 Qt GUI) contains no codec source, and the benchmark's format table marks HALIC as not open source, so the code cannot be inspected or rebuilt and has_code is false even though the licence file says MIT. The measured binary is HALIC072e.exe/HALIC072d.exe from the benchmark's codec folder, with no compiler or flags. The PNG baseline is Pillow's zlib-based encoder (default level), not libpng, and WebP lossless also runs through Pillow 10.1.0 (method 1 and 5). The harness runs Pillow codecs in-process but launches HALIC as one process per image through os.system, so HALIC's times include process start-up and the comparison is conservative for HALIC. On tiny images PNG decodes faster (Kodak: PNG optimize=False 0.484 s versus HALIC 0.615 s), so the decode win shows only on large images. The benchmark author also wrote the competing NBLI/fNBLI codecs (fNBLI is smaller and decodes slightly faster than HALIC on CLIC2021). The author's own README charts carry no numbers.

name: meshoptimizer (vertex codec used as a lossless float-image compressor)
baseline: OpenEXR 3.4.0 ZIP compression at level 4 (deflate through OpenEXR's bundled libdeflate, OPENEXR_FORCE_INTERNAL_DEFLATE ON); the same harness also runs EXR RLE, PIZ, HTJ2K_32/HTJ2K_256 (OpenJPH inside OpenEXR) and libjxl lossless at efforts 1/3/4/7/8. No standalone zstd, fpzip or zfp baseline in this harness.
workload: Lossless round trip of 10 floating-point EXR images (3122.4 MB raw; RGB/RGBA half and float, multi-layer renders with up to 37 channels, two Poly Haven HDRIs) into and out of an in-memory stream. The meshoptimizer path ('Mop') splits pixels into 16K-pixel chunks, encodes each with meshopt_encodeVertexBufferLevel (vertex codec, levels 0-3, encoding version 1; pixels treated as vertices padded to a multiple of 4 bytes; no meshopt filters), optionally followed by a zstd pass (levels 1/3/10/20), chunks run in parallel on 16 threads; OpenEXR uses setGlobalThreadCount(16). Save and load times include container writing; every codec's output is checked bit-exact with CompareImages; best of 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: From img/win-ryzen5950x-20250908.html (Ryzen 9 5950X, 16 threads, 10 files 3122.4 MB, best of 3 runs): meshoptimizer vertex codec level 2 (Mop2) ratio 2.011 at 1.600 GB/s compress and 7.861 GB/s decompress versus EXR ZIP level 4 ratio 1.873 at 1.172 GB/s compress and 2.526 GB/s decompress, i.e. about 1.37x compression and 3.1x decompression throughput at a 7% better ratio (derived from page data). Mop1: 2.004 GB/s compress (1.71x, derived) and 8.016 GB/s decompress at ratio 1.966. Mop2 plus zstd level 1: ratio 2.248, 1.533 GB/s compress, 6.739 GB/s decompress. EXR HTJ2K_256: ratio 1.947, 0.709/1.045 GB/s; libjxl effort 7: ratio 2.180, 0.050/0.382 GB/s. On Apple M4 Max (img/mac-m4max-20250908.html): Mop2 3.104 GB/s compress and 14.808 GB/s decompress versus ZIP4 1.723 and 5.993 GB/s (1.80x and 2.47x, derived from page data). README conclusion: mesh optimizer is 'very far ahead of others towards top right of the chart'.

name: OpenJPH (HTJ2K encoder and decoder)
baseline: OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000 Part 1)
workload: dicom-codecs tests/main.cpp: each codec encodes the raw test image from dicom-codecs/test-data (US1-640-480-3-8-0, MR4-512-512-1-12-0, CT1-512-512-1-16-1, MG1-3064-4664-1-12-0) with its own encoder, then the timed loop decodes its own codestream once after one warm-up decode (iterations = 1). OpenJPH writes an HTJ2K (Part 15) codestream, reversible, RPCL, 64x64 code blocks, decomposition count chosen so the lowest level is at most 64 px (3 for US/MR/CT, 6 for MG), no colour transform; OpenJPEG writes a JPEG 2000 Part 1 J2K codestream, reversible, RPCL, 64x64 blocks, 5 decompositions, RCT on the colour image. Both are single-threaded and lossless; round trips are checked before timing.
claimed_speedup: dicom-codecs README (MacBook Pro M1 Pro), lossless decode time per image: OpenJPH 4.09 ms versus OpenJPEG 24.73 ms (8-bit color US 640x480), 1.43 versus 15.65 ms (12-bit gray MR 512x512), 1.53 versus 22.27 ms (16-bit gray CT 512x512), 89.20 versus 1447.63 ms (12-bit gray MG 3064x4664): about 6.0x, 10.9x, 14.6x and 16.2x (derived from page data). OpenJPH also beats CharLS JPEG-LS lossless (7.46, 3.14, 3.46, 212.92 ms; about 1.8x to 2.4x, derived) but Kakadu is faster still (1.13, 0.51, 0.64, 29.36 ms). Encode times are measured by the harness but not published in the README.
compiler_and_flags: build.sh: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, on arm64 also -DOJPH_DISABLE_INTEL_SIMD=ON; OpenJPEG compiled from source with -ffast-math in Release and threading stubbed out (MUTEX_stub); compiler not stated. Submodules pinned at OpenJPH 5aab43f and OpenJPEG 41c25e3 (updated 2023-12-14)
hardware: Apple MacBook Pro M1 Pro
stars_or_usage: 296 stars; packaged in several distributions per the README's repology badge
tradeoffs: Implements High-Throughput JPEG 2000 (Part 15, ITU-T T.814) only, with Part 1 wavelet and coding features reused; it cannot read ordinary Part 1 JPEG 2000 files, so adoption needs HTJ2K-encoded data. The HT block coder trades some compression ratio for speed.
caveats: The two libraries decode different codestreams: OpenJPH decodes HTJ2K (Part 15 block coder) while OpenJPEG decodes JPEG 2000 Part 1 (EBCOT/MQ coder), so most of the gap is the HT format rather than the library; OpenJPEG at the pinned commit also contains an HTJ2K decoder (ht_dec.c) but it was not timed on OpenJPH's stream. Settings differ slightly (decomposition levels 3 versus 5 on three images, RCT only for OpenJPEG on the colour image). Compressed sizes are not reported (the ratio printout is commented out), so the speed versus size trade-off is unknown. One iteration per case, compiler unstated, OpenJPH built with Intel SIMD disabled on arm64, OpenJPEG built single-threaded with -ffast-math. The dicom-codecs repository calls itself WIP (10 stars, last commit 2023-12-14). The libjpeg-turbo8 row (4.06 ms on the US image) is lossy baseline JPEG and not comparable. The OpenJPH README publishes no numbers of its own.

caveats: Snippet only: the paper could not be opened (arXiv, ar5iv, ADS, hgpu.org, encode.su, the Mainz HPC group page, Hugging Face and OpenAlex are all blocked here); benchmark_url is the arXiv PDF URL as it appears in search results, not opened. name: bc7enc (rgbcx BC1 and bc7enc16 BC7 encoders)
baseline: libsquish (BC1 cluster fit); Intel ispc_texcomp (BC7); also AMD Compressonator and DirectXTex CPU BC7
workload: Encoding 31 images (Kodak corpus plus others) to BC1 and BC7, comparing total encode time and average PSNR at matched quality settings (multithreaded with OpenMP).

BC7 (31 images, kodim plus others, multithreaded, encode time only), perceptual mode scored on REC709 luma PSNR: ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s 48.6 dB vs bc7enc16 uber0/max_partitions 64 38.3 s 49.6 dB (9.3x faster, derived from page data); ispc_texcomp fast 41.5 s 48.0 dB vs bc7enc16 uber0/16 20.8 s 49.3 dB (2.0x faster, derived from page data). Non-perceptual (RGB PSNR): ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s 46.8 dB vs bc7enc16 uber4/64 51 s 46.1 dB (7.0x faster at 0.7 dB lower, derived from page data); the later update at matched RGB PSNR shows parity: ispc_texcomp fast 41.45 s 46.09 dB vs latest bc7enc16 uber4/64 41.42 s 46.03 dB, or 38.78 s 45.94 dB with filterbank optimizations (1.07x, derived from page data); ultrafast: ispc_texcomp 1.9 s vs bc7enc16 3.8 s at 42.7 dB (ispc_texcomp 2x faster). DirectXTex CPU (locally patched) default 9485.1 s 45.6 dB vs bc7enc16 uber1/64 36 s 46.0 dB (263x faster, derived from page data); DirectXTex mode-6-only 466.4 s 41.9 dB vs bc7enc16 6.7 s 42.8 dB (70x faster, derived from page data).

hardware: dual Xeon workstation (CPU model not stated)

At matched RGB PSNR the later update shows parity with ispc_texcomp fast, and in the ultrafast rows ispc_texcomp is faster (1.9 s vs 3.8 s at 42.7 dB non-perceptual; 1.9 s vs 8.9 s perceptual, where bc7enc16 scores 48.4 vs 46.2 dB). The repo publishes no PNG or JPEG numbers.
compiler_and_flags: clang on macOS 12.5 (version and flags not stated); command lines not given. ECT defaults to single-threaded deflate (--mt-deflate is opt-in in src/main.cpp), so the ECT runs were probably single-threaded like zopfli, but the README does not say.

name: etcpak
baseline: Etc2Comp (effort=0, error metric rgba) and ETCPACK 4.0.1 (reference ETC2 encoder in Arm Mali Texture Compression Tool 4.3.0), as measured in the QuickETC2 paper (ACM TOG 2020); the current README only cites the NVIDIA in-driver ETC2 decoder (42.5 Mpx/s) for decompression, and the 2016-2018 README (etcpak 0.5) timed PVRTexToolCLI 3.5, Mali etcpack 4.2, etc2comp and crunch (rg-etc1) 1.04.
workload: Paper: compression of 64 test textures (256x256 to 8192x8192; 55 RGB, 9 RGBA) with each encoder at its fastest setting, highest-performance (16 threads, SIMD) and baseline-control (1 thread, no SIMD) settings, PSNR and SSIM reported. README: ETC1, ETC2, BC1, BC3 and BC7 compression and decompression of a non-public real-life RGBA 16K x 16K atlas, single-threaded and multithreaded.
claimed_speedup: QuickETC2 paper Table 1 (Ryzen 7 3700X, fastest settings, 55 RGB textures): etcpak 0.7 ETC1 3250 Mpx/s and ETC2 planar-only 1931 Mpx/s (16 threads, SIMD) vs Etc2Comp ETC2 3.8 Mpx/s (16 threads) and ETCPACK ETC2 1.4 Mpx/s (single-threaded); with one thread and SIMD disabled, etcpak ETC1 44.6 and ETC2(p) 28.9 Mpx/s vs Etc2Comp 3.1 and ETCPACK 1.4 Mpx/s. Ratios (derived from page data): ETC2(p) about 508x vs Etc2Comp and 1379x vs ETCPACK at highest-performance settings, 9.3x and 20.6x single-thread scalar. Quality is lower: etcpak ETC2(p) 36.82 dB PSNR vs 37.89 dB (Etc2Comp) and 38.09 dB (ETCPACK); etcpak ETC1 35.87 dB. The paper's SIGGRAPH 2020 talk table gives etcpak 0.6.1 1782 Mpix/s vs Etc2Comp 4.0 and ETCPACK 1.3 Mpix/s. First-party README (Ryzen 9 7950X, 16K x 16K atlas): ETC1 797 Mpx/s ST / 9613 MT, ETC2 356/6378, BC1 5730/10174, BC3 2437/8568, BC7 12.1/225; ETC2 decode 599 Mpx/s ST vs 'Nvidia in-driver ETC2 decoder can do only 42.5 Mpx/s' (about 14x, derived from page data; no machine given for the NVIDIA figure). Historical README table (etcpak 0.5, 2016, Xeon E3-1230 v3, 8192x8192 RGB): etcpak 0.5 AVX2 ETC1 872.6 Mpx/s vs crunch (rg-etc1) 1.04 11.53, etc2comp effort=0 1.96, PVRTexToolCLI 3.5 1.3 (total time including image decode) and Mali etcpack 4.2 0.777 Mpx/s.
hardware: QuickETC2 paper: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X @3.6 GHz, 8 cores with SMT, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04. README: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel i7 1185G7, Apple M3 Max (historical README: Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3).
stars_or_usage: 331 stars, 50 forks; README says it is used in production builds by millions of users; the QuickETC2 paper says Unity integrated etcpak (alongside ETCPACK and Etc2Comp) since Unity 2017.3
tradeoffs: Quality is explicitly not the goal ('best suited for rapid assets preparation during development, when graphics quality is not a concern'). Handles ETC1, ETC2, BC1-BC7 and decoding; Benchmarked on x86 (Ryzen, Intel) and Apple M3 Max.
caveats: Speed comes at lower quality: in the QuickETC2 paper etcpak's ETC2 mode is planar-only (no T- and H-modes at version 0.7), so it searches a smaller mode space than Etc2Comp and ETCPACK and scores about 1.1-1.3 dB lower PSNR; compare at matched quality before treating the ratios as like-for-like. In the paper's highest-performance setting ETCPACK ran single-threaded while etcpak used 16 threads; the single-thread scalar ratios (9.3x, 20.6x) are the fair algorithmic comparison. Compiler and flags are not stated anywhere; etcpak's CMakeLists.txt enables -march=native by default. The README's own benchmark (Application.cpp -b mode) uses a non-public atlas and times no competitor; the competitor table was removed from the README in 2018 and the NVIDIA decoder figure has no stated machine. The paper's numbers are for etcpak 0.7 / 0.6.1, not the current 2.1. BC1/BC3/BC7 speed claims have no competitor numbers.

name: fNBLI (NBLI lossless image codec)
baseline: PNG encoded and decoded through Pillow 10.1.0's own PNG codec (PngImagePlugin over Pillow's zlib-based 'zip' codec, not libpng), optipng 0.7.7 for optimized PNG encoding, and libwebp lossless via Pillow 10.1.0
workload: Single-threaded lossless compression and decompression of the CLIC2021 training set (585 RGB 24-bit .pnm images, 4.1 GB) and six other datasets, timed per dataset with file I/O included, in the author's Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout (RunBenchmark.py, which checks the round trip is lossless).
claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark README, CLIC2021 totals (585 images, 4.1 GB, single-threaded): fNBLI 43.164 s compress, 27.450 s decompress, 1,337,587,020 bytes; Pillow PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes; PNG optipng -o2 4395.069 s, 26.625 s, 1,905,215,734 bytes; Pillow WebP lossless m5 1112.134 s, 49.442 s, 1,475,908,700 bytes. That is 7.8x faster encode and 1.23x faster decode than Pillow PNG with 33% smaller files, and 25.8x faster encode and 1.80x faster decode than WebP lossless m5 with 9% smaller files (derived from page data); decoding is slightly slower than optipng-optimized PNG (27.450 s vs 26.625 s at -o2 and 25.799 s at -o5). NBLI README restates these as fNBLI 94.8 MB/s compress and 149.1 MB/s decompress, 29.79% smaller than optipng PNG, vs PNG 12.2 / 121.5 MB/s and WebP -5 3.7 / 82.8 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Prebuilt fNBLI.exe v0.4 (banner 'v0.4, 202409', needs AVX2); compiler and flags for that binary are not stated, and the README gives a build command (g++ -O3 -static) only for the NBLI prototype in src/NBLI, not for src/fNBLI. Baselines: Pillow 10.1.0 on Python 3.9, optipng 0.7.7.
hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10, single-threaded with SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Custom non-PNG format for 8-bit gray and 24-bit RGB; GPL-3.0 (copyleft); fNBLI needs AVX2. The slower prototype NBLI (-g, 14.7 MB/s compress, 17.0 MB/s decompress) compresses to -30.37% but decodes far slower than PNG. Includes PNG and PNM input.
caveats: Author-run benchmark of the author's own codec. The timing harness is asymmetric: Pillow codecs run in-process through exec(), while fNBLI.exe is launched with os.system once per image, so fNBLI also pays process start-up per file (this handicaps fNBLI, not the baselines). The PNG baseline is Pillow's own zlib-based PNG codec, not libpng. Decoding is not faster than optipng-optimized PNG (27.450 s vs 26.625 s / 25.799 s on CLIC2021). The fNBLI source was published on 2026-07-18 (commit 6561fc8, 2,804 added lines under src/fNBLI including AVX2 and rANS code) and carries the same 'v0.4, 202409' banner as the benchmarked binary, but the binary predates the source, the README still links fNBLI.exe, the shootout's format table still marks fNBLI as not open source, and there is no build recipe for it, so binary-to-source correspondence is unverified. Single benchmark machine (i7-12700H, Windows 10).

name: gif_load
baseline: giflib 5.2.2 (also stb_image)
workload: Wall-time decode of every frame of 6 synthetic animated GIFs (320x240 x100, 640x480 x200, 1920x1080 x150; flat shapes and incompressible noise), file read into RAM with read() or mmap(), cold and warm page cache.
claimed_speedup: README tables (best of two runs, wall time in ms): warm cache, gif_load read() beats giflib 5.2.2 stream by 1.28x-1.72x and mmap() by 1.42x-1.78x (derived from page data; README says 1.3x-1.7x), and beats stb_image by 1.4x-2.5x per the README (derived from page data: 1.39x-2.42x for the +RGBA rows, which composite like stb_image), e.g. 1080p shapes 668 ms (read) vs giflib stream 1149 ms vs stb_image 1829 ms. Cold cache vs giflib stream: 1.3x-1.5x faster on the 3 shape GIFs (derived from page data: 1.42x-1.51x with read()) but slower on the 3 noise GIFs; the README states 0.83x-0.85x, while its own table gives 0.89x-0.91x with read() and 0.75x-0.79x with mmap() (derived from page data). Author says the 1.3x-1.5x cold claim also holds on real giphy GIFs (no numbers). Peak memory: one frame plus a 16 KB code table; at 1080p giflib slurp holds 296 MB and stb_image 1254-1611 MB, while giflib stream holds a single row and is lower than gif_load.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5 -O2, Linux 6.4
hardware: CPU model not stated (RAM latency 128 ns, 8 GB/s sequential read, EXT4 cold disk read 342 MB/s)
tradeoffs: Whole file must be in memory before decoding (cannot overlap I/O with decode, which is why cold noise cases lose to giflib). Callback API, header-only, under 300 lines, no libc dependency apart from realloc. Interlaced GIFs are the caller's job to unwind (giflib's DGifSlurp does it). Public-domain dedication (no patent grant).
caveats: The README says 'take everything below with a grain of salt' and that the harness is not published, so the numbers are not reproducible from the repo; no CPU model is given (only RAM latency 128 ns, 8 GB/s sequential read, EXT4 cold read 342 MB/s); synthetic GIFs only; best of two runs; timing includes file acquisition. The README's cold-cache noise ratio (0.83x-0.85x) does not match its own table. Work is comparable only because the test GIFs are not interlaced: gif_load leaves deinterlacing to the caller while giflib DGifSlurp does it; the plain rows return palette indices, so only the +RGBA rows match stb_image's composited output. giflib stream uses less memory than gif_load. Recent fixes landed around the measurement: int32 overflow and null-palette fix (2026-09-27) and a 1-byte out-of-bounds read at GIF_EHDM (2026-10-01, after the numbers were published). Public-domain dedication (Unlicense text in gif_load.h): no patent grant.

name: giflib-turbo
baseline: giflib
workload: GIF LZW decoding through the unchanged giflib API; the decoder uses the output image buffer as the LZW dictionary instead of a linked-list string table.
claimed_speedup: First-party source comment in gif_lib.c (DecodeLZW): 2.5x to 30x faster than giflib, with no harness, machine, test images or giflib version. The author's blocked blog post 'A Big Memory GIF Decoder' (2021-03) is summarised by search snippets as 2x/5x/20x.
stars_or_usage: 39 stars; drop-in for giflib, which is packaged in vcpkg and Conan
tradeoffs: Uses more RAM than giflib (the author's own description: 'It uses more RAM, but you get more speed'); the README lists possible security vulnerabilities and CPU incompatibilities as not yet tested, and says it may take a long time before big projects adopt it.
caveats: Snippet only and unverified: the 2x/5x/20x figures come from a WebSearch summary of the blocked blog post 'A Big Memory GIF Decoder' (2021-03); the '2.5x to 30x' figure comes from a deepwiki machine summary (blocked). The README, repo page and the AnimatedGIF wiki (which describes the same Turbo-mode idea) contain no numbers. Repo harness: the Makefile builds gif_test_old (system giflib from /opt/homebrew, -lgif) and gif_test_new (this gif_lib.c), both with gcc -O3, but test.c has no timing code, its 100-iteration DGifSlurp/EGifSpew decode and re-encode loop is unreachable because main() returns right after DoGifWedge(), and the Makefile references gifwedge.c, gifsponge.c and getarg.c that are not in the repo. No CPU, compiler version, giflib version or test images are stated. The README itself names possible security vulnerabilities and CPU incompatibilities as open risks; the decoder parses untrusted GIF input and has only 10 commits (last 2024-03-22). Only decoding speed is claimed. [retier] Number is a source-code comment with no setup. Memory safety from code reading (not run): the frame buffer is W*H+8 rounded up to 64 KiB but 256 root-dictionary bytes are written after W*H, so valid GIFs whose W*H mod 65536 falls in 65281-65528 (for example 300x218) overflow the heap; DecodeLZW ignores iLZWSize and reads past the file buffer; sub-block and extension parsing is unbounded; the LZW code size is unchecked; a file descriptor is closed twice; mallocs are unchecked. Partial drop-in only: DGifOpen is a stub returning NULL, the DGifGet* functions are absent, and six declared functions (GCB helpers, EGifPutExtension, GifFreeSavedImages) are undefined.
found_via: giflib is a vcpkg and Conan port; WebSearch 'giflib-turbo GIF decoder faster than giflib SIMD github' surfaced the drop-in replacement; repo page and commits opened on github.com

verification.tier_reason: No page that could be opened carries a number: the README, repo root and the author's AnimatedGIF wiki only say giflib-turbo is faster, and the 5x/20x figures appear only in a WebSearch summary of the blocked blog post. name: Goofy (realtime DXT1/ETC1 encoder)
baseline: stb_dxt (ryg DXT1, STB_DXT_NORMAL); also rgbcx 1.08, icbc 1.0 and rg_etc1 1.04
workload: Single-thread compression of the repo's 42 test images (24 Kodak images, lena, baboon, monarch, peppers, sail, tulips, parrot_red, patterns, five PBR textures including a normal map, six Roblox images; list in Src/main.cpp), best of 128 runs per image, averaged speed (MP/s) and RGB-PSNR, each encoder at its fastest or lowest-quality setting.
claimed_speedup: Goofy DXT1 1429 MP/s at 37.02 dB vs rgbcx v1.08 level 0 60 MP/s (40.85 dB), ryg stb_dxt 43 MP/s (40.82 dB), icbc v1.0 24 MP/s (41.00 dB); Goofy ETC1 1221 MP/s (36.30 dB) vs rg_etc1 v1.04 3 MP/s (40.87 dB). Ratios derived from page data: about 24x vs rgbcx, 33x vs stb_dxt, 60x vs icbc, 407x vs rg_etc1.
hardware: i7-7820HQ 2.9 GHz, single thread, fastest of 128 runs
tradeoffs: Speed over quality by design: about 37.0 dB RGB-PSNR for DXT1 versus roughly 40.8-41.0 dB for the compared encoders (only 3.6 dB above the downsample-to-RGB565 baseline at 33.39 dB). One heuristic, DXT1 and ETC1s only, poor on normal maps; DXT5 and ETC2 alpha are future work. Header-only, needs SSE2 (NEON not implemented).
caveats: Speed-quality trade, not equal quality: the compared encoders score about 3.8-4.6 dB higher RGB-PSNR (Goofy DXT1 37.02 dB vs 40.82-41.00 dB; Goofy ETC1 36.30 dB vs rg_etc1 40.87 dB), and Goofy's ETC1 output is restricted to the ETC1S subset, so it does less search work than rg_etc1. The harness (Src/main.cpp) calls icbc::init_dxt1(), rgbcx::encode_bc1_init() and rg_etc1::pack_etc1_block_init() inside every timed call, so those competitors' times include one-time table setup; the stb_dxt wrapper has no such call, so the 33x ratio vs stb_dxt is the cleanest. Compiler and flags are not stated (the repo ships a VS2017 Win64 CMake generator script and CI builds Release with MSVC, GCC and Clang, but the README does not say which build produced the table). test-results/ holds only keep_me.txt, so no raw result files are published. Not suited to normal maps per the README.
found_via: github.com/topics/texture-compression?l=c%2B%2B page led to SergeyMakeev/Goofy; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

verification.tier_reason: First-party README table on a named CPU (i7-7820HQ, single thread, best of 128) with public benchmark code (Src/main.cpp times Goofy, stb_dxt, rgbcx, icbc and rg_etc1 on 42 test images and averages PSNR and time), but compiler and flags are not stated, so not A; no independent measurement found.

name: LERC (Limited Error Raster Compression)
baseline: zlib deflate level 9 (labelled 'LZW' in the benchmark document; called through compress2)
workload: Tile-by-tile (max tile 1024) encode and decode of geospatial rasters with LERC against zlib compress2 level 9: four 4600x4300 float scientific rasters and two interpolated float DTED surfaces (3612x3612 and 10812x10812), lossy only (MaxZError 0.01 to 1.0); four DTED-1 (1201x1201) and four DTED-2/ASTER (3601x3601) 16-bit elevation tiles, lossless and at MaxZError 5; six multispectral 11/16-bit aerial and satellite images (UltraCam, QuickBird, RapidEye), lossless and at MaxZError 2 and 4.
claimed_speedup: From doc/LercBenchmarks_Feb_2016.pdf, times against zlib compress2 level 9 (labelled 'LZW'), tiled at 1024. Lossless (MaxZError 0) rows only: DTED-2 16-bit 3601x3601, average encode 231 ms vs 2484 ms and decode 51 ms vs 130 ms (about 10.8x and 2.5x, derived from page data); DTED-1 16-bit 1201x1201, encode 23 ms vs 274 ms and decode 7 ms vs 16 ms (about 11.9x and 2.3x, derived from page data); multispectral 11/16-bit images, encode 2.4 s vs 30.5 s and decode 0.7 s vs 1.8 s (about 12.7x and 2.6x, derived from page data; the document's prose says 'the much faster encoding speed of 5-10x'). Lossless compression-ratio averages are 5.1 vs 4.2, 6.2 vs 5.8 and 2.1 vs 1.8, but zlib compresses better on the flat Georgia tiles (4.9 vs 4.6 and 7.1 vs 5.3). Lossy rows (not the same work as lossless zlib): float scientific rasters at MaxZError 0.01 encode 0.3 s vs 8.1 s and decode 68 ms vs 424 ms; interpolated float DTED surfaces at 0.01 encode 0.4 s vs 4.3 s and 3.4 s vs 40.5 s. README: encode about 20-30 ms and decode about 5 ms per megapixel per band (no machine stated).
stars_or_usage: 215 stars; vcpkg port lerc and Conan recipe lerc; README says it is used in Esri software
tradeoffs: Special-purpose raster codec for 16-bit and larger or float data with a bounded per-pixel error (MaxZError); lossless only for integer types with MaxZError 0 and only slightly better ratio than zlib there. The README itself says PNG can compress 8-bit data better.
caveats: LERC is lossy-by-tolerance: the caller sets MaxZError, and only MaxZError 0 is lossless, so only the DTED-1, DTED-2 and multispectral LERC (0) columns do the same work as lossless zlib. All float-raster rows were run lossy (0.01 to 1.0), since lossless float/double compression only arrived in LERC 4.0 (2022-07-15). The PDF dates from 2016-02-23, before LERC 1.0 (2016-11-30), so it measured a much older codec than the current Lerc2 v6. It states no CPU, OS, compiler or flags; the benchmark driver and the ZLibAccess.h wrapper are not in the repo, and the large test rasters (UltraCam, QuickBird, RapidEye, DTED and ASTER tiles) are not in testData/, so the run cannot be reproduced. The baseline is zlib level 9 (its slowest level) on raw samples with no TIFF predictor; the PDF says level 6 gave a similar overall picture but gives no level-6 numbers. Not a general photographic codec; for 8-bit data the README says PNG can compress better.

name: libjpeg-turbo
baseline: IJG libjpeg (libjpeg 6b reference)
workload: JPEG compression and decompression on systems with common CPU architectures, SIMD-accelerated Huffman and DCT paths.
claimed_speedup: README: 'generally 2-6x as fast as libjpeg, all else being equal' on systems with SIMD; on other systems it 'can still outperform libjpeg by a significant amount' thanks to optimized Huffman coding. ChangeLog.md (1.5 beta1, AltiVec SIMD): compression about 3-4x and decompression about 2-2.5x faster relative to libjpeg v6b on PowerPC. Search snippet only (libjpeg-turbo.org/About/Performance, blocked): 2.1-6.0x as fast as libjpeg across platforms; versus libjpeg v6b 3.47-6.00x for compression and 2.08-3.43x for decompression on x86-64 Linux, measured with tjbench (Mpixels/sec) using a TurboJPEG wrapper built against libjpeg v6b and v8d.
tradeoffs: Drop-in libjpeg API and ABI plus the simpler TurboJPEG API; SIMD per architecture (x86, ARM and others); the README lists performance pitfalls: decompression can drop by as much as 20% (still far above libjpeg) for JPEGs with restart markers, and compression can drop by as much as 40% when the fast integer forward DCT is used at JPEG quality 98 to 100.
caveats: First-party claim. The detailed tables (machines, compilers, libjpeg v6b and v8d baselines measured with tjbench through a TurboJPEG wrapper) are on https://libjpeg-turbo.org/About/Performance, which is blocked from this environment, so the per-platform numbers come from a search snippet only and were not checked against the page. libjpeg-turbo is itself one of this category's listed baselines; it is recorded here against the IJG libjpeg incumbent it replaced (zlib-ng precedent). The 2-6x figure dates from the libjpeg v6b/v8 era and says nothing about how it compares with newer decoders. Independent runs that do not use IJG libjpeg as baseline: gereoffy/jpeg-nitro README table (Intel i9 13th gen) has libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (AVX2) at 124 ms per image versus stb_image 175 ms and Wuffs 159 ms; google/decoder-benchmarks-for-rust (2.6 GHz 6-core Intel Core i7, macOS) has turbojpeg at 84.25 ms versus the Rust jpeg-decoder crate at 126.2 ms on venice-2000x3000.jpg. LICENSE.md now describes two licenses (IJG for the libjpeg API library, Modified BSD for TurboJPEG) with SIMD code under Zlib and components under libpng-2.0 and BSD-2-Clause; the README still says three.

baseline: libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (decode) and 3.2.0 (encode)
workload: JPEG decode (TurboJPEG-style decompress to RGB, quality 75) of in-repo fixtures tests/fixtures/photo_*.jpg from 64x64 to 3840x2160 at 4:2:0, 4:2:2 and 4:4:4 (the 640x480 4:2:0 row is gradient_640x480.jpg), and encode of the same set at 320x240 to 1920x1080; Rust vs C in microseconds per image on Intel i5-10400, AMD EPYC 7763/9V74 runners and Apple M1 Pro.
claimed_speedup: README decode table, Intel i5-10400 vs C libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2: time ratios 0.77x (320x240 4:2:0), 0.87x (1280x720 4:2:0), 0.90x (1920x1080 4:2:0), 0.93x (2560x1440), 0.88x (3840x2160), but 1.23x (64x64) and 1.05x (640x480 4:2:0), i.e. about 3 to 23% faster on most sizes. Encode on Zen 3 and Zen 4 runners: stock build is 1.05 to 1.10x C 3.2.0's time at 1080p (slower); the target-cpu=native i5-10400 build is 2 to 7% faster than C 3.1.2. Apple M1 Pro: 0.99 to 1.07x of C.
compiler_and_flags: Decode table: stock cargo build --release (Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true), runtime AVX2/SSE2 dispatch; rustc version and the C libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 build not stated. Encode portable table: rustc 1.98.1, no RUSTFLAGS, C harness compiled with cc -O2 against the official libjpeg-turbo 3.2.0 .deb (perf-portable-vs-native.yml). Supplementary i5-10400 encode table: RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native.
hardware: Intel Core i5-10400 @ 2.90GHz (turbo off); AMD EPYC 7763 (Zen 3) and Zen 4 GitHub runners; Apple M1 Pro
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust port of libjpeg-turbo with NEON, AVX2, SSE2 and WASM SIMD128 kernels, byte-for-byte cross-validated against C in CI; ships C ABI shims (TurboJPEG 3 and libjpeg-compatible) so C++ can link it. MSRV 1.87. Lossless transforms and progressive supported.
caveats: Pure-Rust reimplementation (port) of libjpeg-turbo, not an FFI binding: no C dependency, byte-for-byte cross-validated against C in CI. Under the ports rule it may fold into libjpeg-turbo (zlib-rs precedent); it is listed here because it is measured against the original. First-party harness, tiny project (9 stars); recent commits are co-authored by Claude. The x86_64 decode win (README table, i5-10400 turbo off, C 3.1.2) is 3 to 23% on most sizes but 64x64 (1.23x) and the 640x480 gradient (1.05x) lose; that table is undated and does not state rustc or the C build. An earlier report on the same CPU (experiments/x86_64_avx2_final_report.md, 2026-04-12) gives different absolute times but the same direction (0.83 to 0.98x on most cases, progressive 0.83 to 0.91x). The stock portable encoder is 1.05 to 1.10x C 3.2.0's time at 1080p on Zen 3/Zen 4 runners (slower); only the target-cpu=native i5-10400 build beats C 3.1.2 by 2 to 7%. Apple M1 Pro: decode 0.99 to 1.07x, encode 1.03 to 1.07x of C (not faster). README says no memory-safety guarantee yet (unsafe SIMD under audit) and the classic libjpeg ABI is experimental.

The repository's lodepng_benchmark.cpp is the stock lodepng benchmark: it includes only lodepng.h and times lodepng encode/decode, so nothing in the repo measures libpng. A stated ratio without methodology is tier C.

name: MANGO image codecs
baseline: libpng (via find_module(PNG), version and zlib build not stated); 'libjpeg' is whatever jpeglib.h find_module(JPEG) linked, used through the libjpeg API one scanline at a time. Every current install path in docs/installation/setup.md and vcpkg.json installs libjpeg-turbo, but the library used for the i9-8950HK table run is not recorded.
workload: One timed run per library on one image each: PNG decode from memory and RGBA8 encode to a file (2560x1600 and 4833x5875 PNGs on an i7-11800H); JPEG decode from file and encode to file (5184x3456 and 2560x1600 JPEGs on an i9-8950HK). Milliseconds per image plus output size.
claimed_speedup: README tables: PNG decode 3.2 ms vs libpng 57.3 ms (2560x1600) and 53.7 ms vs 379.5 ms (4833x5875); PNG encode 57.2 ms vs 820.5 ms and 287.0 ms vs 14051.3 ms; JPEG decode 23.3 ms vs libjpeg 197.8 ms (5184x3456) and 3.2 ms vs 32.9 ms (2560x1600); JPEG encode 18.5 ms vs 70.1 ms and 4.3 ms vs 16.3 ms. That is about 18x PNG decode and 8.5x JPEG decode on the first image of each pair (derived from page data). Mango ran its default multi-threaded path; the baselines ran single-threaded.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README runs. Repository defaults: CMake Release build, ENABLE_SSE4 on and AVX/AVX2 off for the mango library, and png_benchmark adds -mavx2 -mpclmul on x86.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30GHz (PNG tables); Intel Core i9-8950HK @ 2.90GHz (JPEG tables)
tradeoffs: Large C++20 graphics library (vector math, SIMD abstraction, virtual filesystem, Vulkan text) with image codecs inside, not a standalone codec. Mango's PNG encode output is larger than libpng's (3531 KB vs 2843 KB on the first image) and its JPEG output is slightly larger than libjpeg's.
caveats: Both benchmark programs run mango multi-threaded by default (g_option_multithread / args.multithread = true, --nomt to disable) against single-threaded libpng and libjpeg, and no single-threaded mango numbers are published. The PNG decode figures most likely apply to mango-written files: mango's encoder by default (ImageEncodeOptions::parallel = true) writes a custom pLLD chunk with independently compressed segments, its decoder then takes the parallel decode_plld path, and both test images have an input size equal to mango's own encoded size (3531 KB and 33598 KB). Ordinary PNGs go through the single-stream decode_std path, so the 18x decode lead does not carry over to arbitrary PNGs. In PNG encode mango uses zlib level 4 with parallel segments against libpng defaults, and its output is about 24% larger on the first image (3531 vs 2843 KB) and 19% larger on the second (33598 vs 28180 KB) (derived from page data). In JPEG encode libjpeg runs at quality 95 and mango at quality 0.70. Each library is timed once, including file I/O. png_benchmark prints the fractional digit as microseconds mod 10 rather than tenths of a millisecond (cosmetic, under 0.1 ms). Commit 2a974fb (2026-09-29) fixed a wrong-operand bug in the SSE/AVX2/AVX-512 JPEG iDCT that produced incorrect output, and 17c019c fixed the NEON iDCT; whether that bug was present when the JPEG tables were measured is not established (jpeg_idct.cpp was refactored on 2026-08-15). The two table pairs use different CPUs, and the README itself quotes randy408 (the libspng author's handle): 'I'm skeptical of those benchmarks.' The license is the standard zlib text under a 'MANGO' header; bundled third-party code was not audited.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'github image codec faster than libjpeg-turbo OR faster than libpng ...' surfaced LibMango as a JPEG codec faster than libjpeg-turbo; README opened
Prior knowledge of C++ image libraries (not surfaced by a search query); opened the t0rakka/mango github.com page, README, license and commits page

verification.tier_reason: All README table numbers match the record and come from public first-party programs examples/image/png_benchmark/png_benchmark.cpp and examples/image/jpeg_benchmark/jpeg_benchmark.cpp with the CPU named, but the compiler and the exact flags used for the README runs are not stated, so it falls short of A and stays C.
verification.notes: Numbers are real and code-backed, but the headline gaps come mostly from multi-threading plus mango's own parallel-segment PNG layout (the test PNGs appear to be mango-encoded), and JPEG encode compares different quality settings; the enricher should say so. The JPEG baseline is most likely libjpeg-turbo going by the current build docs, but the README run's library is unrecorded. Recent iDCT correctness fixes (2026-09-29) should be noted; no evidence ties them to the 8950HK numbers.

corrected_fields.baseline: libpng and libjpeg (version not stated in README; possibly libjpeg-turbo)
corrected_fields.workload: Decode and encode time in milliseconds of one 2560x1600 and one 4833x5875 PNG, and one 5184x3456 and one 2560x1600 JPEG, against libpng, lodepng, stb, spng, fpng, Wuffs and libjpeg, toojpeg.
corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: README table, 2560x1600 PNG: mango decode 3.2 ms vs libpng 57.3 ms (about 18x, derived from page data) and encode 57.2 ms vs 820.5 ms (about 14x, derived). 4833x5875 PNG: decode 53.7 vs 379.5 ms, encode 287.0 vs 14051.3 ms. JPEG 5184x3456: decode 23.3 vs libjpeg 197.8 ms (about 8.5x, derived), encode 18.5 vs 70.1 ms (about 3.8x, derived). JPEG 2560x1600: decode 3.2 vs 32.9 ms, encode 4.3 vs 16.3 ms.
