Mango's decode may use multiple threads; not stated. In both PNG tables the mango output size equals the quoted input file size (3531 KB and 33598 KB), so the input PNGs may themselves be mango-produced, which could favour its decoder. README quotes a sceptical comment from libspng's author.

name: msf_gif
language: C (single header, compiles as C99 or C++98)
baseline: gif.h (Charlie Tangora's single-header encoder, named gif_h in the timings file) and jo_gif
workload: Encoding the author's sample animations (in/ directory of msf_gif-testing; test.cpp lists 13 clips such as bouncy 576x360x417 frames and tiles 384x240x625 frames, quality 16, alpha threshold 128). timings.txt itself does not state the input set, so it is not certain that these are the clips behind the totals.
claimed_speedup: README: 'uses SSE where available to encode at hundreds of megabytes a second, several times faster than comparable gif libraries'. msf_gif-testing timings.txt (nine lines, first-party): jo_gif2 ~1160 s, jo_gif ~425 s, gif_h dithered ~315 s, gif_h dithered 7bpp ~240 s, gif_h ~75 s, msf_gif ~14 s, msf_gif simd ~8 s, msf_gif threaded ~4 s, msf_gif simd threaded ~2 s. Single-threaded scalar msf_gif vs gif_h: 5.4x undithered, 22.5x vs gif_h dithered (msf_gif always dithers, so the dithered line is the closer match); vs jo_gif 30x; single-threaded SSE build vs gif_h 9.4x (all derived from page data). The threaded lines compare multi-threaded msf_gif against single-threaded baselines and do not correspond to the shipped single-threaded library. No numbers against giflib, gifski or ffmpeg were found (gifski comparison is a TODO in notes.txt).
compiler_and_flags: msf_gif-testing build.sh / build.bat: clang -march=native -std=c++17 -Os (MSVC /Ox and /O2 configs commented out); timings.txt does not say which configuration produced it
license: Dual: MIT or Unlicense-style public-domain dedication (text at the bottom of msf_gif.h)
tradeoffs: Uses one fixed constant-quality palette-and-dither scheme per frame instead of adaptive quantization; delta encoding between frames for smaller files. SSE on x86 only (NEON listed as a TODO). Public domain, also available under MIT.
caveats: timings.txt is a nine-line first-party note with no hardware, date, compiler or input description, and the gif_h/jo_gif timing code is not in the public msf_gif-testing repo (test.cpp times msf_gif only). The label gif_h is presumably Charlie Tangora's gif.h, but the file does not say. The 'threaded' rows describe a multithreaded variant that the shipped msf_gif.h v2.4 does not contain (notes.txt says multithreading was left out), so only the ~14 s scalar and ~8 s SSE rows describe the library as published. Output size and quality differ between encoders (msf_gif uses a fixed constant-quality palette with ordered dithering and inter-frame delta encoding; the README's smaller-file and quality claims come with no size or PSNR numbers against gif.h or jo_gif). A Handmade Network post (blocked here, search snippet only) cites about 500 MB/s average and 300 MB/s worst case on an unnamed laptop, with no baseline. A gifski comparison is a TODO in notes.txt. The public-domain alternative has no patent grant.

name: mtpng (parallel PNG encoder with C API)
baseline: libpng
workload: Re-encoding a dual-4K screenshot PNG at default options, single-threaded and multi-threaded, compared with libpng built by gcc and clang.
claimed_speedup: docs/perf.md 'Old performance data' (2018-era), dual-4K screenshot at default options. Single-threaded vs libpng: MacBook Pro 2015 Linux x86_64 libpng gcc 850 ms vs mtpng 555 ms (1.53x); macOS libpng clang 943 ms vs 563 ms (1.67x); Xeon E5520 Linux libpng gcc 1695 ms vs 1124 ms (1.51x); Raspberry Pi 3B+ aarch64 4692 ms vs 4311 ms (1.09x); Raspberry Pi 3B+ armhf 5368 ms vs 6068 ms (mtpng 0.88x, slower). Multi-threaded vs single-threaded libpng: MacBook Linux 2 threads 302 ms (2.81x), 4 threads with HT 248 ms (3.43x); Xeon E5520 8 threads 165 ms (10.3x), 16 threads 155 ms (10.9x); Pi 3B+ armhf 4 threads 1875 ms (2.86x), aarch64 4 threads 1416 ms (3.31x). All ratios derived from page data; the 1.0x/1.8x/2.2x factors printed on the page are mtpng thread scaling relative to mtpng on one thread, not ratios against libpng. README: single-threaded ~30-40% faster than libpng (Rust 1.29.0, 26 Sept 2018). The '2026 data' section has mtpng times only (e.g. Apple M3 Max 237 ms on 1 thread, 23 ms on 16; Ryzen 9 5950X Linux 301 ms on 1 thread, 25 ms on 32) and no libpng column.
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release (Rust); libpng built with gcc or clang, versions and zlib not stated
hardware: MacBook Pro 13in 2015, 5th-gen Core i7 3.1 GHz, 2 cores plus Hyper-Threading (libpng comparison); several newer machines for mtpng-only timings
tradeoffs: Encoder only; input must be pre-packed pixels. Compression ratio is a tiny fraction worse than libpng at the default 256 KiB chunk size (closer with larger chunks). Files under 128 KiB uncompressed see no threading gain. Rust library with a C API that the README says is still unstable; pulls libz_sys. Small-file and ancillary-chunk support needs work.
caveats: perf.md says '@fixme how did I measure those libpng times? need to recreate that', so the libpng baseline has no published harness, version, zlib build or flags, and all libpng numbers date from 2018. The work differs from libpng: mtpng's adaptive filter scores only Sub/Up/Average/Paeth (src/filter.rs filter_adaptive), while libpng 1.6's default PNG_ALL_FILTERS selection also scores None (pngwutil.c png_write_find_filter); the README says a 0.3.5 change (crates.io 2021-04-22, after these timings) altered the heuristic to match libpng in some cases, so the timed builds chose filters differently from libpng on the screenshot input. Deflate runs in independent 256 KiB chunks, which the README says compresses a tiny fraction worse than libpng. Multi-threaded rows are many threads against single-threaded libpng. On 32-bit ARM mtpng is slower than libpng single-threaded. The repository now lives at github.com/bvibber/mtpng (brion/mtpng redirects); crates.io's latest published version is 0.4.1 while the repo is at 0.5.0.
found_via: github.com/topics/png-encoder page listed brion/mtpng; README and docs/perf.md read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: oxipng
baseline: OptiPNG
workload: hyperfine wall-clock time to optimize one repository test PNG (tests/files/rgb_16_should_be_grayscale_8.png) without writing output (oxipng -P versus optipng -simulate) at the default level and at -o4; the independent op111.net blog adds web images (d3js.org.png, powertoys.png) at default and maximum settings.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark (tags v9.0.0 through v10.0.0): Oxipng 9.0.0 versus OptiPNG 0.7.7 on one test image, hyperfine wall clock, Intel Core i7-12700: default level 59.6 ms versus 132.4 ms ('2.22 +/- 0.29 times faster'); -o4 88.7 ms versus 444.9 ms ('5.01 +/- 0.25 times faster'). CPU time is closer at -o4: user 270.3 ms versus 444.8 ms, about 1.65x (derived from page data). Older run in the same README (oxipng 5.0.0, AMD Ryzen 7 4800H, rustc 1.55.0-nightly): 1.97x at default and 5.16x at -o4. Independent op111.net blog, search snippet only: d3js.org.png default oxipng 0.764 s for 29.14% reduction versus optipng 2.638 s for 25.42% (about 3.5x, derived from snippet data); powertoys.png 0.266 s for 17.62% versus 0.960 s for 5.85% (about 3.6x, derived from snippet data).
compiler_and_flags: Oxipng: rustc 1.74.0-nightly (7b4d9e155 2023-09-28), cargo release profile from Cargo.toml at commit c16519b (lto = "thin", strip = "symbols", default opt-level 3), default features including parallel (rayon). OptiPNG 0.7.7 as packaged by Debian unstable (distribution build flags).
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700 (8 performance cores, 4 efficiency cores, 20 threads), DDR5-5200 dual channel, Linux 6.5.0-2-amd64 (README run); op111 blog hardware unknown (page blocked).
tradeoffs: Rust command-line tool and library (not a C or C++ API); multithreaded by design, the README says it began as a Rust rewrite of OptiPNG to add multithreading. Optimizes existing PNG/APNG files, it is not a general encoder. Higher levels and --zopfli are slow.
caveats: Rust, not C++ (the search's C++ language filter does not match); OptiPNG is not one of the category's listed baselines (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif). The README benchmark is first-party, uses a single small test image, does not report output sizes, and was removed from the README after v10.0.0 in favor of a link to the op111.net blog. Most of the wall-clock gain comes from multithreading on a 20-thread CPU against single-threaded OptiPNG (user CPU time at -o4 is only about 1.65x lower); oxipng also uses libdeflate and its own trial heuristics, so -o4 does not run the same trial set as optipng -o 4 (different work, not an identical algorithm made faster). The README names Oxipng 9.0.0 but Cargo.toml at the cited commit still says 8.0.0. The op111.net numbers are snippet only (page blocked); per the snippet oxipng also compresses better at default settings.
found_via: WebSearch 'oxipng and friends: A comparison of PNG optimization tools'; oxipng README Benchmarks section links the blog

name: pngenc
baseline: libpng 1.6 (with zlib)
workload: Encode one 1920x1080 24-bit image to PNG in three low-compression modes (uncompressed, Huffman-only, RLE).
claimed_speedup: README table (ms, libpng 1.6 vs pngenc 1 thread vs pngenc multi-threaded, 1920x1080x24-bit image, Ryzen 7 3700X): Uncompressed 9 vs 0.8 vs 0.2; Huffman Only 82 vs 7.3 vs 1.2; RLE 84 vs 30 vs 4; Full LZ77 ~150 vs N/A vs N/A. That is about 11x (uncompressed), 11x (Huffman only) and 2.8x (RLE) single-threaded, and 45x, 68x and 21x multi-threaded (derived from page data). README says 'up to an order of magnitude faster' at 'the same compression rates' as libpng/zlib.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README table. The repo's CMakeLists.txt builds pngenc with -march=native -mtune=native -O3 -fopenmp (GCC/Clang) or /openmp /arch:AVX2 (MSVC); how libpng was built is not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X
tradeoffs: Encoder only. Supports only uncompressed, Huffman-only and RLE modes (full LZ77 is 'N/A'), so it does not replace libpng at default compression levels. Needs OpenMP for the multi-threaded numbers; tested with gcc/mingw, clang and MSVC. Author calls it a hobby project; the CRC32 code is adapted from Mark Adler under a zlib-compatible license.
caveats: Single first-party table, one unpublished image and one CPU; compiler, flags and the libpng timing harness are not published (tests/perf_mt.c times pngenc only, on a data.bin file that is not in the repo). PNG trade-off: pngenc only implements stored, Huffman-only (Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY) and RLE deflate with a fixed horizontal (Sub) row filter (no filter for the uncompressed mode), so its output is much larger than libpng at its default LZ77 level; the README's Full LZ77 row (libpng ~150 ms) has no pngenc counterpart, and the table gives no file sizes to back the 'same compression rates' claim. The comparison is against libpng's low-effort strategies, which the README itself calls a valid trade-off. The multi-threaded column uses OpenMP across the image, while libpng is single-threaded. A later mode (PNGENC_AUTO, Huffman-only falling back to RLE) is not in the README table. Hobby project for learning, per the README.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result GregorBudweiser/pngenc); opened readme.md, LICENSE and commits page

verification.tier_reason: The README table (1920x1080x24-bit image, AMD Ryzen 7 3700X) compares libpng 1.6 with pngenc single- and multi-threaded and the numbers match the record, but it is first-party and states no compiler, flags or harness. The repo has pngenc-only timing tests (tests/perf_mt.c, tests/perf_huffman.c, which read an unpublished data.bin image) and no libpng timing code, so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: Numbers, hardware, license (zlib license; crc32 code by Mark Adler under a zlib-compatible license), 3 stars and last commit 2024-08-10 (stale) all check out. The speed comes from skipping LZ77 entirely, so it suits fast snapshot or screenshot dumps rather than size-competitive PNGs.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: README table (ms, libpng 1.6 vs pngenc 1 thread vs pngenc multi-threaded): Uncompressed 9 vs 0.8 vs 0.2; Huffman Only 82 vs 7.3 vs 1.2; RLE 84 vs 30 vs 4. README says 'up to an order of magnitude faster' at the same compression rates in those modes.
corrected_fields.caveats: Single first-party table, one image and one CPU; compiler, flags and benchmark harness are not stated. The comparison is against libpng's low-effort strategies (Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY, Z_RLE) which the README itself calls a valid trade-off. No libpng-at-default-level comparison is given for any mode that pngenc supports.

name: ptpng
baseline: Decoder: libpng 1.6 (vendored libpng16 branch) with zlib-ng 2.2.4 in ZLIB_COMPAT mode. Encoder: libpng with the vendored stock zlib (develop branch) at level 6 and libpng with zlib-ng 2.2.4 at level 6, both with PNG_ALL_FILTERS adaptive filtering.
workload: PNG decode (27 cases: nine fixtures in native, RGB8 and RGBA8 output, median of 12 alternating rounds) and PNG encode (nine generated fixtures, median of five rotated rounds with a round-trip check) on five GitHub-hosted CI platforms. Fixtures are generated gradients, graphics and random noise at 3200x2400, except the two RGBA16 fixtures and noise_rgba8, which are 1024x768.
claimed_speedup: README: decoder geometric-mean speedup over libpng + zlib-ng 2.2.4 across 27 cases is 1.80x Linux x64 (27/27 faster), 1.64x Windows x64 (26/27), 1.59x Linux ARM64 (27/27), 1.62x macOS ARM64 (27/27) and 1.46x Windows ARM64 (26/27) in the 30 Sep 2026 nightly run 36753946386. Encoder (1 Oct change, nightly run 36791257328 per PERFORMANCE.md) averages 2.25-2.98x stock zlib level 6 and 1.14-1.52x zlib-ng level 6 across five platforms, faster than zlib-ng in only 4-6 of the 9 fixtures per platform, with PNGs at most 2.4% larger than zlib-ng level 6.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build with no explicit -O level in CMakeLists.txt (CMake's defaults, -O3 -DNDEBUG for gcc/clang and /O2 for MSVC), plus per-file -mavx2 or /arch:AVX2 and -mpclmul -msse2 kernels. The nightly matrix uses gcc (ubuntu24 x64 and arm64 images), clang (macos-14) and MSVC cl (win25-vs2026, win11-vs2026-arm64); compiler versions are not stated. PERFORMANCE.md quotes -O3 for paired runs and MSVC /O2 /Ob2 for local runs.
hardware: GitHub-hosted runners logged in gh-pages bench/data.js. 30 Sep decoder run 36753946386: Linux x64 and Windows x64 AMD EPYC 7763 (4 logical CPUs), Linux ARM64 Neoverse-N2, Windows ARM64 Cobalt 100, macOS Apple M1 (Virtual). Encoder run 36791257328: same, except Windows x64 was AMD EPYC 9V45. Local runs used an Intel Core i7-1355U.

name: qoi (qoi-rust)
baseline: QOI reference C implementation (phoboslab/qoi qoi.h, commit 00e34217 as of the 2022-01-06 measurement; the README later relabelled it 8d35d93 without re-measuring)
workload: Encode and decode of 2846 PNG images from the upstream QOI benchmark suite (1.32 GPixels, 4.46 GB of raw pixels), via the repo's bench/src/main.rs: per image and codec, repeated timed encodes and decodes filling a default 1-second budget (at least 2 runs each), median by default, with a round-trip pixel check; totals are sums of per-image medians.
claimed_speedup: Decode 427.4 Mp/s versus 282.9 Mp/s for qoi.h and encode 290.0 Mp/s versus 225.3 Mp/s (1477.7 versus 978.3 MiB/s decode, 1002.9 versus 778.9 MiB/s encode), about 1.5x decode and 1.3x encode (derived from page data); measured 2022-01-06 against qoi.h 00e34217.
compiler_and_flags: qoi.h (phoboslab/qoi submodule at 8d35d93) compiled by the cc crate at opt_level 3 with QOI_NO_STDIO and QOI_IMPLEMENTATION (libqoi/build.rs); rustc version, C compiler and Rust build profile not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 laptop
stars_or_usage: 129 stars; crates.io crate qoi with 68.4M downloads (17.4M recent)
tradeoffs: Pure safe Rust (unsafe forbidden), no_std support; usable from C++ only through FFI, there is no C API in the README. Same QOI format and compression ratio as the reference.
caveats: Rust, not C++ (the search's C++ language filter does not match). An independent safe-Rust re-implementation of the QOI format, not an FFI binding or wrapper of qoi.h, so like wx257osn2/qoixx it can sit beside phoboslab/qoi rather than fold into it as a duplicate. Baseline is the QOI reference qoi.h (commit 8d35d93), not a listed category baseline (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif). First-party numbers from one Apple M1 laptop with no rustc or C compiler version. By default the encoder emits QOI_OP_INDEX instead of a length-1 QOI_OP_RUN where allowed, so its byte stream can differ from qoi.h's (same size, still valid QOI; the 'reference' feature restores identical output), and each codec decodes its own encoder's output. The README says it is the fastest of the Rust QOI crates but gives no table for the others. The crates.io release (0.4.1) dates from 2022-10-16.

name: TinyTIFF
baseline: libTIFF (libtiff 3.8.2 and 4.6.0)
workload: Writing many small uncompressed 16-bit frames (64x64, 10 to >100000 frames) and frames of 64x64 to 4096x4096 into one multi-frame TIFF, compared with libTIFF and with raw fwrite(), using the repo's tests/tinytiffwriter_speedtest program.
claimed_speedup: Per-frame write times in doc/images/performance_measure_ssd.ods (Ryzen 7 5800H, Win11, SSD, 64-bit Release, libTIFF 4.6.0; units not labelled): 64x64 16-bit frames, speedup column 1.59x at 10 frames, 2.63-2.78x at 100 to 10,000 frames, 1.79x at 100,000 and 3.10x at 1,000,000; frame-size sweep 32x32 to 4096x4096: 5.11x, 1.67x, 3.11x, 5.15x, 4.49x, 2.06x, 1.81x, 1.51x (4096x4096: 70.2 vs 106.2 per frame). README prose: 1.5-3x over frame count and 1.5-5x over frame size on the SSD. Hard-disk run in doc/images/performance_measure.ods (Ryzen 5 3600, Win10, 32-bit Release, libTIFF 3.8.2): speedup grows with frame count from 1.77x at 10 frames to 2421x at 100,000 frames (libTIFF 205.8 vs TinyTIFF 0.085 per frame) and is 289-3674x for 32x32 to 256x256 frames, because libTIFF 3.8.2's per-frame time grows with the number of frames already written; for large frames TinyTIFF was slower there: 0.19x at 1024x1024 (22.28 vs 4.21), 0.96x at 2048x2048, 0.73x at 4096x4096. Write side only.
compiler_and_flags: Release builds (32-bit on the Win10 run, 64-bit on the Win11 run); compiler and flags not stated
hardware: Ryzen 5 3600+, Win10, hard disk, libTiff 3.8.2; Ryzen 7 5800H, Win11, SSD, libTiff 4.6.0
tradeoffs: Basic TIFF only: uncompressed pixel data, limited tag set and pixel formats; the writer pre-reserves a fixed header block per frame. LGPL-3.0 licence.
caveats: First-party; compiler and flags are not stated ('Release-build' only), so not tier A. The harness writes all TinyTIFF configurations, then all raw fwrite() configurations, then all libTIFF configurations, one run each; TinyTIFF beating raw fwrite() in several SSD rows (256x256: 0.103 vs 0.373 for raw) shows run-to-run noise of the same order as some of the gaps. The files are equivalent in kind (uncompressed, stripped, contiguous 16-bit greyscale on both sides), but libTIFF writes TIFFDefaultStripSize strips (about 8 KB, so many strips per large frame) while TinyTIFF writes one strip per frame, and the libTIFF helper TIFFTWriteUint16 copies each strip into a freshly allocated buffer inside the timed region. The very large ratios (up to 2421x and 3674x) come only from the 32-bit libTIFF 3.8.2 hard-disk run; with libTIFF 4.6.0 the per-frame time stays flat as frames accumulate, so against current libTIFF the gain is 1.5-5x. The 1,000,000-frame SSD row writes about 8.2 GB of 64x64 16-bit pixels, past the 4 GB classic-TIFF limit of both writers (TinyTIFF has no BigTIFF support), and I found no file-size check in src/tinytiffwriter.c, so that row does not compare valid files. On the hard disk TinyTIFF was slower than libTIFF 3.8.2 for 1024x1024 to 4096x4096 frames, which the README describes as 'in the same range'. No read-speed comparison against libTIFF is published, although the README calls the reader very fast compared to libtiff. TinyTIFF handles only uncompressed, stripped, non-BigTIFF files whose frames share one size and type.

name: wpd (WebP decoder)
language: Rust with x86 assembly, C ABI (wpd.h)
baseline: libwebp at pinned revision 94d3c4a (decoder version 1.6.0), static libwebpdecoder plus libwebpdemux built through Meson's CMake subproject, single-threaded
workload: Median wall-clock time of one process doing 48 decodes (hyperfine -N, 3 warmups, 20 runs; wpd --threads 1, libwebp use_threads off; output discarded to /dev/null but the requested format conversion still runs) on 7 files from halidecx/wpd-test-data. Both decoders request the same output format per row: planar YUV420P/YUVA420P for lossy stills, RGBA for lossless stills and composited animations. Decode defaults match libwebp's (loop filtering and fancy upsampling on). image-webp 0.2.4 appears only in RGBA rows.
claimed_speedup: README table (median ms per 48-decode run, libwebp / wpd): lossy.webp YUV420P 180.40/173.56 = 1.04x; simplelf-lossy.webp YUV420P 174.43/162.07 = 1.08x; anim_yuv.webp RGBA 190.90/169.18 = 1.13x; lossless.webp RGBA 195.75/111.27 = 1.76x; anim_rgb.webp RGBA 104.47/62.56 = 1.67x; a_lossy.webp YUVA420P 50.70/36.38 = 1.39x; anim_yuva.webp RGBA 494.37/374.46 = 1.32x. image-webp is slower than libwebp on every RGBA row (e.g. lossless 231.50 ms, anim_yuva 776.54 ms). With both decoders forced to RGBA on the same machine (AVX2_BENCHMARKS.md at commit 0a453d8) the lossy stills give 195.16/189.38 = 1.03x (lossy.webp), 188.91/179.66 = 1.05x (simplelf-lossy.webp) and 71.78/60.37 = 1.19x (a_lossy.webp).
compiler_and_flags: Meson release build (default buildtype=release, assembly enabled, -Dtrim_dsp=false); Rust release profile with lto=fat, codegen-units=1 and opt-level 3 for dependencies (Cargo.toml); libwebp built through the Meson CMake subproject (libwebp's CMake default build type is Release); rustc, C compiler and NASM versions are not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-13700K, Linux x86-64, benchmark pinned to CPU 0 (named in the README at commit 64273a2 and in AVX2_BENCHMARKS.md at commit 0a453d8; the 2026-10-01 README reformat 85e77ee dropped the machine paragraph but kept the same table numbers)
tradeoffs: Decoder only. Needs the Rust toolchain plus nasm on x86 (Meson build). Assembly is on by default; building with -Denable_asm=false gives memory-safety guarantees at the cost of speed. C API in include/wpd.h, installs static and shared libraries plus wpd.pc, so it is callable from C++. Streaming and cropping/scaling options exist.
caveats: First-party numbers on very fresh code: measured 2026-09-30 on wpd 59a1c12 plus then-uncommitted AVX2 changes (landed as a78b2c4 on 2026-10-01). Lossy stills gain only 1.04x-1.08x (1.03x-1.05x when both output RGBA); the larger wins are lossless (1.76x) and animation (1.13x-1.67x). Earlier README tables showed much larger ratios: the 2.38x and 4.56x figures in the search snippet come from the c91dc1e table (2026-09-17) and are relative to image-webp, not libwebp (libwebp/wpd in that table is 1.10x-1.85x, derived from page data); the f5c5b33 table gave libwebp/wpd 1.26x-3.07x (derived from page data); the 54d03ee table, run before f5c5b33 pinned wpd to one thread, reached 17.19x versus image-webp. Those runs were on an Apple M5 Pro and the old scripts/bench.sh asked libwebp and image-webp for RGBA while wpd emitted its native output (planar YUV for lossy), so wpd skipped the YUV-to-RGB conversion the baselines performed. Commit 0a453d8 ('bench: compare matching formats and expose libwebp threading') fixed the harness, and AVX2_BENCHMARKS.md states that the corrected x86 numbers miss the old ARM ratios on six of seven images. The current README still says 'reproduce the CPU affinity above' although the machine line was removed. Test files live in a separate repo (halidecx/wpd-test-data). Language is Rust plus hand-written assembly (NASM on x86, ARM/AArch64 directories) with a C ABI (include/wpd.h); C appears only in headers, tools and test harnesses. It is not C++, so it falls outside the C++ language filter, but C++ code can call it through wpd.h. name: zenjpeg
baseline: libjpeg-turbo (mozjpeg-sys 2.2 with nasm_simd, C+NASM)
workload: JPEG decode to RGB of 10 CID22-512 training photos (512x512) re-encoded by mozjpeg-rs at Q85 4:2:0, baseline and progressive, timed in interleaved zenbench A/B runs (zenjpeg/benches/decode_zenbench.rs). The parallel-decode table uses synthetic noise+patches images with restart markers at 1024, 2048 and 4096 px (CLAUDE.md Parallel Decode, 2026-02-15).
claimed_speedup: README (Ryzen 9 7950X, single-threaded, 10 CID22 512x512 photos at Q85 4:2:0): baseline decode 73.8 MiB/s with default Triangle upsampling vs libjpeg-turbo/mozjpeg 78.1 MiB/s (0.94x, slower); 80.4 MiB/s with NearestNeighbor (box) upsampling (1.03x, but that skips the fancy upsampling C performs); progressive decode 46 vs 34 MiB/s (1.35x faster), the one single-thread like-for-like win. Parallel decode with DRI (rayon, --features parallel) vs single-threaded libjpeg-turbo: 1.56 vs 3.86 ms at 1024, 3.05 vs 15.8 ms at 2048, 8.74 vs 65.3 ms at 4096 (about 2.5x, 5.2x, 7.5x, derived from page data); this compares a multi-core decode with a single-thread one. The same synthetic set run single-threaded (CLAUDE.md, 2026-02-15, commit 39f012f) gives 3.66 vs 3.86, 14.8 vs 15.8, 61.9 vs 65.3 ms (about 1.05 to 1.07x faster, derived from page data), and progressive 0.60 to 0.69x of mozjpeg's time on synthetic images.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --release, default target (no -C target-cpu=native), runtime SIMD dispatch via archmage; rust-toolchain.toml pins channel 'stable' only and the rustc version is not recorded; C reference is mozjpeg-sys 2.2 with nasm_simd, built by its build script with unstated C compiler and flags
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (WSL2)
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 or paid commercial licence. Pure Rust, so C++ needs bindings. Baseline decode is slightly slower than libjpeg-turbo with libjpeg-compatible upsampling; the large win needs restart markers (DRI) and the parallel feature (multi-threaded versus single-threaded libjpeg-turbo). Decoder API is prerelease. Encoder lands within about 15 to 20% of jpegli at matched quality.
caveats: First-party benchmark; tiny project (15 stars). The C reference is mozjpeg-sys 2.2 (mozjpeg's libjpeg-turbo-derived decoder via FFI), not stock libjpeg-turbo 3.x. Single-thread baseline decode is 6% slower than C on CID22 with the default Triangle upsampling; NearestNeighbor only matches C by doing cheaper upsampling. The default decoder uses the 'Jpegli' integer IDCT, not libjpeg's ISLOW; the README says the pixel-exact Libjpeg IDCT adds about 37% overhead, so the progressive 1.35x win is measured with output that differs slightly from libjpeg-turbo (like-for-like margin unmeasured). The parallel table compares rayon multi-threaded zenjpeg with single-threaded libjpeg-turbo, against the repo's own benchmarks/README rule never to compare single-threaded and thread-pooled contenders; its libjpeg-turbo column comes from synthetic noise+patches images (Feb 2026), not CID22. The Feb 2026 synthetic single-thread table shows zenjpeg 5 to 7% faster on baseline, the newer CID22 run shows it 6% slower. rustc version not recorded. AGPL-3.0 copyleft (commercial license sold separately).

name: zune-png (zune-image workspace)
language: Rust (C bindings via the zune-capi crate)
baseline: libspng 0.6.3 through the Rust spng 0.1.0 binding (spng-sys 0.1.0, 2021) linked to bundled stock zlib via libz-sys (zlib-ng feature off); libpng is not measured
workload: Criterion decode from an in-memory buffer of four PNG files from the zune-image test-images set (speed_bench.png, speed_bench_interlaced.png, speed_bench_16.png, speed_bench_palette.png), one thread per decode for all three libraries: zune-png decode_raw with default DecoderOptions, image-rs/png 0.18.0-rc.3 with EXPAND and ignore_checksums(true), and the spng 0.1.0 binding with Format::Png (native layout), TRANSPARENCY and IGNORE_ADLER32. Outputs are not cross-checked, and their layouts differ.
claimed_speedup: benchmarks/benchmark-results.md (Darwin, criterion mean, ms; spng vs zune-png): baseline 297.4 vs 135.0 (spng 2.20x slower, as printed); interlaced 8bpp 378.0 vs 139.7 (2.71x, as printed); 16 bpp 541.2 vs 186.3 (2.9x, derived from page data); palette 53.59 vs 35.21 (1.5x, derived from page data). image-rs/png beats zune-png on 16 bpp (163.7 ms; zune 1.14x slower) and palette (28.31 ms; zune 1.24x slower). These ratios overstate the library gap: the spng side is libspng 0.6.3 (2021) on stock zlib with its ARM NEON path disabled, and it verifies chunk CRCs while zune-png verifies neither CRC nor Adler-32.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench with criterion 0.8.1 (20 s measurement time) under the workspace bench profile (release opt-level 3 plus debug info, no target-cpu flags); libspng compiled by the cc crate in spng-sys build.rs (SPNG_SSE defined only for x86 targets with ssse3/sse4.1); rustc and C compiler versions not stated
hardware: Unnamed Darwin (macOS) machine; CPU model not given (the benchmarks README's Homebrew /opt/homebrew setup suggests Apple Silicon). The benchmarks README also lists an AMD EPYC-Rome KVM Linux box, but the results file has only Darwin columns.
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust decoders with minimal unsafe (only SIMD intrinsics); C access only through the separate zune-capi crate, so it is not a drop-in libpng or spng replacement for C++ code. The workspace also contains zune-jpeg, zune-inflate, zune-qoi, zune-heif and image filters.
caveats: The measured code does different work from the baseline. Checksums: zune-png's default options skip both chunk CRC and zlib Adler-32 checks, image-rs/png is told to ignore both, but spng only ignores Adler-32 and keeps libspng's default CRC verification of critical chunks (crc_action_critical = SPNG_CRC_ERROR). Baseline build: the spng crate pinned is 0.1.0 from March 2021 with libspng 0.6.3 (current libspng is 0.7.x), linked to stock zlib through libz-sys with the zlib-ng option off, and its ARM NEON unfilter path is commented out in that libspng version, so on an Apple machine spng runs scalar filters on stock zlib inflate. Output layouts differ: spng's Format::Png returns native rows (palette indices with tRNS not applied, host-endian 16-bit samples), while zune-png and image-rs expand palettes to RGB(A) and keep 16-bit samples big-endian. libpng, the category incumbent, is not measured at all. Single results file, Apple hardware, no CPU model, criterion timings on the maintainer's own image set. In the same file zune-jpeg is slower than mozjpeg on most cases (1.1x-1.3x slower on baseline and subsampled decodes, about 1.0x-1.1x faster only on some progressive cases), zune-inflate is 1.5x-2.5x slower than libdeflate, and zune-qoi is 1.88x slower than rapid-qoi, so the claim holds only for PNG against this spng build, not for the zune family generally. The README only promises 'on par with or better than reference libraries'. Language is Rust; a C API exists in crates/zune-capi (library name zil_c, wrapping zune-image), so it sits outside the C++ language filter unless used through that C API.

name: Basis Universal (bc7f and etc1f real-time encoders)
baseline: bc7e.ispc level 1 (BC7); etcpak and rg_etc1 (ETC1)
workload: Analytical, non-SIMD real-time BC7 (bc7f) and ETC1 (etc1f) block encoders in the transcoder module; no benchmark figures given.
claimed_speedup: Directional only, no numbers. Wiki: 'Even without any SIMD, bc7f is several times faster than our bc7e.ispc encoder at level 1, with a slightly lower average PSNR' and 'bc7f is essentially like bc7e.ispc level ~.8'; 'etc1f is significantly faster and more portable than etcpak, with substantially higher visual quality' and 'significantly faster than ... rg_etc1'. v2.0 release notes: bc7f and etc1f are 'significantly faster than other SIMD encoders, including our own previous SIMD encoders such as bc7e.ispc'.
tradeoffs: bc7f is portable (no SIMD needed), strictly bounded O(1) per block and thread-safe, and uses the whole BC7 format; fully analytical mode gives a lower PSNR than the partially analytical mode. Encoders live in the single-file transcoder basisu_transcoder.cpp.
caveats: First-party directional claim with no numbers, machine, compiler or benchmark harness anywhere reachable (README, wiki Transcoder Internals page with its embedded copy of the bc7f blog post, wiki Release Notes, GitHub releases, issues, and the bc7e and bc7enc_rdo READMEs that point to bc7f as 'an even faster alternative'). The original blog post on richg42.blogspot.com is blocked here; the wiki copy has no figures. bc7f trades slightly lower average PSNR than bc7e.ispc level 1 for speed, and its default XUBC7 use runs in partially analytical mode. The encoders are internal transcoder APIs (transcoder/basisu_transcoder.cpp) that the authors say may change at any time; they require basist::basisu_transcoder_init() first. Not a duplicate of bc7e or etcpak: bc7f and etc1f are separate, newer non-SIMD encoders. Texture encoders have baselines outside the category list.

name: Anti-Grain Geometry (AGG 2.6)
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo 1.18.4
workload: Blend2D bl_bench suite as run by LaurenzV (vello_chart): 29 tests (FillRectA/U/Rot, FillRoundU/Rot, FillTriangle, FillPoly NZ/EO with 10/20/40 vertices, Fill/Stroke Butterfly, Fish, Dragon, World, and the matching stroke tests) x paint styles x 6 sizes 8x8 to 256x256, SrcOver, 512x600 PRGB32 target, single thread, best of repeated runs reported as render calls per ms. The AGG backend supports only Solid, Linear and Radial styles (87 of 174 test/style rows). It fills integer-aligned solid rectangles through Agg2D::fillRectangleI (a direct span blend with no rasterizer) and draws radial gradients as centred radials, while Skia and Cairo draw a two-point conical gradient with a focal point.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 Pro, 2026-06-08 run, single-threaded, geometric mean of per-cell rcpms ratios over the 522 cells AGG shares with each baseline (29 tests x Solid/Linear/Radial x 6 sizes; derived from page data): 1.21x Skia (faster in 66% of cells; strokes 1.39x, fills 1.08x; 1.03x at 8x8, 1.02x at 16x16, 1.22x at 32x32, 1.39x at 64x64, 1.34x at 128x128, 1.28x at 256x256) and 2.29x Cairo 1.18.4 (faster in 94% of cells). The three earlier M1 runs (2025-09-24, 2026-01-22, 2026-05-17) give 1.20-1.21x Skia and 2.27-2.30x Cairo. Intel Core i9-14900K Windows run of 2026-01-22 (no Skia in that dataset): 1.87x Cairo 1.18.2 (1.89x on 2025-09-14). Slower than Blend2D 0.12.0 single-threaded (0.30x). All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the result files. Harness: Blend2D bl_bench from LaurenzV/blend2d-apps built with CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (C++17); AGG compiled from source as the copy bundled in blend2d-apps/3rdparty/agg plus the Agg2D wrapper in 3rdparty/agg2d; Skia linked from the vcpkg unofficial-skia package and Cairo from pkg-config, both prebuilt with unrecorded build flags; compiler and version unstated. The exact harness commit used for the 2026 runs is not recorded.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64, macOS); second dataset Intel Core i9-14900K (x86_64, Windows)
stars_or_usage: 367 stars, 92 forks (GitHub copy of the SourceForge AGG SVN); AGG 2.4 itself is widely vendored, e.g. by matplotlib's Agg backend
tradeoffs: Header-heavy C++ template library, CPU only, run single-threaded in this harness. Older, lower-level API than Skia or Cairo. The upstream SourceForge AGG 2.4 and this 2.6 mirror are dual licensed under a Modified BSD License or the Anti-Grain Geometry Public License.
caveats: Measured code is not this repository but the AGG 2.4-line copy bundled in blend2d-apps/3rdparty/agg, driven through the Agg2D wrapper; its hot-path headers (agg_basics.h, agg_rasterizer_scanline_aa.h, agg_rasterizer_cells_aa.h, agg_pixfmt_rgba.h) match ghaerr/agg-2.6 except for std:: qualifiers and a configurable cell_block_limit, so the result transfers. Against Skia (rows = test x style, geomean over sizes) AGG wins 67 of 87 rows: the polygon and path fills (FillPoly 1.06-1.35x by test, only FillPolyNZi10/Radial slightly behind at 0.98x; FillFish 1.54x, FillDragon 1.30x, FillWorld 1.27x, FillButterfly 1.21x) and every stroke except StrokeRectA (StrokeWorld 1.92x, StrokeFish 1.82x, StrokeButterfly 1.67x, StrokeRectU 1.60x); it loses the simple-shape fills FillRectA (0.84x, except solid), FillRectU (0.90x), FillRectRot (0.85x), FillRoundU (0.80x), FillRoundRot (0.94x), FillTriangle (0.94x) and StrokeRectA (0.52x). At 8x8 and 16x16 it is only at parity overall. Against Cairo it wins 84 of 87 rows, losing StrokeRectA/Solid (0.33x), FillRectU/Solid (0.46x) and FillRectA/Linear (0.91x). Both libraries run single-threaded and anti-aliased; AGG's radial gradient is the simpler centred form (radial rows 1.13x vs linear 1.25x against Skia), and output equivalence is not checked in the published data. This GitHub copy was cloned from the SourceForge SVN at r132 (2019-05-06) and last changed on 2023-08-21; the SourceForge SVN continued to r145 (2024-09-28: C++20/23 warning fixes, and r144 moved the bundled General Polygon Clipper to MIT). In this copy GPC is still under its non-commercial licence, so do not copy agg-src/gpc (the core is BSD-3-Clause or the AGG Public License). Skia's version is not recorded in the data.

name: Blend2D
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also AGG, JUCE, Qt6, CoreGraphics
workload: Time for 1000 render calls of a single shape (rectangles, polygons, curves, strokes; solid/gradient/image paints) at sizes 8x8 to 256x256 on a 512x600 pixmap, single-threaded and 8-thread.
claimed_speedup: Third-party thesis (ETH Zurich, Vello CPU author): Blend2D is 'the clear winner', needing the shortest time 'for nearly all configurations' versus the C++ and Rust renderers. Fill-Solid-RectU 256x256 single-threaded: Blend2D 10.8 ms vs Skia 50.3 ms (about 4.7x faster, derived from page data) and Cairo 21.9 ms (about 2.0x faster, derived from page data) per 1000 renders. Across the thesis data set (vello_chart data/arm/2025-09-24.json, M1 Pro), Blend2D ST is faster than Skia in 1032 of 1044 test x size cells (geometric mean about 4.1x) and faster than Cairo in 863 of 870 cells (geometric mean about 7.2x) (derived from page data). Blend2D 8-thread mode reaches 4.7x over its own single-thread time at 256x256 in Fill-Solid-RectA.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the thesis. The harness README builds with CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release and Blend2D's CMakeLists adds -O2 for release builds; the compiler is not named, Skia comes from vcpkg's unofficial-skia package with unstated version and flags, and Cairo is found via pkg-config (version 1.18.4 per the result JSON).

name: JUCE software renderer (juce_graphics)
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo 1.18.4
workload: Same bl_bench suite as above (JUCE 8.0.8 through juce::Graphics on a juce::SoftwareImageType image): 29 fill/stroke shape tests x five paint styles (solid, linear, radial, two image-pattern filters; no conic) x six sizes 8x8 to 256x256, SrcOver, 512x600 target, render calls per ms.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 Pro, 2026-06-08 run, JUCE 8.0.8 software renderer, single-threaded, geometric mean of per-cell rcpms ratios over 870 cells (29 tests x Solid/Linear/Radial/Pattern_NN/Pattern_BI x 6 sizes; derived from page data): 1.68x Skia (faster in 84% of cells; strokes 2.10x, fills 1.40x; 1.26x at 8x8, 1.32x at 16x16, 1.69x at 32x32, 2.02x at 64x64 and 128x128, 1.97x at 256x256) and 2.93x Cairo 1.18.4 (faster in 95% of cells). Excluding the three StrokeRect tests, which JUCE draws as four filled rectangles instead of a stroked path: 1.64x Skia and 2.90x Cairo. Earlier M1 runs give 1.61-1.70x Skia and 2.79-2.94x Cairo. Slower than Blend2D 0.12.0 single-threaded (0.41x). No JUCE run in the x86 data. All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the result files. Harness: Blend2D bl_bench from LaurenzV/blend2d-apps, CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (C++17); JUCE 8.0.8 compiled from source via JUCE_DIR/add_subdirectory with -DJUCE_USE_CURL=0 -DUSE_COREGRAPHICS_RENDERING=0 and a juce::SoftwareImageType surface; Skia from the vcpkg unofficial-skia package and Cairo from pkg-config, both prebuilt with unrecorded flags; compiler and version unstated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64, macOS)
tradeoffs: The renderer is part of the large JUCE application framework (juce_graphics, juce_core, juce_events), not a standalone library; it is single-threaded and CPU only. Dual licensed: AGPLv3 or a paid commercial JUCE licence, so closed-source use needs the commercial licence.
caveats: Some tests do different work from the baselines. JUCE's Graphics::drawRect fills four rectangles inside the shape bounds (LowLevelGraphicsContext::drawRect) instead of stroking a centred mitred path, so StrokeRectA/U/Rot are not like-for-like (StrokeRectU 3.44x Skia). JUCE's radial paint is a centred radial with no focal point, while Skia and Cairo draw a two-point conical gradient. JUCE's EdgeTable rasterizer is anti-aliased but uses its own approximate coverage (8-bit fixed-point x with adaptive vertical sub-steps), and output equivalence is not checked in the published data. All renderers here run single-threaded. Against Skia (rows = test x style, geomean over sizes) JUCE wins 134 of 145 rows, with the largest gains on strokes (StrokeWorld 3.08x, StrokeFish 2.47x, StrokeDragon 2.33x) and complex polygon fills (FillPolyEOi40 2.03x). Against Cairo it wins 138 of 145 rows, losing FillRectA (0.43-0.45x), FillRectU (0.59-0.68x) and StrokeRectA/Solid (0.71x). Only one machine (M1 Pro). JUCE 8.0.8 was measured; the repository is now at 9.0.3 (2026-09-28). name: LunaSVG

hardware: Apple M4, macOS 26.5.1

tradeoffs: Lightweight SVG 1.1/Tiny 1.2 renderer on top of the plutovg rasterizer. No filters, no SVG inside <image>, no WebP images, no CSS transform property, no transform-origin, no mix-blend-mode, no context-fill. Only 59% of resvg's feature tests match resvg output at 1% pixel tolerance (cairosvg 53%).

The pipeline is timed through Python: about 89% of pillow-lunasvg's 1.00 ms is Pillow load plus PNG encode (render only 0.11 ms), and the three tools use different PNG encoders (Pillow zlib, cairo's PNG writer, resvg's encoder), while cairosvg parses SVG in Python, so the gap over cairosvg reflects front-end and encoder overhead more than Cairo's rasterizer versus plutovg. On the resvg test corpus LunaSVG does less work: it lacks filters, the CSS transform property, transform-origin, mix-blend-mode, context-fill and SVG/WebP inside <image> (59% loose fidelity match against resvg), and per-renderer medians cover different file subsets. Filter tests are not timed. On simple-icons fidelity is comparable (99.0% vs cairosvg 99.4% strict). name: raqote
baseline: Cairo (image surface; 1.18.4 on the M1 Pro run, 1.18.2 on the Windows x86 run); not faster than Skia once the broken rotated tests are excluded
workload: Blend2D bl_bench suite with the raqote backend from LaurenzV/blend2d-apps (benching branch, bl_bench/backend_raqote.cpp) calling raqote 0.8.5 through the LaurenzV/raqote_c C bindings: 29 fill/stroke tests x six paint styles (Solid, Linear, Radial, Conic, Pattern_NN, Pattern_BI) x six sizes 8x8 to 256x256, SrcOver, 512x600 target, single thread, render calls per ms. In the rotated tests the raqote backend uses a random angle about each shape's own centre (as intended), unlike the incrementing angle about the screen centre used by the other backends, and its transform composition is wrong (see caveats).
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 Pro, 2026-06-08 run, single-threaded. As published, geometric means of per-cell rcpms ratios are 1.08x Skia (1044 cells, faster in 57%) and 1.84x Cairo 1.18.4 (870 cells), but the four rotated tests are inflated by a harness bug. Excluding FillRectRot, FillRoundRot, StrokeRectRot and StrokeRoundRot: 0.93x Skia (900 cells, faster in 51%; fills 1.08x, strokes 0.77x), i.e. not faster than Skia, and 1.48x Cairo (750 cells, faster in 76%; fills 1.86x, strokes 1.11x). The earlier M1 runs give the same picture (0.92-0.93x Skia, 1.46-1.49x Cairo). Intel Core i9-14900K Windows run of 2026-01-22 (no Skia): 1.09x Cairo 1.18.2 as published, 0.89x with the rotated tests excluded (fills 1.19x, strokes 0.61x). Slower than Blend2D 0.12.0 single-threaded (0.26x as published). All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Rust crates (raqote 0.8.5 through the raqote_c staticlib, cargo build --release) built with target-feature=+avx2 on x86 and default NEON on ARM (LaurenzV master thesis Section 5.2); C++ harness CMake Release; Skia from the vcpkg unofficial-skia package and Cairo from pkg-config, both prebuilt with unrecorded flags; rustc and C++ compiler versions are not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64, macOS); second dataset Intel Core i9-14900K (x86_64, Windows)
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars, 65 forks; README lists resvg, Servo and orbtk as users (the list may be dated)
tradeoffs: Rust crate (needs the raqote_c bindings or FFI from C++); no explicit SIMD, 4x4 multi-sampled anti-aliasing (lower quality than analytic coverage), single-threaded.
caveats: Harness bug: backend_raqote.cpp builds the rotation as rq_transform_multiply(rq_transform_multiply(translate_to_centre, rotate), translate_back), and raqote_c implements rq_transform_multiply(a, b) as euclid a.then(b). Each shape is therefore rotated about the canvas origin by a random angle in [0, 6.28), so most rotated shapes land off the 512x600 canvas and are clipped. The data shows it: raqote's FillRectRot at 256x256 (29.4 calls/ms) is 4.3x faster than its own FillRectU (6.82), and FillRoundRot (32.2) is 4.8x faster than FillRoundU (6.76), while every other single-threaded renderer is slower on the rotated variants at 64x64 and 256x256. That is where the published 3.16x/3.09x/2.59x/2.12x wins over Skia on FillRectRot/FillRoundRot/StrokeRectRot/StrokeRoundRot (and 9.49x on FillRectRot over Cairo) come from. With those tests excluded raqote wins only 75 of 150 test x style rows against Skia (99 of 125 against Cairo): path and complex-polygon fills (FillWorld 1.77x, FillPolyEOi40 1.44x, FillFish 1.43x, FillButterfly and FillDragon 1.35x). It loses StrokeRectA (0.28x), FillRectA (0.68x), StrokeWorld (0.55x), StrokeRoundU (0.65x), StrokeRectU (0.69x), StrokeTriangle (0.71x), FillRoundU (0.79x) and FillRectU (0.86x), and is 0.90x at 256x256. Against Cairo the wins are fills; it loses rectangle fills (FillRectA 0.57x, FillRectU 0.61x), StrokeRectA (0.37x), StrokeRectU (0.71x) and StrokeWorld (0.64x), and on the x86 run it is slower overall. raqote anti-aliases with 4x4 multisampling (thesis Section 4.1, coarser coverage than analytic rasterizers) and has no SIMD code or threading; output equivalence is not checked in the data. Language is Rust: it falls outside the C++ filter, and from C++ it is reachable only through the unofficial raqote_c shim ('not meant for production'). raqote 0.8.5 (2024-07-24) was measured; the last commit was 2025-02-11. The runner (Vello CPU author) wrote both the raqote backend and the bindings; the Skia version is not recorded.

name: Vello CPU (sparse strips renderer)
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also Rust tiny-skia, raqote, AGG, JUCE
workload: Time for 1000 render calls of a single shape (rectangles, many-segment polygons, curves, strokes; solid/gradient/image paints) at sizes 8x8 to 256x256 on a 512x600 pixmap, single-threaded and 8-thread, in a fork of the Blend2D benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: Thesis: Vello CPU 'outperforms nearly all other renderers, including Skia or Cairo, as the shape size increases'; Blend2D still wins in 'the vast majority of cases'. Fill-Solid-RectU 256x256 single-threaded: Vello CPU 14.2 ms vs Skia 50.3 ms (about 3.5x faster, derived from page data) and Cairo 21.9 ms (about 1.5x faster, derived from page data) per 1000 renders; Blend2D 10.8 ms. Across the thesis data set (vello_chart data/arm/2025-09-24.json), vello-cpu ST is faster than Skia in 954 of 1044 test x size cells (geometric mean about 2.4x) and faster than Cairo in 822 of 870 cells (geometric mean about 4.0x) (derived from page data). At small sizes (8x8, 16x16) Skia, AGG and JUCE are faster in some tests. Multi-threaded: the 8-thread mode reaches up to 5.3x over Vello CPU's own single-thread time (Fill-Solid-PolyNZi40, 5.1x at 256x256), 4.6x on Fish and 4.1x on Linear RectA at 256x256, but only 3.4x on Fill-Solid-RectA 256x256.
compiler_and_flags: Rust crates built with target-feature=+avx2 on x86 (no extra flags on ARM); build flags of the C++ baselines (Skia, Cairo, Blend2D) not stated in the thesis
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (8 cores: 6 performance + 2 efficiency, 16 GB, macOS) for the thesis results; an Intel Core i9-14900K (Windows) run in vello_chart data/x86 has no Skia or JUCE column
tradeoffs: Rust crate (vello_cpu); C bindings exist in a separate repo (LaurenzV/vello_cpu_c) so C++ use needs FFI. Weak for very small shapes because of the fixed 4x4 tile size. Supports multi-threading and NEON/AVX2 SIMD.
caveats: Evidence is an ETH Zurich master's thesis (PDF checked into LaurenzV/master-thesis, read via raw.githubusercontent.com) by the Vello CPU author, so the benchmark is first-party for Vello CPU even though the harness is a fork of Blend2D's; the vello-cpu harness backend is not in the public fork, only the C binding crates (vello_cpu_c, which its README says is not meant for production). Blend2D is faster in nearly all tests, so this is not a win over the category's best. Thread counts are not like for like: Vello CPU's nT mode uses n worker threads plus a main thread, Blend2D's uses the main thread as one of n. Raw results for M1 Pro and i9-14900K are in the public LaurenzV/vello_chart data/ JSON files; the 2026-06-08 M1 Pro run shows vello-cpu ST at 9.26 ms on Fill-Solid-RectU 256x256, ahead of Blend2D 0.12.0 at 10.8 ms, so later Vello versions improved. name: Marlin renderer (Java 2D)
baseline: OpenJDK 8 Pisces and Oracle JDK 8 Ductus (the Java 2D antialiasing rasterizers)
workload: MapBench 0.4 (Java 2D rendering of serialized GeoServer map drawings, maps/ in the mapbench repo) at 1, 2 and 4 threads: longer shared profile (one image per test, 10 s per test; 27 tests, 9 per thread count) for the 0.5.6 summary; default and shared profiles for the wiki's 0.3 and 0.5.4 comparisons.
claimed_speedup: MapBench 0.5.6 summary (longer shared profile, 9 maps at 1, 2 and 4 threads, ratio = baseline time / Marlin time): overall score versus Ductus 228.90% and versus Pisces 223.85%; per-test ratios versus Ductus range from 99.75% to 598.66%. Summary Pct95 ms/op at 1/2/4 threads: Ductus 157.616 / 263.145 / 645.566, Pisces 345.619 / 373.08 / 477.03, Marlin 0.5.6 129.718 / 130.557 / 131.877, i.e. about 1.22x / 2.02x / 4.90x faster than Ductus and 2.66x / 2.86x / 3.62x faster than Pisces (derived from page data). Wiki Benchmarks page, Marlin 0.3 tables (same ratio direction, checked against the linked compareResults page: Pisces 173.103 ms vs Marlin 102.149 ms gives 169.46%): versus OpenJDK 8 Pisces 'score small' Tavg 163.28% (1 thread), 162.93% (2), 164.92% (4), 'score big' 327.59%, 372.77%, 391.64%; versus JDK 8 Ductus 'score small' 96.28%, 134.03%, 186.95%, 'score big' 128.67%, 164.76%, 386.80%. Wiki headline: 'Marlin 0.5.4 is 17% to 25% faster than marlin 0.3 and is as fast as Oracle ductus !'
compiler_and_flags: 0.5.6 summary: Oracle Java SE 1.8.0_60-ea-b05 (HotSpot 25.60-b05), plus an internal OpenJDK 1.9.0 build of 2015-02-24 for the extra 'Marlin JDK9' column; JVM tuning -server -Xms2048m -Xmx2048m -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC; Pisces via -Xbootclasspath/a:../lib/openjdk8-pisces.jar -Dsun.java2d.renderer=sun.java2d.pisces.PiscesRenderingEngine; Marlin via -Xbootclasspath/p:../lib/marlin-0.5.6-Unsafe-sun-java2d.jar -Xbootclasspath/a:../lib/marlin-0.5.6-Unsafe.jar -Dsun.java2d.renderer.useThreadLocal=true -Dsun.java2d.renderer.useSimplifier=false -Dsun.java2d.renderer.useRef=soft -Dsun.java2d.renderer.pixelsize=2048 -Dsun.java2d.renderer.tileSize_log2=5 -Dsun.java2d.renderer=org.marlin.pisces.PiscesRenderingEngine; MapBench 0.4. Wiki 0.3 tables: custom OpenJDK8 b65 build (Pisces and Marlin), JDK8 b121 (Ductus), heap 2g, minimum 5000 ms per test.
hardware: 0.5.6 summary: Intel i7 4800 (as written on the page; host HP ZBook 15), 4 CPUs at a fixed 2 GHz, HyperThreading and turbo boost disabled, Linux 3.13.0-47 (Ubuntu). Wiki 0.3 tables: 4 virtual CPUs on Linux 2.6.35 (Fedora 14), CPU model not stated.
stars_or_usage: 197 stars; default Java 2D antialiasing renderer in OpenJDK 9+ (JEP 265) and in OpenJFX as Marlin-FX
tradeoffs: Java only; no GC pressure thanks to pooled array caches; scales near-linearly across threads where Ductus had synchronised singleton native structures; derived from OpenJDK 8 Pisces source and licensed GPLv2 with Classpath Exception.
caveats: Java, not C++: a pure-Java Java 2D RenderingEngine plugged into the JDK through sun.java2d.renderer, derived from the OpenJDK 8 Pisces source (GPL-2.0 with Classpath exception). Pisces (OpenJDK 6-8) and Ductus (closed-source, Sun/Oracle JDK up to 8) were the default Java 2D antialiasing rasterizers before Marlin replaced them in OpenJDK 9 (JEP 265, per the README's JDK table), so they are recognisable incumbents for Java but not catalogue baselines (Skia, Cairo, Blend2D): baseline_in_list false. All numbers are first-party and from 2014-2015 builds (Marlin 0.3 to 0.5.6; current release 0.9.4.9) on early-access or internal JDK builds; since Marlin is now the JDK default, the comparison is historical and Ductus is only available as a binary in Oracle JDK 8. Summary ratios are Pct95 per-op times under concurrent threads, so the 4-thread gain over Ductus largely reflects Ductus's poor multi-thread scaling; single-thread gain over Ductus is about 1.2x (0.5.6) or none (0.3 'score small' 96.28%). The two PRs were timed under different conditions (PR #3's master time for 23.svg 3x, 19.1 ms, is below PR #2's optimized 24.3 ms), so the speedups should not be multiplied.

name: NV_path_rendering (NVpr)
language: C (OpenGL extension in the NVIDIA driver)
baseline: Cairo 1.9.6, Skia (circa May 2010, CPU raster backend), Qt 4.5.x, Direct2D and the OpenVG 1.1 reference implementation (the nvpr_svg comparison backends in the NVprSDK)
workload: GPU stencil-then-cover path rendering of SVG-like scenes, compared in the NVprSDK nvpr_svg demo and the SIGGRAPH Asia 2012 paper 'GPU-accelerated Path Rendering' (Kilgard and Bolz).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (search summaries of the blocked paper PDF and ResearchGate page): the paper gives performance ratios of NV_path_rendering at 16 samples per pixel over Cairo, Skia, Qt, Direct2D and the OpenVG reference implementation for SVG scenes at window sizes from 100x100 to 1100x1100; one snippet attributes 8.69 ms at 1000x1000 with 16 samples against Cairo's 909 ms at 1000x1000 to a complex clipping scene (about 105x, derived from snippet data). The ratio tables themselves were not seen.
hardware: GeForce 650 GPU and an unnamed 'fast Core i7' CPU for the ratio benchmarks; a GeForce 560M laptop for the Snail Bob (5 ms) and SIGGRAPH web page (4.8 ms) frame timings (all per search snippets of the paper)
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and driver exposing GL_NV_path_rendering; vendor-specific extension, not usable on AMD or Intel; the NVprSDK samples are NVIDIA-distributed, not an OSI-licensed repo that was opened here.
caveats: Paper-only entry for the research section. The paper PDF (developer.download.nvidia.com), the GTC 2012 slides and ResearchGate are blocked, so all numbers are from search-result snippets. NV_path_rendering is implemented inside NVIDIA's proprietary driver, so the renderer itself cannot be copied; only the SDK example code is public. An unofficial mirror of the July 2011 NVprSDK (github.com/victusfate/nvpr_demo, 1 star, no license file seen) carries nvpr_svg with -benchmark (best frames/second over 6-second intervals) and a key to benchmark the Qt/Cairo/Skia software renderer, but no recorded results. The CPU baselines are 2009-2010 versions (Skia's CPU raster path, not Ganesh/Graphite), the README notes Cairo 1.9.6 had a path-clipping bug, and the hardware is 2012-era. NVIDIA-only (GeForce 8 or later, driver 275.33+).

name: ragg
baseline: Cairo (R grDevices png(type = 'cairo') anti-aliased raster device)
workload: R graphics primitives (1000 random points with pch 1, 19, 4, 0, 15, 2 and '#', lines with and without dash patterns, polygons, even-odd paths, rotated and interpolated rasters, text strings), a prebuilt layered ggplot2 plot (hexbin, points, smooth, facets) and grid clipping paths, masks, gradients and patterns, rendered to PNG and timed with bench::mark (min_iterations 10) per device: agg_png() vs png(type = 'cairo') with antialias none, gray and subpixel; void_dev() time marks non-rendering overhead; Xlib omitted on the build machine.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Faster (up to 40% faster than anti-aliased cairo device)'; no number in the vignette backs the 40%. Vignette conclusion: 'a general speed gain of around ~33% compared to cairo' among anti-aliased devices. Rendered plots (pkgdown build of 2026-04-08), read approximately: complex ggplot2 composite ragg about 245 ms vs anti-aliased cairo (gray and subpixel) about 320-325 ms, about 1.3x (derived from page data, plot readings), with the void_dev() non-rendering baseline at about 130 ms; unfilled circles about 5.5 ms vs about 7.3 ms; filled complex polygon about 38 ms vs about 48 ms. Non-anti-aliased cairo beats ragg on single primitives (about 3.1 ms unfilled circles, about 6.5 ms filled polygon) but is slower on the composite (about 265 ms). Cairo is about twice as fast to open and close a device, slightly faster for non-rotated rasters, and about on par for gradients; ragg is clearly faster for clipping paths, masks and patterns.
compiler_and_flags: not stated (package built on the CI runner with R's default toolchain and flags; session info lists no compiler)
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 x86_64 runner (pkgdown article build of 2026-04-08: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, R 4.5.3, ragg 1.5.2 per session info); CPU model not stated
license: MIT; bundled AGG 2.4 sources under a BSD-style license (LICENSE.note)
stars_or_usage: 184 stars, 30 forks; on CRAN; README documents use as a knitr device (dev = 'ragg_png') and as the RStudio AGG graphics backend
tradeoffs: R graphics-device package, not a standalone C++ API; the rasterizer is the AGG library (already catalogued as AGG 2.6) wrapped with FreeType/HarfBuzz text and libpng/libjpeg/libtiff output. Always anti-aliases fills, so the win is partly a quality difference.
caveats: Language mismatch with the C++ filter: ragg is an R package. Its C++ core (src/ragg.h includes Rinternals.h and R_ext/GraphicsEngine.h) implements R's graphics-device API and cannot be called from plain C++ without R; the reusable C++ piece is the bundled AGG 2.4 rasterizer. Baseline is R's cairo device (grDevices png(type = 'cairo')), not Cairo called from C++, and both sides include R graphics-engine overhead. Numbers are first-party and shown only as ridge plots from a CI runner (no CPU model, no compiler flags); the README's 'up to 40%' has no backing figure and the vignette's '~33%' is summary prose. Gains are smallest on fills because grDevices cairo does not anti-alias fills; non-anti-aliased cairo is faster on single primitives, and cairo is about twice as fast to open/close a device and slightly faster on non-rotated rasters. The vignette is excluded from the CRAN tarball (.Rbuildignore) and rendered only on the pkgdown site; the rendered copy is on the gh-pages branch.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/vector-graphics (C++ filter), surfaced r-lib/ragg; CRAN is the registry

verification.tier_reason: The benchmark code is public (vignettes/ragg_performance.Rmd, bench::mark per device against png(type='cairo') with antialias none/gray/subpixel), but results exist only as ridge plots in the rendered article, built on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 x86_64 runner with no CPU model or compiler flags stated, and the ~33%/40% figures are first-party summary prose; C.
verification.notes: Benchmark code is the R script in vignettes/ragg_performance.Rmd; the machine is a GitHub Actions ubuntu-24.04 runner per the rendered article's session info (raw.githubusercontent.com gh-pages copy, since ragg.r-lib.org is blocked), CPU model unstated. Language should be 'R (C++ core on AGG 2.4)' via a decisions.json override, since 'language' is not a correctable field; the C++ filter mismatch is in caveats. CRAN was blocked (403), so CRAN usage figures were not checked.

Performance vignette conclusion: 'a general speed gain of around ~33% compared to cairo' among anti-aliased devices; clipping paths and patterns clearly faster, gradients roughly on par, plain raster blits slightly slower than cairo.

corrected_fields.workload: R graphics-device primitives (lines, points, polygons, paths, text, clipping, gradients, patterns) and a layered ggplot2 plot rendered to PNG, timed with bench::mark against void_dev() overhead baseline.
corrected_fields.caveats: Benchmark code is public (vignette) but the numbers are rendered plots; the vignette source does not state CPU or compiler flags (session info is generated at build time). Baseline is R's cairo device, not Cairo called from C++. Gain is smaller where Cairo skips fill anti-aliasing; cairo is faster for opening/closing a device and slightly faster for non-rotated raster blits. The 33% and 40% figures are the author's summary prose, not tabulated numbers. Usable from C++ only by reusing the AGG-based device code, so this mainly counts as evidence that AGG-class scanline rasterizers beat Cairo in an R workload.

name: Rive Renderer (rive-runtime)
baseline: Skia (and Flutter Impeller, per the same post); Skia backend and configuration unstated
workload: Animated vector tiles drawn on an iPhone 12 (many path-heavy tiles per frame), Rive Renderer vs Skia/Impeller.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (LinkedIn post by Rive's Guido Rosso, not opened): on an 'iPhone 12 Max', Skia renders 9 animated tiles in about 100 ms (10 fps) while the Rive Renderer renders 100 tiles in about 16 ms (60 fps), stated as '66x faster here, 6000 tiles/sec vs 90 tiles/sec'; the post adds that two tiles with Skia/Impeller already exceed 16 ms per frame.
hardware: iPhone 12 (per snippet)
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars, 122 forks; renderer used across Rive's Apple, Android, Flutter, Unity, Unreal and web runtimes
tradeoffs: GPU renderer (Metal, Vulkan, D3D12, D3D11, OpenGL/WebGL, per the README) built around a geometric reduction of anti-aliased paths into triangle patches and best with pixel local storage support; not a CPU rasterizer. Designed for Rive content and its runtime, with an abstract renderer interface (a Skia integration layer and a CoreGraphics renderer also exist in the repo).
caveats: Vendor claim by the company selling the product (C), snippet only: the LinkedIn post and Rive's blog are blocked or unopened. The rive-runtime README and renderer/README.md contain no benchmark numbers, and tests/bench holds only internal micro-benchmarks without a Skia baseline. The test is animation-heavy tile grids on one mobile GPU, not a general path-rendering benchmark; Skia configuration (Ganesh or Graphite, GPU or CPU) is unstated, and 'iPhone 12 Max' is not a real model name (probably iPhone 12 Pro Max). Search-snippet discussion in the March 2024 open-source announcement thread on HN says performance depends on hardware pixel-local-storage support, with Apple Silicon the best case, so the gap on other GPUs may be smaller.

name: stilus
baseline: golang.org/x/image/vector (the Go project's rasterizer) and gogpu/gg v0.52.5 CPU rasterizer
workload: Synthetic print-style scenes on an A3 landscape page at 150 dpi (2481x1754 px) from internal/scenes: Hatch (2,000 parallel 45-degree hairlines spanning the page, drawn one device pixel wide) and Short (20,000 random 2-8 mm strokes, 0.35 mm wide). stilus draws through its Canvas with a page clip; the x/image/vector run strokes each line with stilus's own stroker and fills each outline with one vector.Rasterizer reset to that outline's bounding box; gogpu/gg strokes each line with no clip.
claimed_speedup: README comparison table: 2 000 hatch lines: stilus 70 ms, x/image/vector 33 400 ms, gogpu/gg 14 800 ms; 20 000 short strokes: stilus 55 ms, x/image/vector 111 ms, gogpu/gg 2 090 ms. About 477x and 2.0x versus x/image/vector (derived from page data). Separate 'Numbers' table: stilus 1 core 67 ms (2 000 hatch lines at 0.35 mm) and 41 ms (20 000 short strokes), 4 cores 19 ms and 12 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Go; the comparison lives in the separate bench module (bench/go.mod: go 1.26.0, golang.org/x/image v0.46.0, github.com/gogpu/gg v0.52.5; the core module's go.mod says go 1.24); exact toolchain version for the table not stated; run with `cd bench && go test -bench .` (bench/compare_test.go).
hardware: 'Same machine' as the Numbers table: cloud Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (exact model not stated), minimum of 15 runs; some speed levers were measured on a Ryzen 7 5800H
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo, no dependencies, builds for all GOOS/GOARCH including js/wasm; zero allocations after warm-up; sparse cost model (edge length plus covered spans); exact-area coverage like FreeType/AGG; optional AVX2/AVX-512 compositing under GOEXPERIMENT=simd; it is only the rasterizer core of a planned PDF renderer (no fonts, colour spaces or display lists).
caveats: The 477x hatch ratio is not a fair measure of x/image/vector: that rasterizer is a dense area accumulator whose cost is proportional to the canvas it is sized to, and the harness resets and draws one rasterizer per 45-degree page-spanning line, so each of 2,000 lines pays for a bounding box of up to about 1754x1754 px; a single page-sized rasterizer filled with all outlines (same result for opaque black) would very likely narrow the gap by orders of magnitude, but that was not measured. The short-stroke row (about 2.0x, derived from page data: 111 ms vs 55 ms) is the representative comparison, and it includes stilus's own stroker on both sides. x/image/vector is the Go project's glyph-oriented rasterizer and gogpu/gg a community library, neither a catalogue baseline (Skia, Cairo, Blend2D), so baseline_in_list is false; quality is only checked against PDFium (mean deviation 0.3-1.5/255, SSIM at least 0.998). The comparison's stilus hatch time (70 ms) does not match the Numbers table's hairline hatch (53 ms), so the tables were likely measured at different times. First-party, one author, repo created days ago (0 stars), CPU model not named exactly, benchmark source read but not run.

name: tdewolff/canvas
baseline: Inkscape and Cairo (named in the README as 'existing solutions'; which Cairo-based tool was run, e.g. rsvg-convert or CairoSVG, is not stated on any readable page)
workload: End-to-end conversion of one very large SVG (score.svg attached to issue #280, a bug report about a pathIntersections panic) to a raster image; this includes SVG parsing, path processing and rasterization, so it is not a rasterizer-only comparison with Cairo. The comparison comment itself could not be read.
claimed_speedup: README (directional, no number on the page): 'Execution performance is actually really good, especially the rasterizer is highly optimized with ASM. See for example a comparison of an extreme case in issue #280 (comment 1995990038), where this library is at least twice as fast as existing solutions, and can handle bigger images than the likes of Inkscape and Cairo.' The linked comment could not be read, so no timing, ratio or image size is verified.
tradeoffs: Pure Go vector graphics with raster, SVG, PDF, EPS, HTML Canvas and Gio outputs; assembly-optimised rasterizer is architecture specific; Fribidi and HarfBuzz can be CGO or native Go.
caveats: No numbers verifiable: the README links a single issue comment (issue #280, comment 1995990038, March 2024) that does not render outside a browser; no benchmark code, hardware, Go version or command lines for the rasterization comparison are public in the repo. One extreme-case file only; the issue's own opening post says canvas 'takes ages' on that file while JSVG (Java) takes 'a second or two', i.e. before the fixes canvas was slower than another renderer. The README's 'highly optimized with ASM' wording describes the golang.org/x/image/vector backend in use in March 2024 (whose accumulation loop has amd64 assembly); since commit 'Use Scanx rasterizer, fixes #334' (2025-02-06) the default renderers/rasterizer path uses the pure-Go srwiley/scanx scanner (rasterizer.go even carries a TODO to add an ASM version), after issue #334 reported x/image/vector as 500-1000x slower than scanx for GUI rounded-rectangle workloads. So the 2x claim, if it was ever measured, was measured on a superseded backend. The separate tdewolff/canvas_benchmarks repo covers polygon boolean operations only (canvas is slower than iOverlay there and comparable to Clipper2), not rasterization. First-party, no methodology. The code is MIT, but the README warns that FriBidi (used for text bidirectionality) is LGPL. Language is Go.

name: TFT_eSPI
baseline: Adafruit_GFX (Adafruit-GFX-Library) with the Adafruit_ILI9341 driver
workload: Arduino_GFX README 'Performance' table: per-primitive drawing benchmark (screen fill, text, pixels, lines, horizontal/vertical lines, rectangles, triangles, circles, arcs, rounded rectangles; filled and outline variants) pushed to an ILI9341 over SPI, comparing Adafruit_GFX, Arduino_GFX, LovyanGFX and TFT_eSPI.
claimed_speedup: Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ result.txt (reproduced in the Arduino_GFX README Performance table), one pass per test, microseconds (lower is faster), TFT_eSPI versus Adafruit_GFX with the Adafruit_ILI9341 driver: Text 21,752 vs 97,662 (4.5x); Lines 264,950 vs 1,062,311 (4.0x); Circles (outline) 25,269 vs 118,125 (4.7x); Triangles (outline) 16,277 vs 58,843 (3.6x); Rounded rects (outline) 15,371 vs 43,185 (2.8x); Pixels 775,781 vs 1,365,211 (1.8x); Screen fill 155,938 vs 195,782 (1.3x); Rectangles (filled) 323,908 vs 406,817 (1.3x); ratios derived from page data. TFT_eSPI is fastest of the four on Pixels, Lines and Circles (outline) and beats LovyanGFX on Text, but trails LovyanGFX on the other rows by up to 17% (Rounded rects (outline) 15,371 vs 13,089) (derived from page data). The TFT_eSPI README says its speed additions make it 'typically 3 to 10 times faster' than the Adafruit libraries it derives from, without a benchmark or numbers behind that statement.
compiler_and_flags: Arduino IDE 1.8.15 with the arduino-esp32 1.0.6 default toolchain; compiler flags not stated
hardware: TTGO T8 v1.8 (ESP32) board, PSRAM disabled, ILI9341 240x320 panel in 16-bit RGB565 on 4-wire SPI at 40 MHz (User_Setup.h: ILI9341_DRIVER, SPI_FREQUENCY 40000000, GLCD font), no DMA; Arduino IDE 1.8.15, arduino-esp32 1.0.6; test date 2021-06-16 (benchmark repo commit 8798d61); exact ESP32 CPU clock not stated
stars_or_usage: 4.9k stars; widely used Arduino and PlatformIO TFT library
tradeoffs: Grew out of Adafruit_ILI9341 and Adafruit_GFX; DMA on ESP32, RP2040 and STM32, 8 and 16-bit parallel interfaces, sprites for flicker-free updates, smooth anti-aliased arcs, circles and rounded rectangles, anti-aliased TrueType via the OpenFontRender add-on; user-setup header files select the display and processor; generic processors fall back to slow Arduino SPI calls.
caveats: Measured by the author of a competing library (Arduino_GFX), not by the TFT_eSPI project; the result is against that author's interest since TFT_eSPI beats Arduino_GFX on most rows. The README table does not link its code, but the sketches and raw output are in moononournation/Arduino_graphicstest_PDQ (result.txt matches the table; units are microseconds). The TFT_eSPI sketch runs the identical test body as the Adafruit_GFX and Arduino_GFX sketches at the same 240x320 resolution, RGB565 colour and 40 MHz SPI, with no DMA and no bus held across tests (TFT_eSPI's DMA mode was not used); Arcs are N/A because TFT_eSPI lacked arc calls at the time. Single pass per test, no repeat count or variance; the TFT_eSPI version is not recorded and an earlier 2020-10-15 run gives notably different numbers (Lines 308,601, Circles 44,739), so results move with library versions. Compiler flags and Arduino board-menu settings are not stated. Screen fill is bound by the SPI link: five full-screen fills of 240x320x16 bits at 40 MHz need 153,600 microseconds (derived from page data). TFT_eSPI's own TFT_graphicstest_PDQ example divides fill time by 5, so its own output is not comparable to this table. Weak category fit: an embedded SPI/parallel display driver stack with drawing primitives, not a general path rasterizer comparable to Skia, Cairo or Blend2D. Maintenance: last commit 2026-04-03; the February 2026 commits include a code fix ('Fix DMA on ESP32 C3 and S3 for board packages 3.x.x') besides README and board-header updates; 278 open issues and 75 open pull requests, and a closed June 2025 issue (#3770) called the library abandoned and suggested LovyanGFX. license.txt combines the FreeBSD two-clause licence for the original code with the Adafruit BSD and MIT notices of the code it started from; the bundled fonts have separate licence files.

name: TGFX (Tencent Graphics)
baseline: Skia (m136)
workload: ParticleBench-Rect from libpag/tgfx-benchmark and libpag/skia-benchmark (the same source with each engine's API): animated anti-aliased filled rectangles of 4-14 px (times screen density) in three colours, drawn one drawRect call each; the rectangle count ramps up every frame until FPS falls below 59.5 with average draw time above about 14.7 ms, and the count held at that point is reported. This is a GPU-backend comparison (TGFX GPU renderer vs Skia Ganesh), run in the browser via WebGL/WebAssembly at tgfx.org/benchmark or natively on Windows/macOS.
claimed_speedup: '510,308 Rectangles at 60 FPS' for TGFX versus '34,721 Rectangles at 60 FPS' for Skia; announcement text: 'renders rectangles at least 10 times faster than Skia's m136 version - reaching up to 16 times faster' and 'Basic graphics (such as Rect) rendering is 10x faster compared to version 1.2' (ratio of the two counts is about 14.7x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the posted numbers. Benchmark repos: TGFX built as a CMake Release target (C++17); Skia built with gn is_official_build=true is_debug=false skia_enable_ganesh=true (web build: target_cpu=wasm, skia_use_webgl=true, Emscripten).
hardware: Not stated (device, GPU and browser behind the 510,308 vs 34,721 numbers are unknown; the online benchmark runs on the viewer's own device)

tradeoffs: GPU-only (OpenGL 3.2+/ES 3.0+, WebGL 2, Vulkan 1.1+, WebGPU; Metal in progress); no CPU/software rasterizer; much smaller feature set than Skia (README: 'a compelling alternative to the Skia graphics library while maintaining a much smaller binary size'); runs on iOS, Android, HarmonyOS, macOS, Windows, Linux and the Web.

name: ThorVG
baseline: Skia (CPU raster backend, Skia v148)
workload: thorvg.benchmark CPU backend at 2560x1440: 5,000 retained shapes per frame (rects with alpha 240-255, rotated rects, strokes, circles, PNG images with bilinear filtering, linear/radial gradients), per-frame translate/scale (and rotation in rotation mode), 120 warmup + 1000 measured frames, frame time includes SDL_UpdateWindowSurface for both engines.
claimed_speedup: README: 'an average of ~2.9x faster' than 'a widely-used vector graphics engine' (Skia v148 in the test conditions), CPU backend, 2560x1440, 5k primitives. Chart table (fps, ThorVG vs Skia): Rects 76.0 vs 17.2 (4.4x), Rotated Rects 36.0 vs 10.1 (3.6x), Stroke 55.7 vs 17.2 (3.2x), Rects+Stroke 41.8 vs 10.5 (4.0x), Rotated Rects+Stroke 25.0 vs 4.5 (5.6x), Circles 38.5 vs 10.4 (3.7x), Images (PNG) 6.4 vs 6.0 (1.1x), Rotated Images 4.4 vs 4.4 (1.0x), Linear Gradient 9.0 vs 8.5 (1.1x), Radial Gradient 6.9 vs 6.0 (1.2x). The 2.9x is the arithmetic mean of the ten per-test ratios (2.89, derived from page data); image and gradient cases are roughly at parity.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated (macOS build, presumably Apple Clang). thorvg.benchmark README: harness built with CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; ThorVG built with meson using project defaults (buildtype=debugoptimized, optimization=3); Skia installed from vcpkg (arm64-osx triplet), its build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M2 Pro (macOS 26) per README test conditions
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; used by Canva (Lottie), SEGGER, Lottie Creator per README
tradeoffs: Smaller feature set than Skia (core binary about 170KB per README); focused on SVG and Lottie, with software, OpenGL and WebGPU backends. Per the VGCPU-Benchmark README its CPU rasterizer uses a sum-then-saturate coverage model (not exact union), so self-overlapping paths can differ from Skia and Cairo. The gain is large for rect, stroke and circle workloads but only 1.0x to 1.2x for images and gradients.
caveats: First-party benchmark (thorvg/thorvg.benchmark, MIT, 6 stars). Thread asymmetry: the harness initialises ThorVG with opts.threads worker threads, default 4 since commit 2f87860 'thorvg: fine-tuned options' (2026-08-31; before that the default was hardware_concurrency), while Skia renders through a single-threaded raster surface (SkSurfaces::WrapPixels). The README chart was last updated the same day (2026-08-31) and the README does not state the thread count, so the ~2.9x compares multi-threaded ThorVG with single-threaded Skia; the gains are largest in geometry-heavy tests and near 1x for images and gradients. Compiler not named; Skia's vcpkg build flags unverified. The headline sentence does not name Skia (only the test conditions do). The stroke workload was replaced on 2026-09-21 (designer stroked paths) and the harness says new stroke results are not comparable with earlier runs, so the chart's Stroke row predates the current code. Per-test numbers exist only as an image.
