name: tiny-skia
baseline: Cairo (and raqote); slower than Skia
workload: CPU 2D rendering of common operations (fills, strokes, gradients, patterns, clipping) in the project's benchmark set.
claimed_speedup: README: 20-100% slower than Skia on x86-64 and about 100-300% slower on ARM, 'still faster than cairo and raqote in many cases'. Results pages (gh-pages x86_64.html, July 2021; arm.html, Aug 2022): tiny-skia AVX2 beats cairo in 41 of 49 x86 tests (geometric mean 2.27x, range 0.31x-11.9x) and tiny-skia beats cairo in 46 of 49 ARM tests (geometric mean 2.7x) (derived from page data). Cairo wins on x86 Rect fills (tiny-skia 0.37-0.45x), Nearest pattern (0.39x) and Source Over/Destination Over/Plus blending (0.31-0.58x); tiny-skia wins most on non-separable blend modes (4.5-9x), bicubic patterns (11.9x) and AA hairlines (4.4x). Against Skia AVX2 tiny-skia wins only 5 of 50 x86 tests (geometric mean 0.68x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: x86 page (committed 2021-07-04): benches/README at that time lists Rust 1.53 (nightly cargo bench), clang 12, tiny-skia -Ctarget-cpu=x86-64 (SSE2) or haswell (AVX2), Skia built with clang -march=x86-64/haswell plus -DSK_FORCE_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLITTER and is_debug=false gn args, cairo 1.16.0 Gentoo system build with gcc -march=native (gcc version and -O level not stated). Current benches/README (ARM update 2022-08-27): Rust 1.62, clang 13, Skia v90; no extra flags on ARM.
hardware: AMD 3700X (Ryzen 7, Gentoo Linux) for x86-64 results; Apple M1 for ARM results
tradeoffs: A minimal Skia subset ported to Rust (about 14k lines, about 200KB, no text, no GPU); not a Skia replacement. Needs FFI from C++.
caveats: Rust library (language-filter mismatch). Slower than Skia on its own benchmarks; the claim is relative to cairo (and raqote) only. Results are old (x86 page July 2021, ARM page Aug 2022) and the current benches/README environment block (Rust 1.62, clang 13, Skia v90) was written for the 2022 ARM run, not the x86 page; cairo's build is a distro package with only -march=native stated (macOS cairo build for the ARM run not described). Cairo is faster on solid rect fills and nearest-neighbour patterns in tiny-skia's own data. The Vello CPU master thesis (LaurenzV/master-thesis main.pdf, M1 Pro, Blend2D harness with tiny_skia_c bindings, times per 1000 render calls) shows the same split: cairo faster on Fill-Solid-RectA (256x256: 18.6 ms vs 136 ms) and RectU, nearest-neighbour patterns and larger linear-gradient rects, while tiny-skia is about 1.1-2.3x faster than cairo on PolyNZi40 (small sizes), Fish and World fills and on World and Butterfly strokes; tiny-skia is slower than Skia and Vello CPU in most shown tests.

name: tiny-skia-cpp
baseline: Rust tiny-skia (linebender/tiny-skia, a Skia subset)
workload: 512x512 FillRect and FillPath rendering, C++ SIMD backend vs the Rust tiny-skia implementation, normalized to Rust = 1.0x (ARM measured on Apple Silicon NEON, x86 on Intel/AMD with AVX2+FMA).
claimed_speedup: README: up to 1.9x faster than Rust tiny-skia at 512x512, normalized to Rust = 1.0x: FillRect 1.9x ARM (NEON) and 1.3x x86 (AVX2+FMA); FillPath 1.4x ARM and 1.2x x86; C++ SIMD over C++ scalar up to 2.3x (x86) and 1.9x (ARM). The x86 ratios compare an AVX2+FMA C++ build with a Rust build that has no AVX enabled. The regression test's calibrated baselines (tests/benchmarks/run_render_perf_regression_test.sh) match the README on x86 (simd_over_rust 1.18 FillPath, 1.29 FillRect) but not on arm64 (simd_over_rust 2.90 FillPath and 3.50 FillRect; simd_over_scalar 2.80 and 3.90), so the README's ARM figures and the calibration disagree. No raw result files are published.
compiler_and_flags: Bazel -c opt. C++ library copts: -std=c++20 -ffp-contract=off -Wall -O3, plus -mavx2 -mfma for the native x86 build (bazel/defs.bzl); host C++ compiler and version not stated (CONTRIBUTING lists GCC 11+, Clang 14+ or MSVC 19.30+ as supported). Rust tiny-skia 0.12.0 is built through rules_rust 0.71.3 as a rust_static_library with no rustc target-cpu or target-feature flags (tests/rust_ffi/BUILD.bazel, MODULE.bazel), so it runs SSE2 code on x86-64; tiny-skia's README says AVX needs -Ctarget-cpu=haswell. Google Benchmark 1.9.5: 5 repetitions, min_time 0.2 s, mean real time; the Rust time is the average of its runs in the native and scalar binaries.
hardware: Apple Silicon (NEON) and Intel/AMD (AVX2+FMA), exact CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: CPU-only C++20 port of the Skia-subset algorithms with x86-64 AVX2+FMA and ARM64 NEON backends plus a scalar fallback, zero dependencies, Bazel or CMake. Output is near-pixel-accurate against Rust tiny-skia, not bit-exact (extra analytic AA and filter primitives). Only a subset of Skia features.
caveats: C++ port of linebender/tiny-skia, benchmarked only against its own Rust original, not against Skia, Cairo or Blend2D. On x86 the comparison is unequal: the C++ side is compiled with -mavx2 -mfma, the Rust side without AVX. On FillPath the two sides run different anti-aliasing algorithms: the C++ port fills anti-aliased paths with analytic AA (src/tiny_skia/scan/PathAa.cpp, ported from Skia's SkScan_AAAPath.cpp), which the README names as one reason its output is not bit-exact with Rust tiny-skia. The README's ARM ratios disagree with the arm64 baselines in the regression test (2.90x and 3.50x). Only two workloads at one size; CPU models and compiler versions not stated. Rust tiny-skia's README says it is 20-100% slower than Skia on x86-64 and 100-300% slower on ARM, so a 1.2-1.9x gain over it does not show the port beats Skia (inference). 9 stars, 156 commits; the latest commits (2026-07-04) are mostly renovate[bot] dependency bumps alongside one author commit.

name: libopus-rs
baseline: libopus, Opus trunk commit 03647f524a40b05a1898522e92033810b58103c7 (static .libs/libopus.a from an autotools tree; configure flags not recorded), called through the full opus_encode/opus_encode24 and opus_decode/opus_decode24 API
workload: 48 kHz stereo CELT-only, 5 ms (240-sample) frames, OPUS_APPLICATION_AUDIO, fullband, complexity 10, 16-bit and 24-bit PCM, CBR and constrained VBR at 192/256/320 kb/s. Direct in-process encode and decode of four 10 s excerpts from the private SoundKit diverse-v1 corpus. A 5 s warm-up, three alternating Rust/C rounds of seven internal repeats, the median per source, and four source medians summed per cell (40 s of audio). The C side runs the full Opus encoder/decoder layer (opus_encode with OPUS_SIGNAL_MUSIC). The Rust side runs the crate's own CELT-only raw-frame Encoder/Decoder.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.19-2.36% less time and decode 1.50-4.64% less time than trunk libopus in all 12 aggregate cells (e.g. 16-bit CBR 192 kb/s: encode 371.9 ms vs 380.9 ms, decode 95.3 ms vs 100.0 ms per 40 s of audio); Rust encoder 96.8-107.6x realtime, decoder 338-430x realtime.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1 / Cargo 1.97.1: release mode, ThinLTO, codegen-units=1, -C target-cpu=native. C driver tools/raw_celt_bench.c: GCC 12.2.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native, linked against the static libopus.a from the trunk commit. The libopus library's own configure string (optimisation level, intrinsics, --enable-float-approx) is recorded as unavailable. The final timing JSON records both build-flag fields as unknown because the binaries were reused.
hardware: GCP c4-highcpu-4 (4 vCPUs), Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C; measured processes pinned to CPU 2 with taskset; one x86 host only
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks, 53 commits; archived 2026-08-25. crates.io libopus-rs 0.0.2 (2026-06-30, before the benchmarked August checkpoint), 4,277 downloads.
tradeoffs: Incomplete codec: only 48 kHz CELT-only raw frames are supported; no SILK, hybrid or Ogg Opus. Not a drop-in replacement for libopus, no C API, and encoder packets are not byte-identical to libopus. Encoder is marked experimental. Uses a private SIMD kernel path dependency crate.
caveats: The gain is small (encode 1.19-2.36%, decode 1.50-4.64%) and covers one configuration family (48 kHz stereo CELT, 5 ms frames, maximum complexity, 192-320 kb/s) on one x86 host. The libopus.a build configuration was not recorded, and the project's own README warns that intrinsics and --enable-float-approx materially change the C baseline. Meanwhile the Rust side was built with target-cpu=native, ThinLTO and one codegen unit. At a 1-2% margin, build asymmetry cannot be ruled out. The work is not identical. C goes through the full opus_encode/opus_decode layer, including the 4 ms OPUS_APPLICATION_AUDIO delay compensation: the quality gate aligns C at 312 samples versus 120 for Rust. Rust is a CELT-only raw-frame codec that ports the tonality analysis but not that lookahead. Output is not bit-exact with libopus, and the README says the encoder does not target byte identity. CBR byte totals match (fixed by the bitrate), constrained-VBR totals differ by 350-527 B over 400 s, aligned SNR is within about 0.04 dB, and ViSQOL MOS-LQO is 4.5731 versus 4.5724. The packet-identity gate compares Rust with its own previous checkpoint, not with C. The codec is incomplete (no SILK, hybrid, Ogg Opus or other sample rates), and the README says it is not a production replacement for libopus. The timing corpus is licensed local audio that is not in the repo, and the raw timing JSONs are published only as SHA-256 hashes, so the run cannot be reproduced as published. The repository was archived on 2026-08-25 in favour of wavey-ai/soundkit (soundkit-opus). The README's soundkit-opus/libopus-rs link returned 404 on main. The crates.io release predates the measured optimisations.

name: opus-pure
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (float build)
workload: Encode and decode of generated, bit-reproducible 48 kHz test signals (speech for the SILK/hybrid rows with application voip and signal voice; music for the CELT rows with application audio, fullband, signal music), 20 ms frames, complexity 9 (plus complexity 0/5/10 rows), 8 s of audio per case. Fastest of 12 passes, a fresh encoder per pass built outside the timed region, OPUS_SET_LSB_DEPTH(24), and libopus constrained VBR at its default. Covers SILK, hybrid and CELT modes, mono and stereo.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.09-1.76x faster than libopus (SILK 1.09-1.12x, e.g. 218x vs 195x realtime for SILK NB 8 kb/s mono; CELT 128 kb/s 204x vs 116x realtime = 1.76x); decode slower or at parity, 0.84-1.02x of libopus (e.g. SILK NB 3432x vs 3958x realtime).
compiler_and_flags: Rust: cargo default release profile (no LTO or codegen-units override; the reference harness package adds debug=1 line tables only), no RUSTFLAGS, no target-cpu; the rustc version is not stated (MSRV 1.88.0). libopus 1.6.1 (sha256-pinned tarball) is built by reference/build.sh as a static CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release float build, NEON on with runtime dispatch, plus an OPUS_FIXED_POINT=ON build for the second table. The harness cspeed.c is compiled with cc -O2 -ffp-contract=off. The C compiler is the system cc (clang per the README), version not stated. Neither side uses -march=native.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64 NEON)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars, 3 forks, 19 commits; crates.io opus-pure 0.2.2 (2026-09-28), 15,474 downloads
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no C API or FFI exposed (callable from C++ only by writing a wrapper); no dependencies; hand-written NEON/SIMD kernels for CELT. Decode is not faster than libopus. Chunk-parallel encode is lossy relative to serial encode. Ogg reader seeks only to the start.
caveats: One aarch64 machine (Apple M1 Pro) only, no x86 numbers, and the toolchain versions are not pinned. Decode is slower than libopus in 9 of 10 rows (0.84-0.92x), with parity at 1.02x only for stereo hybrid. The large wins are CELT encode only (1.34-1.76x). The README says hybrid matches neither libopus build exactly. Encoder output is not bit-exact with libopus except SILK, which is byte-exact against fixed-point libopus in 22 configurations. name: opuspp
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 decoder (opus_decode_float), built with identical compiler and flags
workload: Decoding a 60 s mixed-audio stream (tones, noise, transients, orchestral music) encoded by libopus as 48 kHz fullband stereo, 10 ms CELT frames at 320 kb/s and encoder complexity 4; best of 7 passes pinned to one core, packet buffer flushed from cache before each pass. claimed_speedup: Like for like (same compiler and flags) opuspp is 1.27x to 1.48x faster than libopus at 320 kb/s (GCC Size 1.27x, GCC Balanced 1.48x, GCC Fast 1.43x, Clang Size 1.42x, Clang Balanced 1.46x, Clang Fast 1.42x); 1.09x to 1.50x across other bit rates, packet loss and encoder complexities. compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2 and Clang 22.1; Size: -Os, Balanced: -O2, Fast: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -falign-loops=32 (libopus with OPUS_FLOAT_APPROX=ON and OPUS_FAST_MATH=ON, opuspp with OPUSPP_FLOAT_APPROX); all with -DNDEBUG -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections and -Wl,--gc-sections

tradeoffs: Header-only freestanding C++23 decoder specialised to one stream type: CELT-only, fullband, 48 kHz stereo float output, 10 ms frames, prediction disabled, no pitch post-filter, no SILK, hybrid, FEC or DNN extensions. Bit-identical to libopus in strict-IEEE builds (47 encoder configurations, 300k-packet fuzz); the Fast profile is not bit-exact in either decoder. Smaller code (71-198 KB vs 98-236 KB static libopus) and decoder state (18.1 KB vs 26.6 KB), no heap or libm.
caveats: Code was written by Claude Code (the README says so); the repository has one commit (2026-10-02), 0 stars and no users yet. Decoder only, and only for one stream configuration: OPUS_APPLICATION_RESTRICTED_CELT, fullband, 10 ms frames, 48 kHz stereo float output, prediction disabled, encoder complexity 0-4, no SILK/hybrid/FEC/pitch post-filter; other packets are rejected. The comparison is like for like: both decoders decode the identical packet buffer, built with identical flags per profile (libopus with its default CMake options apart from hardening off, so its intrinsics/run-time CPU dispatch stay enabled), best of 7 passes with the packet buffer clflushed before each pass. name: rustrtc
baseline: webrtc-rs 0.17.1 (Rust) and pion/webrtc v3.3.6 (Go); no C or C++ stack (libwebrtc, libdatachannel, usrsctp) was compared
workload: WebRTC data-channel loopback benchmark (cargo run -r --example benchmark): 10 concurrent peer-connection pairs in one process (ICE/DTLS/SCTP, each with an idle Opus audio track), each sending 1 KiB messages on one data channel for 10 s. Throughput = bytes received / whole run time including setup (MiB/s, labelled MB/s). 'Setup latency' = time from connected to data-channel open, not ICE/DTLS setup; pion's is truncated to whole ms. CPU and RSS are sampled with ps every 500 ms. rustrtc's channel is reliable unordered (DataChannelConfig default ordered=false); webrtc-rs and pion channels are reliable ordered. The pion sender throttles on a 100 KB bufferedAmount threshold, while the Rust senders yield every 32 sends.
claimed_speedup: README, release 0.3.141: throughput 549.04 MB/s vs 165.98 (webrtc-rs) and 169.58 (pion), about 3.3x and 3.2x; message rate 562,214 vs 169,967 and 173,648 msg/s; data-channel open latency 0.45 ms vs 25.64 and 3.00 ms; peak RSS 21 MB vs 44 and 48 MB; CPU 739.62% vs 677.95% and 555.20% (higher for rustrtc); throughput per CPU-percent 0.74 vs 0.24 and 0.31 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.97.1 (8bab26f4f 2026-07-14) with Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto="fat", codegen-units=1, strip=symbols. This applies to both rustrtc and webrtc-rs, which are built into the same example binary by cargo run -r --example benchmark. go 1.24.4 linux/amd64, default go build for the pion program.
hardware: Intel Core i7-9700T @ 2.00GHz (8 cores), Debian 13, kernel 6.12.101+deb13-amd64
stars_or_usage: 110 stars, 20 forks, 352 commits; crates.io rustrtc 0.3.145 (2026-10-03), 15,220 downloads
tradeoffs: Pure Rust WebRTC, RTP/SRTP, T.38 fax and UPnP stack, no C API; claims interoperability with Chrome and pion. Uses more CPU than pion in the same run.
caveats: This is networking, not audio or video coding. The benchmark measures WebRTC data channels (SCTP over DTLS over UDP loopback), with no RTP media, codec or SRTP work in the timed path. The baselines are a Rust stack (webrtc-rs) and a Go stack (pion v3.3.6, an old major version), not C or C++; libwebrtc, libdatachannel and usrsctp were not compared. The configurations differ. rustrtc's channel is reliable unordered (DataChannelConfig derives Default, so ordered=false), while webrtc-rs and pion default to ordered reliable channels. The throughput workload is a near-unity ratio (1 + 200 ppm), not 44.1/48 kHz conversion. Quality pairing: soxr HQ (20-bit precision, about 120 dB rejection, passband to 91.3% of Nyquist per soxr.h) vs libsamplerate MEDIUM (filter table 120.61 dB stop band, 90% bandwidth per its docs) is a fair match; soxr VHQ (28-bit, about 170 dB, passband 91.3%) vs libsamplerate BEST (154.67 dB, 97% bandwidth) gives soxr more rejection but a narrower preserved band (about 21.9 kHz vs 23.3 kHz at 48 kHz, derived), both flat past 20 kHz; the page's AES17-style THD+N test puts soxr VHQ and libsamplerate sinc_best both at the format ceiling (-143.8 vs -143.5 dB, 24-bit I/O). Supporting evidence at a real conversion ratio: the python-soxr README (Google Colab, CPU unspecified, through Python bindings) times 10 s of 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz at 10.8 ms (soxr HQ) vs 223 ms (samplerate sinc_medium) and 14.5 ms (VHQ) vs 794 ms (sinc_best). soxr's speed comes with large latency (424-788 frames at HQ in this test), so it suits offline or batch work, not 1-2 ms live paths. The GitHub repo mirrors SourceForge; both end at 2018-02-24 (0.1.3); the maintained patched fork dofuuz/soxr (bundled by python-soxr) fixes integer-output dithering and enables NEON on AArch64, neither of which affects these float x86 numbers.

name: r8brain-free-src

name: edge264
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec H.264 decoder (README chart also shows LibAVC and OpenH264)
workload: Decoding the 1080p 10 s Big Buck Bunny H.264 clip (30 MB, converted to Annex B), median of 5 runs, every decoder single-threaded: edge264_test -by (n_threads 0, YUV comparison off; wall clock via CLOCK_MONOTONIC), ffmpeg -benchmark -threads 1 -c:v h264 -f null (the script reads the utime field, i.e. user CPU time), LibAVC avcdec with --num_cores 1 (wall clock around the process), OpenH264 h264dec (its own reported time); run on GitHub-hosted runners ubuntu-latest (x86-64) and ubuntu-24.04-arm (arm64).
claimed_speedup: README-benchmark.svg ('Decoding time measured on 27/07/2026 (lower is better)', median of 5 runs, all decoders single-threaded): x86-64 edge264 Clang 3.9 s, GCC 4.5 s, WASM 5.2 s, FFmpeg 4.6 s, LibAVC 6.4 s, OpenH264 8.2 s; arm64 edge264 Clang 3.8 s, GCC 3.9 s, WASM 5.0 s, FFmpeg 4.7 s, LibAVC 4.5 s, OpenH264 6.8 s. Clang build about 1.18x faster than single-threaded FFmpeg on x86-64 and 1.24x on arm64; the GCC build roughly ties FFmpeg on x86-64 (4.5 vs 4.6 s) and is about 1.2x faster on arm64 (derived from page data). FOSDEM'24 talk title linked from README: reach 10% faster speed and 3x code reduction over the state of the art.
compiler_and_flags: Stock GCC and Clang from the runner's Ubuntu apt packages (versions not pinned or stated), make STATIC=yes with Makefile flags -march=native -std=gnu11 -O3 -flax-vector-conversions; WASM via emmake with -mrelaxed-simd under Node; FFmpeg is the Ubuntu apt package (version not stated), LibAVC built with CMake Release, OpenH264 with its default make.
hardware: GitHub-hosted runners (ubuntu-latest for x86-64, ubuntu-24.04-arm for arm64) per .github/workflows/benchmarks.yml; CPU model and core count not stated.
tradeoffs: Supports Progressive High and MVC 3D profiles only, 8-bit 4:2:0; interlaced, higher bit depths and 4:2:2 are planned. Uses compiler vector extensions instead of hand-written assembly (SSE and NEON from one code path, WASM via Clang). README targets API freeze in 2027.
caveats: Numbers exist only as labels inside README-benchmark.svg, produced by the project's own CI (workflow_dispatch) on shared GitHub runners whose CPU model is not recorded; compiler and FFmpeg versions are the runner's apt defaults and are not pinned. The comparison is single-threaded only: FFmpeg is run with -threads 1, and stock edge264's multithreading is flagged experimental and is reported broken by the edge264-mvc fork, whose own chart shows multithreaded FFmpeg (2.4 s x86-64, 2.0 s arm64) beating multithreaded edge264-mvc (2.9 s, 2.6 s). Timing is asymmetric: edge264 is wall clock while the FFmpeg figure is the CLI's user CPU time (utime), which excludes system time and includes CLI demux and null-mux overhead. edge264 decodes only 8-bit 4:2:0 progressive High and MVC (no interlaced PAFF/MBAFF, no FMO, no 4:2:2/4:4:4 or high bit depth; 109/224 JVT conformance bitstreams decode), so FFmpeg is a full-featured decoder doing the same work on this progressive clip but covering far more; the benchmark disables output checking (-y). The fork documents correctness bugs in stock edge264 (SSE temporal-direct MV rounding off by up to a quarter pel, PPS scaling-matrix fall-back, high-QP 8x8 dequant overflow); whether the benchmark clip exercises them is not known. Pre-1.0, API freeze targeted for 2027.

name: fast-vad
baseline: webrtcvad (Google WebRTC voice activity detector, C)
workload: Relative processing speed of voice activity detection on speech audio (AVA-Speech and LibriVAD are the accuracy sets; which audio the speed figure used is not stated), with Silero VAD ONNX as the 1x reference. fast_vad offline (VAD.detect, all frames in parallel with rayon on 16 threads) and streaming (VadStateful, one 32 ms frame at a time) against webrtcvad through its Python binding (webrtcvad-wheels in the dev dependencies). The detectors do different work: fast_vad scores 32 ms (512-sample at 16 kHz) Hann-windowed FFT frames with an 8-band log-energy logistic-regression model, while webrtcvad uses its own model on 10, 20 or 30 ms frames; the frame size used for webrtcvad is not stated.

tradeoffs: Logistic-regression VAD on 8 log-energy bands (16 kHz and 8 kHz only, 32 ms frames); no C API (Rust and Python only); offline path uses rayon across cores. Accuracy is lower than Silero on hard audio.

baseline: FFmpeg native flac encoder (libavcodec); the same README table also measures libFLAC and SoX, and libFLAC is faster than go-flac
workload: Encode at level 5, single-threaded, of a deterministic 30-minute mono 48 kHz/16-bit generated mix using scripts/bench-encoders.sh; plus a 2026-09-05 snapshot on real 48 kHz recordings at 16/24/32-bit.
claimed_speedup: Input MB/s on the default input: amd64 (i7-1260P) go-flac 147 vs ffmpeg 128 (about 1.15x, derived from page data), libFLAC 229, SoX 194; arm64 (Cortex-A76) go-flac 51 vs ffmpeg 48 (about 1.06x, derived), libFLAC 76. Real-recording snapshot: 16-bit about 19 ms vs about 71 ms, 24-bit about 25 ms vs about 61 ms for ffmpeg flac (machine not stated). README: 'libFLAC's reference encoder remains about 1.5x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: go-flac built with plain 'go build' (default flags; Go toolchain version not stated, go.mod declares go 1.27). Baselines run as 'ffmpeg -threads 1 -c:a flac -compression_level 5', 'flac -5 -f -s', 'sox -C 5'; their versions and builds are not stated.
hardware: Intel i7-1260P (amd64) and Cortex-A76 (arm64); machine for the real-recording snapshot not stated
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, SIMD kernels (AVX2 on amd64, NEON on arm64) bit-identical to the scalar fallback. Stays bit-exact at 32-bit where the README says ffmpeg's FLAC encoder truncates to 24-bit. Go only, so C++ callers would need a c-shared build or a rewrite.
caveats: First-party claim with a public harness (scripts/bench-encoders.sh). That harness supports only the throughput claim, and modestly: on the harness table go-flac is 1.15x (amd64) and 1.06x (arm64) faster than ffmpeg's flac encoder (derived from page data). libFLAC is about 1.5x faster than go-flac. Each encoder is timed once with GNU time, so the wall time includes process start-up and WAV parsing, and the arm64 margin is within run-to-run noise. All encoders run level 5, single-threaded, on the same file, so they do comparable work. The default input is a synthetic 440 Hz sine plus white-noise mono mix (ratio about 0.85), not music. The README contradicts itself on compression ratio. 'Audio quality' says go-flac 'encodes faster and slightly smaller than ffmpeg's FLAC'. The benchmark section says it 'matches libFLAC's compression ratio exactly and beats ffmpeg on both throughput and ratio on each architecture'. Yet the README's own harness table lists go-flac 0.8523 vs ffmpeg 0.8519 (and SoX 0.8519), so ffmpeg's output is smaller and the ratio claim is contradicted by the only harnessed data. 'Slightly smaller' rests only on the 16-bit row of the 2026-09-05 snapshot (0.45 vs 0.46; 24-bit equal at 0.64; 32-bit 0.51 vs 0.48 where ffmpeg truncates to 24-bit). That snapshot has no script in the repo, no stated machine, and the README calls it 'a small directional sample'; a corpus-based gate is still open as issue #45. Young repo (commits from July 2026).

name: HALAC (High Availability Lossless Audio Compression)
baseline: FLAC 1.5.0 (flac CLI) at -8 and -5. The 0.5.4 notes also list WavPack 5.9.0 -h and HALAC 0.5.1. Monkey's Audio, WavPack and OptimFROG (versions not stated) appear only in the 0.4.8 notes for the 32-bit float set.
workload: Single-thread encode and decode of six BipTunia albums, 24-bit 44.1 kHz stereo, about 5.88 GB, release 0.5.4 notes; a separate 29-song 32-bit float set (about 2 GB) in release 0.4.8 notes.
claimed_speedup: Release 0.5.4 notes, 'AMD Ryzen 9 9600X, Single Thread', six BipTunia albums, 5,883,941,384 bytes of 24-bit/44.1 kHz stereo WAV. HALAC 0.5.4 -plus: 4,232,751,891 bytes, 11.578 s encode, 13.201 s decode. FLAC 1.5.0 -8: 4,243,522,638 bytes, 50.802 s, 14.357 s. That is about 4.4x faster encode and 1.09x faster decode with 0.25% smaller output (derived from page data). HALAC 0.5.4 -normal: 4,268,470,589 bytes, 7.200 s, 9.353 s. FLAC 1.5.0 -5: 4,265,600,750 bytes, 15.857 s, 13.451 s. That is about 2.2x faster encode and 1.44x faster decode with 0.07% larger output (derived from page data). WavPack 5.9.0 -h: 4,263,185,834 bytes, 64.855 s, 49.367 s. Release 0.4.8 notes, 29 tracks of 32-bit float stereo, 2,089,718,160 bytes, 'HALAC AVX2 Single thread', no FLAC row. HALAC normal 1,381,439,835 bytes, 3.050 s / 4.290 s, versus WavPack fast 1,392,225,168 bytes, 20.675 s / 13.914 s, and OptimFROG fast 1,346,477,460 bytes, 39.310 s / 32.179 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. 0.5.4 ships closed Windows executables built for AVX, AVX2 and AVX512, and the notes do not say which was timed; the 0.4.8 notes say 'HALAC AVX2 Single thread'. FLAC 1.5.0 build and options beyond -8/-5 are not stated.
hardware: 'AMD Ryzen 9 9600X' as written in the 0.5.4 notes (AMD sells the 9600X as a Ryzen 5), single thread. OS not stated; the release assets are Windows .exe files.
tradeoffs: Uses ANS (FSE) entropy coding instead of Rice coding, trading a few percent of compression for speed; OptimFROG compresses better. Releases cover 16/24-bit and 32-bit float PCM and up to 128 channels. No SIMD/GPU in early versions, AVX2 and multithreading added from 0.4.3.
caveats: First-party release-note numbers with no benchmark script, compiler, OS or timing method, and the test albums are not distributed, so tier C. The measured code is not public. The repository source is only v0.1.9 (halac_encode/decode_v.0.1.9 plus FSE), last changed 2025-11-17. Its encoder prints 'Only 16 bit, 2 channels .wav types are supported for input!', reads 2-byte samples, and its main() walks a hard-coded Windows test directory, so it cannot even encode the 24-bit benchmark set. The release 'Source code' archives for 0.4.8 and 0.5.4 are that same 2025-11-17 snapshot, and the 0.5.4 encoder exists only as HALAC_ENCODE_0.5.4_AVX/AVX2/AVX512.exe (2026-04-10). The comparison names the machine and the settings (single thread; HALAC -plus vs FLAC -8 and -normal vs FLAC -5, levels paired by similar output size). It does not say whether FLAC's default whole-stream MD5 and per-frame CRCs were left on. The public v0.1.9 encoder computes no MD5 or CRC, so if 0.5.4 also skips them, the two encoders do different integrity work. The headline 4.4x is against FLAC's slowest standard preset; against -5 it is 2.2x encode, and the decode gap is small (1.09x to 1.44x). Releases continue to 0.6.6 (dated 26 Sep, year not shown). name: LibFResample
baseline: libsamplerate (Secret Rabbit Code 0.1.8)
workload: Resampling 16-bit stereo and mono audio from 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz, measured as multiples of real time on four machines.
claimed_speedup: Stereo, System C (3.2 GHz AMD Phenom II, GCC 4.7): LibFResample Q=5 Medium 1276x realtime vs libsamplerate Sinc Med. 35x and Sinc Fast 68x; Q=8 High 318x vs Sinc Best 8.5x; System D (1.7 GHz Core i5, Clang 4.0): Q=5 1247x vs Sinc Med. 39x. Mono Q=2 Low 3195x vs libsamplerate Linear 1112x (System D). Pairs closer in passband width: Q=8 High (19.5 kHz) vs Sinc Med. (90% bandwidth) 318x vs 35x on System C (about 9.1x, derived from page data) and 303x vs 39x on System D (about 7.8x, derived from page data); Q=10 Ultra (21.2 kHz) vs Sinc Best (97% bandwidth) 107x vs 8.5x on System C (about 12.6x, derived from page data) and 87x vs 11x on System D (about 7.9x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.4 (System A), GCC 4.0 (B), GCC 4.7 (C), Clang 4.0 (D); optimization flags not stated
hardware: 1.6 GHz Intel Atom, 2.0 GHz PowerPC G5, 3.2 GHz AMD Phenom II, 1.7 GHz Intel Core i5
tradeoffs: Only 16-bit mono/stereo input, no error reporting, SSE2 and AltiVec only, no Windows port; README itself says it is not release quality. Quality table: Q=5 gives 16.3 kHz bandwidth and 84 dB SNR, Q=8 19.5 kHz and 92 dB; filter is a plain Kaiser-windowed sinc.
caveats: Numbers are from 2005-2012 hardware and libsamplerate 0.1.8. The headline Q=5 Medium setting does less work than the libsamplerate converters it is paired with: by LibFResample's own quality table Q=5 keeps 16.3 kHz at 84 dB SNR, while libsamplerate documents 97 dB SNR at 90% bandwidth for Sinc Medium (about 19.8 kHz at 44.1 kHz output) and 80% (about 17.6 kHz) for Sinc Fast, and its MEDIUM filter table states 120.61 dB stop-band attenuation. Q=8 and Q=10 match libsamplerate's Medium and Best bandwidths more closely but measure 92 dB SNR (limited by the 16-bit dithered test floor), so stop-band parity is unproven. The two sides were timed by different harnesses: LibFResample on 16-bit pink noise (tests/benchmark.py, 20 iterations), libsamplerate by its own throughput test, which in the current libsamplerate source runs mono float data at ratio 0.99 through src_simple, so the stereo SRC rows are likely mono-test figures (not confirmed for 0.1.8). Optimization flags are not stated. The README says the library is not release quality (16-bit mono/stereo only, no error reporting). Baseline is not an FFmpeg component, so baseline_in_list is false. name: minimp3
baseline: keyj's minimp3 (Martin J. Fiedler's fixed-point single-file MP3 decoder, https://keyj.emphy.de/minimp3/)
workload: Decoding the ISO/IEC 11172-4 and 13818-4 MP3 conformance vectors (compl.bit, he_*.bit, si*.bit, sin1k0db.bit); CPU clockticks measured with perf, I/O included.
claimed_speedup: README tables (clockticks, lower is better): compl.bit 14,306,684 vs 31,849,373 for keyj's minimp3 (about 2.2x fewer, derived from page data); he_44khz 21,296,300 vs 41,628,861 (about 2.0x, derived); hecommon 3,169,715 vs 20,437,779 (about 6.4x, derived); sin1k0db 24,842,977 vs 55,569,636 (about 2.2x, derived). Conformance: PSNR 107-144 dB for this minimp3 versus 0.15-72 dB for keyj's, which fails conformance on all vectors.
hardware: i7-6700K, speedstep effects avoided, measured with perf
tradeoffs: Single-header C decoder with SSE and NEON intrinsics, floating-point output; CC0 means no patent grant. The baseline is a fixed-point decoder with no vector code, so the comparison is between different design points.
caveats: Baseline is the original keyj minimp3, a small fixed-point hobby decoder that fails conformance on every vector (PSNR 71-72 dB on most, 27.80 dB on si_huff.bit and 0.15 dB on sin1k0db.bit) and decodes nothing on he_free.bit, so on several vectors it is not producing correct output (sin1k0db sample counts also differ, 730,368 vs 725,760); the speed rows compare a conformant decoder with a broken one. No number against libmpg123, libmad, FFmpeg or dr_mp3 is published in the repo, and none was found elsewhere. The only independent figure found is FastLED's Callgrind count (agents/docs/mp3-decoder-performance.md, its vendored minimp3-float build, scalar -DMINIMP3_NO_SIMD at -O2, x86-64): 202,832,660 instructions vs 222,939,814 for the Helix MP3 decoder, about 9% fewer, instruction counts rather than time. Compiler and flags for the README table are not stated (the CI script scripts/build.sh builds with gcc -O2 -std=c89); the timed process includes file I/O and the PSNR comparison against the reference PCM. name: NonIntegerSRC (Holters-Parker resampler)
baseline: libsamplerate (SRC_SINC_FASTEST)
workload: One timed pass (std::chrono, no warm-up, no repeats) resampling a 1,000,000-sample 100 Hz float sine in 2048-sample blocks, mono, for four ratios (2.0, 0.5, 1.088, 0.919; the 44.1k/48k ratios are rounded), comparing the SSE-vectorised Holters-Parker multi-rate IIR resampler (src/HPResampler.h, src/src_utils/HPFilters.h) against libsamplerate SRC_SINC_FASTEST (src/LibSamplerRateSRC.h), harness src/src_test.cpp.
claimed_speedup: Speed factor of the Holters-Parker resampler over libsamplerate SRC_SINC_FASTEST, from doc/speed_chart.png: 48k to 96k 39.8x, 96k to 48k 16.9x, 44.1k to 48k 21.2x, 48k to 44.1k 21.8x (doc/writeup.md: '10-40x faster'). Not quality-matched: the HP resampler runs a 4th-order IIR filter, libsamplerate SINC_FASTEST is a 97 dB SNR / 80% bandwidth sinc converter.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler and version not stated. Documented build is 'cmake -Bbuild; cmake --build build --config Release'; on a single-config Linux generator '--config Release' is ignored and neither the top-level CMakeLists.txt nor the current libsamplerate and libsndfile CMakeLists.txt set a default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so the optimisation level of the measured build is unknown (possibly unoptimised). libsamplerate is built from the third_party/libsamplerate submodule with the same flags as the HP code.
hardware: Linux machine with an Intel i7 CPU, model not stated (doc/writeup.md); the author also reports comparable results on a Mac and close to 40x on Windows, without numbers.
tradeoffs: Holters-Parker resampler uses SSE-vectorised 4th-order IIR filters (from a DAFx-2018 paper) rather than a windowed-sinc FIR, so quality (aliasing and passband) differs from libsamplerate; the Lanczos resampler and SSE complex classes are borrowed from Surge Synthesizer. GPLv3 copyleft.
caveats: The two sides do different work. The HP resampler uses one 4th-order analog filter (the JUNO-60 bucket-brigade filter poles and zeros from Holters and Parker's DAFx 2018 paper, per src/src_utils/HPFilters.h; the README and writeup call it a 4th-order Butterworth), while libsamplerate SRC_SINC_FASTEST is documented at 97 dB SNR and 80% bandwidth (docs/api_misc.md). The author's own quality plot doc/HP_compare.png shows HP output with spurious components up to about -47 dB against a roughly -10 dB fundamental, where libsamplerate's spectrum stays smooth (read from the plot), and doc/writeup.md says 'I'm primarily interested in speed rather than quality'. In src/HPResampler.h the filter cutoff is set to the input Nyquist (sample_rate*0.5) for every ratio, so for 96k to 48k the anti-aliasing cutoff (48 kHz) sits above the 24 kHz output Nyquist (derived from code reading). Timing is a single pass on a 100 Hz sine with no repeats; quality stats are computed in src_test.cpp but never printed. Compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated. The code uses SSE intrinsics (x86 only) and code from the GPL-3.0 Surge Synthesizer. Last commit 2021-07-12.

name: OpenVVC
baseline: VTM reference decoder and Fraunhofer VVdeC
workload: Software decoding of VVC (H.266) bit-streams on multi-core x86 and embedded ARM platforms; also a live 4K intra end-to-end pipeline paper.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (all papers blocked): the arXiv 2205.12217 abstract says OpenVVC reaches real-time UHD decoding by combining SIMD with frame-level parallelism, decodes faster than VVdeC, and uses less memory than VVdeC by a factor greater than 2.11x. An independent study (Journal of Real-Time Image Processing 2023, 'Performance analysis of optimized versatile video coding software decoders on embedded platforms') found OpenVVC and VVdeC both reach real-time FHD on an 8-core and HD on a 4-core embedded platform with comparable energy (about 26 J and 15 J), with VVdeC needing 2x OpenVVC's memory; that is a memory win, not a speed win. The ACM MMSys 2023 end-to-end pipeline (uvg266 encoder + uvgRTP + OpenVVC) is almost 34,000x as fast as a VTM-based pipeline and 3.3x the fastest VVenC/VVdeC configuration; those are whole-pipeline figures that include the encoder, not decoder-only speedups. The 290 fps FHD / 90 fps UHD figures in the original record did not appear in any snippet this verifier saw.
tradeoffs: Supports 8-bit bit-streams, frame and tile parallelism, RPR; README says it is still under development. Lightweight, lower memory than VVdeC.
caveats: Snippet only: every number comes from search snippets of blocked papers (arXiv 2205.12217; ACM MMSys 2023 'Open-Source Toolkit for Live End-to-End 4K VVC Intra Coding'; Springer JRTIP 2023 independent study at https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11554-023-01376-7); none was opened, and the repo README has no numbers or benchmark harness. The baselines are the VTM reference decoder and Fraunhofer VVdeC, not FFmpeg; no comparison against FFmpeg's native VVC decoder was found. The independent study shows parity in speed with VVdeC and a 2x memory advantage, so the speed claim rests on the authors' own paper. The 34,000x figure is an end-to-end pipeline result dominated by the encoder choice. Last commit on master is 2022-03-22 (2,197 commits), so the code may lag the papers' decoder; README still says 'still under development' and supports only 8-bit bitstreams. LGPL-2.1.

name: pedalboard
baseline: pySoX (Python wrapper that runs the SoX command-line program), SoxBindings (Python bindings to libsox) and librosa.load (audio file reading)
workload: Python audio effect processing for single transforms and audio file reading, compared against pySoX, SoxBindings and librosa.load.
claimed_speedup: README, under 'Even when only using one thread': processes audio up to 300x faster than pySoX for single transforms and 2-5x faster than SoxBindings (via iCorv/pedalboard_with_tfdata), and reads audio files up to 4x faster than librosa.load 'in many cases'. The cited SoxBindings notebook times six single effects on LJ Speech at 22.05 kHz: SoxBindings 73.1/130.8/38.1/38.6/76.7/105.2 s against pedalboard 11.6/26.3/10.9/10.8/32.2/20.9 s (Compressor, Chorus, HighpassFilter, LowpassFilter, Phaser, Reverb), i.e. 2.4-6.3x (derived from page data). But pedalboard ran with tf.data num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE while SoxBindings ran serially, and a single Pedalboard effect chain was slower than the SoxBindings chain (357.2 s vs 305.2 s, 0.85x, derived from page data); only splitting the chain into parallel tf.data stages won (82.1 s). PR #85 first claimed 'up to 20x faster than librosa.load in certain cases', later tempered; no method given.
tradeoffs: Python-first API on a JUCE C++ core; GPL-3.0 (copyleft, commercial licensing through JUCE terms may apply); releases the GIL so multiple cores can be used; wheels cover macOS, Windows and Linux.
caveats: First-party claims without benchmark code, corpus, machine or compiler in the repo; no FFmpeg, libsamplerate or resampling comparison anywhere in the README, so the video-audio category fit is weak (the baselines are Python audio-effect and file-loading wrappers, not FFmpeg, x264/x265 or Opus). The 300x figure against pySoX includes pySoX launching a SoX subprocess and file I/O per transform, so it mostly measures process overhead. The only public numbers behind the SoxBindings claim (iCorv/pedalboard_with_tfdata notebook) ran pedalboard multi-threaded via tf.data AUTOTUNE against serial SoxBindings, contradicting the README's 'even when only using one thread', compared SoX and JUCE effects at default parameters (different algorithms), and showed a single Pedalboard chain slower than SoxBindings (357.2 s vs 305.2 s). The librosa figure traces to PR #85 ('up to 20x... in certain cases', later tempered to 4x) with no method. The C++ core is a pybind11 extension module (C++17, -O3 release builds) and is not shipped as a standalone C++ library; C++ users would use JUCE directly. GPL-3.0, with JUCE, Rubber Band and LAME linked in under GPL terms.

name: remade_ffmpeg_rs
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec native MP3 decoder and native AAC encoder; libvorbis
workload: MP3 decode of a 27.5-minute stream, decode-and-discard on the same physical cores, 15 pairs; AAC-LC encode of a 60 s stereo clip with frame-parallel encoding; Vorbis encode of stereo music on 24 cores.
claimed_speedup: Per component, all first-party. MP3 decode (crate rusty_mp3, crates/rusty_mp3/README.md) vs the FFmpeg CLI's native libavcodec MP3 decoder (`-f null -`, not libmp3lame or mpg123), 27.5-minute stream, decode-and-discard, wall clock, 15 alternated pairs: 1 physical core 1,952 vs 2,431 ms (1.24x, 15/15, z = -3.87); 2 physical cores, pipelined build 1,017 vs 1,455 ms (1.39x); total CPU on one core 1,875 vs 2,125 ms (1.13x less CPU, derived from page data). The same table's control row shows the serial rusty_mp3 build on 2 cores at 1,807 ms against FFmpeg's 1,445 ms, i.e. FFmpeg 1.25x faster (derived from page data), because FFmpeg's CLI spreads work over about 2 cores even with -threads 1. AAC-LC encode (crate rusty_aac) vs FFmpeg 8.1.2's native AAC encoder (`-c:a aac`, not libfdk_aac): main README about 6x faster on a 60 s stereo clip (about 450x realtime) via frame-parallel encoding against FFmpeg's single-threaded encoder, about 1.15x single-thread; the crate README reports 3.2-7.9x (mean 5.0x) on 24 s clips (piano 214x vs 57x realtime, guitar 306x vs 39x, vocal 299x vs 93x), best-of-5, unpinned subprocesses. Vorbis encode (crate rusty_vorbis) vs libvorbis via `ffmpeg -c:a libvorbis`: at about 140 kb/s, 443x realtime on 24 cores vs libvorbis 86x (about 5.2x in docs/benchmarks.md, 5.3x in the README), but single-thread 60x vs 87x realtime (about 1.45x slower than libvorbis), and libvorbis is 0.6-0.7 PEAQ ODG ahead on tonal content at matched bitrate. Image rows (PNG decode 2.55-2.89x, lossy WebP decode 1.24-1.29x vs FFmpeg) are outside video-audio.

name: ruopus
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (SIMD-enabled C)
workload: In-process mono 48 kHz Opus decode and encode of a 6 s synthetic speech/music-like signal (tones under a syllabic envelope plus light noise) in 20 ms frames, one core, reported as x realtime (benches/vs_libopus.rs, timed until each run exceeds about 0.4 s). Decode inputs are libopus-encoded VBR packets for SILK WB 16 kb/s (VoIP), hybrid FB 32 kb/s (VoIP) and CELT FB 64 kb/s (Audio); each repetition builds a new decoder or encoder on both sides.
claimed_speedup: README (x realtime, one pinned core; ratio = ruopus/libopus): decode SILK WB 16 kb/s 2095x vs 1171x (1.79x), hybrid FB 32 kb/s 1199x vs 850x (1.41x), CELT FB 64 kb/s 1389x vs 1566x (0.89x, slower). Encode at matched complexity 0: 734x vs 740x (0.99x), 560x vs 562x (1.00x), 1088x vs 1092x (1.00x). Encode against libopus at complexity 10 (ruopus also set to 10): SILK WB 16 kb/s 703x vs 221x (3.18x), hybrid FB 32 kb/s 424x vs 193x (2.20x), CELT FB 64 kb/s 693x vs 432x (1.60x); ruopus's complexity-10 encoder omits delayed-decision NSQ and warped noise shaping, so these ratios compare unequal work.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench vs_libopus --features std; release profile opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1 (Cargo.toml); libopus 1.6.1 reached through the opus FFI crate against the system libopus, so its build flags are not stated.
hardware: one core pinned to a single performance core; CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 1 star; on crates.io as ruopus (about 6.9k downloads)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust Opus encoder and decoder with Python bindings and wasm32 support; no C API or FFI exposed, so C++ use needs a wrapper. Encoder does not yet implement delayed-decision noise-shaping quantization or warped noise shaping.
caveats: Baseline is libopus itself (not another Rust port), linked via the opus 0.3 FFI crate against the system libopus (1.6.1 per the README); its build flags and SIMD dispatch are not stated, nor are the CPU model, OS or rustc version. Decode is comparable work, but output is not bit-exact PCM: the decoder passes all twelve RFC 8251 vectors at 99.2-100% on opus_compare with bit-exact per-packet final ranges, while PCM differs in float rounding (default spectrograms/rustfft MDCT backend). The encoder produces a different bitstream from libopus, and its quality is checked only by waveform SNR (examples/encoder_quality.rs; the CHANGELOG reports higher SNR than libopus), not a perceptual metric. At complexity 10, ruopus skips delayed-decision NSQ and warped noise shaping that libopus runs, so the 1.6-3.18x encode wins compare unequal work; at matched complexity 0, encode is at parity. In the encode bench, ruopus chooses its mode through encode_auto, while libopus gets an explicit application and VBR setting, and the bench does not check that both pick the same mode. CELT decode is slower than libopus. The signal is synthetic. The library is pure Rust with no C API (Python bindings via PyO3), so C++ use needs a custom FFI shim.

The headline 3.18x encode figure compares ruopus at its fixed effort against libopus complexity 10; at matched complexity 0, encode is at parity. The decode wins (1.41-1.79x on SILK and hybrid) are like-for-like work. verify.py does not apply 'language' from corrections, so record it as a decision override.

name: rusty-av1-toolkit
baseline: stock rav1e (AV1 encoder); decoder side is a fork of rav1d, itself a Rust port of dav1d
workload: Real rav1e CLI: fork at opt-entropy HEAD 885a2887 vs stock rav1e 564ae3b0 (merge-base with xiph/master), both built with 'identical flags'; one synthetic 640x480, 60-frame ffmpeg testsrc2 clip, --speed 6 --quantizer 100 --tiles 1 --threads 1, 7 interleaved rounds, median wall-clock. A QP sweep (QP 60/100/160, 9/5/5 rounds) and the --racecar on ('nitro') runs (5 interleaved rounds) used the same clip on the same unnamed machine, which the ledger says has about 5% thermal noise.
claimed_speedup: Default --racecar off (byte-identical to stock rav1e, 262,180 B): median 7.588 s vs 6.911 s = 1.098x (per-round 1.072-1.117x); QP sweep 1.126x at QP 60, 1.099x at QP 100, 1.058x at QP 160. Opt-in --racecar on (rav1e's existing tx_domain_rate + tx_domain_distortion options plus the kernels): 4.586 s vs 7.745 s for the stock code path = 1.69x (1.61x over the byte-identical mode at 7.399 s), but the bitstream grows from 262,180 to 419,010 B (+60%) and PSNR drops from 44.50 to 42.22 dB (-2.28 dB) at the default tune; with --tune Psnr the probe measured +48% size and -1.13 dB. Decoder: no speed claim ('same as rav1d, profiled at its performance floor').
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the ledger says only that both binaries were 'built with identical flags'. rusty_av1e/Cargo.toml release profile uses lto = "thin" and debug = true; asm feature needs nasm; minimum rust-version 1.83.0, actual rustc version not given.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 1 fork, 112 commits; crates.io rusty_av1e 0.8.0 (1,270 downloads) and rusty_av1d 1.2.0 (1,492 downloads); README banner claims 1,002 active installs (not verifiable).
tradeoffs: Encoder fork of rav1e (not a GitHub fork: the parent code is vendored into rusty_av1e/) with tuned hot kernels and asm; the content-adaptive 'RAV1E_FAST=fast' tier trades quality for speed and is content-dependent (measured +5.3% bus, +3.3% akiyo, -8.7% mobile BD-rate vs the default at speed 6). Rust only; the baseline is rav1e, not libaom, SVT-AV1 or x265.
caveats: First-party, one synthetic 640x480 60-frame testsrc2 clip at speed 6, single thread and single tile; the machine, rustc version and flags are not named, and the A/B script (scratchpad/ab.sh) is not in the repo, although the binary keeps a '--racecar stock' mode that reproduces the stock code paths. The 1.10x gain is content dependent (1.058x to 1.126x by QP) and sits near the box's stated 5% thermal noise. The 1.69x mode is a quality trade, not a free speedup: it turns on rav1e's own tx-domain rate estimation (which stock rav1e leaves off at every speed) and costs +60% bitstream and -2.28 dB PSNR at the default tune; its 1.69x divides by a stock time taken from a separate sweep session. The numbers belong to this fork's own encoder kernels (B7a nz-map stencil, its AVX2 twin, Q2 branchless quantize), not to the vendored rav1e or rav1d projects; the decoder half (rav1d fork) has no speed claim. Not a GitHub fork; is_fork_of rav1e for the encoder, the decoder forks memorysafety/rav1d. Rust code with a Rust baseline (rav1e is not a wave-10 list baseline and not in the catalog). Part of Mata Network's 'Remade With Rust' initiative; README opens with an install-count banner and an advert. AV1 patent grant comes from the AOM Patent License 1.0 in rusty_av1e/PATENTS, separate from the BSD-2-Clause source license.

name: rusty_flac
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 native flac encoder and decoder (libavcodec)
workload: Single-core comparison, both binaries pinned to one core at High priority, ABBA-alternated, 31 pairs, on a 180 s 44.1 kHz stereo music clip (guitar, piano, vocal): encode at -compression_level 8, and decode of an FFmpeg-encoded stream. Per the README, outputs are verified lossless before timing; the public tools/flac_gate.ps1 checks lossless round trips in both directions (SHA-256 of decoded PCM) and sizes on 10 clips x levels 5 and 8, but the timing harness itself is not published.
claimed_speedup: Single-core, pinned, CPU time on one 180 s 44.1 kHz stereo music clip against FFmpeg 8.1.2's native flac: encode at -compression_level 8 672 ms vs 813 ms (0.83x, 17.3% faster), decode of an FFmpeg-encoded stream 266 ms vs 344 ms (0.77x, 22.7% faster), 31/31 paired wins on both (z = 5.57 is the sign-test value for 31/31). Smaller-file claim (20 of 20 gate combos, e.g. stereo guitar s24 L8 539,087 vs 565,122 bytes) is inflated: FFmpeg's flac muxer writes an 8,192-byte PADDING block by default (libavformat/flacenc.c, metadata_header_padding = -1 becomes 8192) plus a Vorbis comment, which flac_gate.ps1 does not disable, while rusty_flac writes only fLaC + STREAMINFO. Subtracting roughly 8.2 KB of metadata (derived from page data): guitar s24 about -3.2% and piano s16 about -1.1% remain, but pink noise s24 (delta 8,100 B), vocal s16 (8,024 B) and silence (7,964 B) become ties or slightly larger for rusty_flac.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the timed builds. Cargo.toml only sets edition 2021 and rust-version 1.85 (minimum); no RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu are given. FFmpeg arm is the prebuilt Gyan 'ffmpeg-8.1.2-full_build' Windows binary (default path in remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/flac_gate.ps1).
hardware: CPU model not stated ('single core, this machine'). The gate script's default FFmpeg path is a Windows Gyan 'ffmpeg-8.1.2-full_build' package, so the box is a Windows x86-64 PC (inferred); four AVX2 kernels are runtime-detected.
stars_or_usage: 1 star, 0 forks; crates.io rusty_flac 1,348 total downloads (0.1.0 on 2026-08-13 to 0.2.0 on 2026-09-30); README claims 321 active installs via one downstream app (RAG Converter), not verifiable
tradeoffs: Pure Rust (no_std plus alloc capable, unsafe only in four AVX2 kernels with scalar twins), no C API, so C++ use needs an FFI shim. FLAC subset with LPC orders up to 12. Part of the Remade With Rust ecosystem, which also ships remade_ffmpeg_rs.
caveats: Rust crate, not C++ (wave language filter mismatch). First-party claim: CPU model, compiler and rustc flags are not stated, and the pinned ABBA CPU-time harness for FLAC is not identifiable in remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/bench (pinab.py reads a self-reported time with a kbps argument; codec-bench.ps1 is a video-frame harness), so its command lines (for example whether FFmpeg got -threads 1) are unknown. Like-for-like on threading: both arms are pinned to one core and FFmpeg's flac encoder is single-threaded; FFmpeg's flac decoder has frame threading (AV_CODEC_CAP_FRAME_THREADS), so without -threads 1 any extra FFmpeg threads would share the pinned core and add overhead to the FFmpeg decode arm. All four timing figures are integer multiples of the Windows 15.625 ms CPU-time tick (43, 52, 17 and 22 ticks, derived from page data), the clock the group's own codec-bench.ps1 calls tick accounting rather than a clock; the gaps are 9 and 5 ticks, so the direction is plausible but each ratio has about 2-6% resolution. Single 180 s clip for speed; the timed clip and the corpus are not published. Compression levels do not do the same work: rusty_flac's level maps to LPC order only with estimate-gated search, FFmpeg's level 8 uses its own order-search method. The smaller-file claim is inflated by FFmpeg's default 8,192-byte PADDING block (see claimed_speedup); on pink noise, vocal and silence rusty_flac's audio payload is not smaller. The baseline is FFmpeg's flac, not the reference libFLAC, which was not tested. Lossless interop is gated in public code (flac_gate.ps1) on 20 clip-level combos. Young project with rapid release churn (48 commits, v0.2.0 on 2026-09-30).

name: SampleRateTap (async engine)
baseline: libsamplerate 0.2.2 (Secret Rabbit Code, MEDIUM and BEST converters)
workload: A fixed, known near-unity ratio (48000 to 48009.6 Hz, 1 + 200 ppm) applied to a 997 Hz float sine streamed in 128-frame blocks, for mono, stereo and 8-channel streams, measured in million output frames per second. SampleRateTap runs only its fractional_resampler datapath with a constant rate deviation; the servo is quiescent and clock recovery is not timed. libsamplerate gets the ratio through src_process. Algorithmic latency is also reported. The embedded rows count QEMU executed instructions per stereo output frame (32-frame blocks; 2 s and 4 s runs separate steady-state from construction cost).
claimed_speedup: COMPARISON.md (host x86, 2026-09-25, million output frames/s, median of 5) reports SampleRateTap 3.1-3.9x faster than libsamplerate 0.2.2 (stereo/mono; 1.5x at 8 channels) at the ~120 dB tier and 6.1x at the ~140 dB tier, with about 2-3.6x less latency. Table rows: balanced vs libsamplerate MEDIUM: mono 20.3 vs 5.2, stereo 14.6 vs 4.8, 8-ch 3.0 vs 1.9; transparent vs libsamplerate BEST: stereo 9.6 vs 1.6. Latency is 24 vs 46 frames (MEDIUM) and 40 vs 143 frames (BEST). The tiers are paired by vendor-stated stopband depth only. On the same page SampleRateTap is SLOWER than soxr HQ (114.3 mono, 52.9 stereo, 12.9 8-ch) and r8brain-free-src 120 dB (35.4 mono, 16.5 stereo, 4.1 8-ch). In embedded steady-state instruction counts (QEMU, stereo, 32-frame blocks), libsamplerate MEDIUM executes 2.7x (Cortex-M55), 3.2x (Cortex-M33) and 3.3x (Hexagon) more instructions per output frame than SampleRateTap balanced float, and BEST executes 7.8-9.8x more.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3 -O3 (CMake Release; the bench target adds only warning flags, no -march). libsamplerate 0.2.2 and soxr 0.1.3 are the Ubuntu 24.04 distro packages, so their build flags are the distro's. r8brain-free-src is at pinned commit 7.5 with Ooura FFT. Embedded counts: arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2.1 and hexagon-clang 19.1.5 at -O3 (CMake Release).
hardware: Host: shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz (exact model not stated), run 2026-09-25. Embedded: QEMU TCG instruction counting on Cortex-M55 (mps3-an547), Cortex-M33 (mps2-an505) and Hexagon (qemu-hexagon 8.2.2) via the manually triggered compare.yml workflow.
tradeoffs: Specialised: near-unity asynchronous ratio (+-1000 ppm default) for clock-domain bridging, not a general-ratio resampler. Header-only C++20. Fixed-point Q15/Q31 paths for FPU-less DSPs. Very low latency (0.5 ms filter, 1.5 ms default).
caveats: First-party: the harness and doc are by the project's author. On x86 host throughput, SampleRateTap beats only libsamplerate; soxr HQ and r8brain-free-src are faster (the author says so openly) but carry 8-33x more latency. The host CPU model is not stated (shared Xeon), and no raw result file is committed; the numbers exist only in COMPARISON.md. The libsamplerate latency rows date from 2026-06-12. The tiers are matched on stopband depth only, so the engines do not do equal filtering work. SampleRateTap balanced is 48 taps with a 20 kHz passband and a 28 kHz stopband edge, above the 24 kHz Nyquist (async/include/tap/sr/async/polyphase_filter.h). libsamplerate MEDIUM is 120.61 dB with a 90% -3 dB bandwidth and about 91 taps per output at this ratio (half length 22437, increment 491 in src/mid_qual_coeffs.h; tap count derived from source data). At the ~140 dB tier, SampleRateTap transparent is 80 taps (20-26 kHz transition, 140 dB), while libsamplerate BEST's table is 154.67 dB at about 286 taps (derived from source data). Part of the speedup therefore comes from a shorter filter with a wider transition band, which lets 20-24 kHz content alias above 20 kHz. No THD+N was measured for libsamplerate MEDIUM. The THD+N table pairs SampleRateTap balanced (-133.9 dB at 24-bit I/O, servo recovering the clock) with libsamplerate sinc_best (-143.5 dB, fed the exact ratio), about 10 dB better. The products solve different problems: the async engine is an ASRC limited to near-unity ratios (default +/-1000 ppm), while libsamplerate is a general fixed-ratio converter (1/256 to 256). The benchmark times only the fixed-ratio datapath, so the clock recovery the libraries lack is not timed, and SampleRateTap cannot replace libsamplerate outside drift correction. On embedded targets, construction costs far more than libsamplerate (870 M vs 20.9 M instructions on Cortex-M33 for balanced vs MEDIUM). The benchmarks are behind TAP_SR_BUILD_COMPARE_BENCH (requires TAP_SR_BUILD_BENCHMARKS), off by default. The repo is young (5 stars, 225 commits, measurements back to June 2026, no issues filed); no correctness bug behind the numbers was found.

The embedded rows are reproducible QEMU instruction counts (.github/workflows/compare.yml, async/bench/icount/cmp_main.cpp, pinned arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2.1 and hexagon-clang 19.1.5 at -O3), but they count instructions rather than time, and the same author ran them.

The doc's ratios agree with its tables to within rounding of the displayed values: 14.6/4.8 = 3.04 and 3.0/1.9 = 1.58 (derived from page data), against the stated 3.1x and 1.5x. The main shortcoming is the quality pairing: the tiers are matched by stopband dB, while libsamplerate's filters keep the transition band below Nyquist with roughly 2x (MEDIUM) and 3.5x (BEST) the taps. The ASRC also solves only the near-unity drift problem, not general rate conversion.

name: Shine (fixed-point MP3 encoder)
baseline: LAME 3.100 (M1 Pro run) and LAME 3.99.5 (outdated Raspberry Pi run) CLI, 128 kbps CBR, qval=3, joint stereo with psychoacoustic model
workload: Encoding a 5 min 18 s 44.1 kHz stereo WAV to 128 kbps MP3 with the shineenc CLI versus lame -b 128.
claimed_speedup: README, first-party, MacBook Pro M1 Pro (arm64), 2022-12-30: LAME 3.100 at 128 kbps qval=3 reports 88.773x realtime (play/CPU; zsh time 3.609 s total) and Shine 318.0x realtime on a 5:18 stereo 44.1 kHz WAV, about 3.6x faster (derived from page data). The 318.0x is 318 s divided by a whole-second timer reading of 1 s (shineenc uses time()), so the true Shine time could be anywhere under 2 s and the ratio is only bounded below at about 1.8x (derived from page data). Outdated Raspberry Pi run (model not named): LAME 3.99.5 1.8216x (3:06) vs Shine 3.6x (1:35) on a 5:39 file, about 2.0x (derived from page data). Nexus 5: Shine 24.2x realtime, no LAME number.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for either README run. The repo's Makefile.am builds libshine/shineenc with -O2 -funroll-loops -fno-exceptions -Wall -fsigned-char (compiler not named); the LAME build is a stock 'LAME 3.100 64bits' binary of unknown origin.
hardware: MacBook Pro arm64 M1 Pro (current numbers); Raspberry Pi with model not named and Google Nexus 5 (Shine only) in the outdated section
stars_or_usage: 422 stars, 77 forks; github.com/savonet/shine resolves to toots/shine; used as FFmpeg's libshine encoder (issues #22, #28) and by Liquidsoap
tradeoffs: Fixed-point encoder for CPUs without an FPU; no psychoacoustic model, so quality at a given bitrate is below LAME; LGPL-2.0 (COPYING is GNU Library GPL v2). README notes the encoder may have latent bugs and that work on this fork was limited to reorganizing code into a shared API.
caveats: Speed is bought with lower quality: Shine has no psychoacoustic model (README 'Limitations' says so and calls the algorithm 'rather simple'), encodes plain stereo, while LAME runs its full psychoacoustic model at qval=3 with joint stereo, so the ratio compares different amounts of work at the same bitrate. No quality measurement exists anywhere in the repo (issue #27 'Quality comparison' open since 2017 with no reply). Single runs from pasted CLI output; shineenc's realtime figure uses whole-second time() resolution (src/bin/main.c), so 318.0x means 'finished within about 1 s' and is imprecise. LAME's figure is CPU-time based, Shine's is wall-clock. The two M1 runs used differently named input files (/tmp/decoded.wav, /tmp/bla.wav) of the same length. Open correctness issues: #24 full-amplitude sine input produces distorted output, #37 final frame may be truncated, #39 padding bit wrong at 32 kHz/48 kbps from float truncation in layer3.c; none touches the timing itself. A third-party ARM NAS anecdote on forum.serviio.org (Shine 42 s vs LAME 6:09 on a 3:48 file, '13x faster', little gain on x86) is search-snippet only. README says the code is Gabriel Bouvigne's late-1990s encoder via Pete Everett's fixed-point RISC OS port; issue #25 asks why it is LGPL when the original Shine seemed GPL. Last commit 2023-01-01, more than three years ago.

name: SuperFast Codecs (fre:ac multi-threaded codec drivers)
baseline: fre:ac's regular single-threaded codec drivers: libopus (Opus), FAAC and Core Audio AAC in the initial release; FDK-AAC, LAME and Speex drivers added later
workload: Converting one input file to one output file (single file mode) or several files in parallel (multi file mode) in fre:ac with 1, 4 or 8 threads, FAAC and Opus only. Each worker runs its own codec instance on overlapping blocks: the 2017 PDF describes 128-frame blocks with 8-frame overlap, while the archived repo's Opus driver uses 256-frame blocks with an overlap of at least 24 frames, and the LAME driver uses 128-frame blocks with 4x1152/frameSize overlap plus a frame repacker. Default thread count is cores + (logical CPUs - cores)/2.
claimed_speedup: Text: 'Using four threads, the conversion is already three times faster than with the regular drivers, which use only a single thread in this mode' (single file mode); in multi file mode the SuperFast drivers are 'only slightly faster'. Chart readings (approximate, unit-less y axis, derived from page data): single file mode, regular drivers about 24 (FAAC) and 29 (Opus) at every thread setting; SuperFast about 8.2 / 9.0 at 4 threads (about 2.9x / 3.2x) and 5.3 / 6.1 at 8 threads (about 4.5x / 4.8x); SuperFast at 1 thread is about 4% faster from decode/encode thread separation. Multi file mode gains are about 1-10%. Only FAAC and Opus are charted; Core Audio, FDK-AAC, LAME and Speex have no published numbers.
hardware: Not stated (the text mentions a 6 core CPU)
stars_or_usage: 65 stars; code merged into mainline fre:ac (BoCA)
tradeoffs: Chunked parallelism over several codec instances, so output is not bit-identical to a single-threaded encode and the 8/128 overlap caps speedup at 16x. Works for Opus, AAC, Speex and MP3 drivers; the author says Vorbis, FLAC and WMA do not fit. Needs the fre:ac BoCA and smooth class libraries to build. It speeds up a driver, not the codec library itself.
caveats: First-party PDF whose numbers are only in chart images with no y-axis unit; CPU model, OS, compiler and codec versions are not stated (the text only says 'even on a 6 core CPU'), and no benchmark script is published, so tier C. The measured code does different work from the baseline: it is the same codec run as several parallel instances against one single-threaded instance, not a faster codec implementation, and total CPU work rises because overlap frames are encoded and then discarded (6.25% at 8/128 in the PDF, about 9.4% at 24/256 in the final Opus driver). Output is not bit-identical to a single-threaded encode: every chunk starts from fresh encoder state, and the PDF's difference-signal plots show residual differences the author calls 'unnoticeable' without any listening test, objective quality metric or bitrate/size comparison. For MP3 the LAME driver unpacks and repacks frames to rebuild the bit reservoir across chunk seams, with rate-control limits and re-encoding when a frame does not fit. In multi file mode the gain is small (about 1-10%). The Opus resampler stays single-threaded, so non-48 kHz input gains less, and conversions are often limited by decoding speed. Repo archived 2020-12-11 (last commit 2020-12-10, last code change 2018-09-01); the code lives on in enzo1982/BoCA.

name: SuperLAME
baseline: LAME (stock single-threaded libmp3lame 3.101 beta)
workload: Multithreaded MP3 encoding of full albums (16-bit/44.1 kHz WAV) at VBR -V2 and CBR 320: SuperFast runs many libmp3lame instances on overlapping chunks and a serial repacker re-chains the bit reservoir. Measured with 16 threads on an 8-core/16-thread CPU against the same LAME r6531 core encoding single-threaded; the v1.1.0 scaling figures use the in-RAM --bench mode at 2 to 16 threads.
claimed_speedup: README: 'roughly 8x faster than stock single-threaded LAME at the same quality'; v1.1.0 on a Ryzen 7 5800X3D, 44-minute album, CBR 320: 13.8 s at 2 threads down to 3.9 s at 16 (~680x realtime), parallel efficiency ~93% at t2 and ~61% at t16 (no stock-LAME time is given for that run). docs/SCALING_NOTES.md (42-minute 440 MB album, mode not stated): stock LAME ~28 s versus SuperLAME ~3.6 s at -t2 to -t16, '~8x'; SuperLAME -t1 takes ~42 s (0.7x stock). docs/COMPARISON_REPORT.md (2026-06-29, pre-v1.1.0 build, 16 threads versus the same patched LAME r6531 core single-threaded, 4 albums): VBR -V2 5.84x to 6.17x (e.g. 4.19 s vs 24.46 s for a 50-minute album), CBR 320 1.49x to 4.73x (e.g. 17.19 s vs 25.60 s). The v1.1.0 CHANGELOG reports multithreaded encodes became 1.8x to 1.9x faster after that report (t16 7.2 s to 3.9 s on the 44-minute CBR 320 album), so the June table understates the current build.
compiler_and_flags: clang 21.1.6 targeting x86_64-unknown-windows-msvc (Windows 11): libmp3lame engines built with -O3 -march=znver5 / znver4 / znver3 / x86-64 (build/build_dispatch.sh; znver3 engine used on the test CPU); frontend clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -march=x86-64 and dr_flac clang -O2 -march=x86-64 (build/build_final.sh). Build flags of the stock-LAME baseline binary (build/phase2-build/lame.exe) are not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D (8 cores / 16 threads, Zen 3), Windows 11
tradeoffs: Runs many libmp3lame instances in parallel on chunks and repairs the bit reservoir, so the gain is thread parallelism. Single-thread output is bit-identical to stock LAME; multi-thread output differs by an inaudible (below -45 dB) reconciliation at chunk seams. Whole input and output are held in RAM (about 1-2 GB input limit). Needs clang to build the SIMD paths; GPL because it combines LGPL LAME and mpg123 with GPL code ported from fre:ac/BoCA.
caveats: First-party numbers only. The win comes from parallelism: 16 threads versus single-threaded stock LAME; per thread SuperLAME is slower (its -t1 is about 1.5x slower than stock LAME). No public script runs the stock-LAME comparison, the baseline binary's build flags are unstated and the test albums are commercial recordings, so the comparison cannot be reproduced. Multithreaded output is not bit-identical to stock LAME (decoded differences of -45 to -87 dB at chunk seams; single-thread output is identical). CBR gains are much smaller than VBR gains (1.49x to 4.73x versus 5.84x to 6.17x in the June report). The docs disagree on scaling: SCALING_NOTES says it plateaus at about 2 workers, while the v1.1.0 README shows gains up to 16 threads after the sleep-poll fix. Earlier builds had a repacker desync bug (fixed by porting fre:ac/BoCA fixes) and v1.1.1 fixed lost frames at low CBR bitrates. The znver4/znver5 engines are unverified; the build and tests are Windows-only (clang, PowerShell). Very new repo (3 stars). Built on LAME r6531 plus a port of fre:ac/BoCA SuperFast (GPL), not a GitHub fork.

caveats: Rust library, not C++ (wave language filter mismatch). First-party results, so tier C: the test files come from the author's personal media library (not published) and only one or two files are used per codec, which the page itself says favours the decoders it was tuned on. The page was last updated 2023-02-03 (rustc 1.67.0, development main of both projects at that date), long before the current v0.6.1, so the numbers may be stale. The FFmpeg C compiler, version and flags are not stated (plain ./configure). Timings are whole-process hyperfine wall times (startup and demuxing included for both; ffbench is statically linked). Results are mixed: Symphonia loses on AAC-LC, Vorbis and MP3 128 kbps everywhere and on ADPCM on some CPUs, and wins mainly on FLAC, ALAC, MP1 and MP2; on the Raspberry Pi the margins are small (10 of 16 rows faster, 0.81-0.96). Like-for-like single thread: ffbench.c opens the decoder with avcodec_open2(dec_ctx, dec, NULL), so libavcodec's default of one thread applies even for FLAC and ALAC, which support frame threading.

name: uavs3e
baseline: HPM 4.0 (the AVS3 reference software) for encoding speed; x265 veryslow for compression at a roughly similar speed
workload: AVS3 encoding (a different codec from HEVC): uavs3e speed level 3 against the HPM 4.0 reference encoder on encode time and BD-rate, and against x265 veryslow on BD-rate at a similar speed. Sequences, thread counts, CPU and compiler were not seen.

No speed ratio over x265 was seen; a later real-time-encoder paper claims a 'significant advantage in encoding speed compared to x265' without a number in the snippets.

name: VVenC
baseline: VTM-19.2 (JVET VVC reference encoder) and HM-17.0 (HEVC reference encoder); x265 v3.5 is also plotted but only in figures
workload: Random-access encoding of JVET common-test-condition sequences (class B HD, classes A1/A2 UHD) at constant QP 22/27/32/37; VVenC v1.14.0 with 8 threads versus single-threaded VTM-19.2 and HM-17.0 (both with MCTF enabled), reported as encoder runtime speedup together with PSNR-YUV BD-rate versus HM-17.0. The x265 3.5 runs in Figure 2 use 8 threads, --tune psnr and CRF 17/22/27/32 instead of constant QP.
claimed_speedup: VVenC v1.14.0 Table III, 8 threads vs single-threaded reference encoders, random access, JVET CTC: HD4K speedup over VTM-19.2 faster 2400x, fast 1100x, medium 330x, slow 87x, slower 19x (HD column 2400x/1100x/280x/74x/15x; UHD column 2500x/1200x/380x/98x/22x); over HM-17.0 the HD4K speedups are 380x/180x/53x/14x/3x with PSNR-YUV BD-rate versus HM of -13.3%/-25.8%/-35.1%/-39.1%/-42.1%. Only the slower preset matches VTM's compression (Figure 1 puts VTM-19.2 at roughly -41% BD-rate versus HM, read approximately from the figure), so the quality-matched speedup over VTM is 15x HD / 22x UHD / 19x HD4K, and it includes 8 threads versus 1. The page prose says 'more than 20x for HD4K' for slower and quotes 2300x/370x/-13.7% (faster) and 280x/45x/-35.8% (medium) for HD4K, which disagree with the v1.14.0 table and look stale. Versus x265 3.5 (8 threads) there are no numbers, only Figure 2: x265's plotted presets sit at about +29% to +42% PSNR BD-rate versus HM at about 0.4% to 6% of HM's runtime, while VVenC's presets sit at -13% to -42% at about 0.26% to 33% of HM's runtime (read approximately from Figure 2, derived from page data), i.e. a compression win at similar runtime rather than a speed win over x265.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502P 32-Core @2.5GHz (Dell servers); VVenC and x265 run with 8 threads, HM and VTM single-threaded
tradeoffs: Encodes H.266/VVC, whose decoder support and patent licensing differ from H.264/HEVC; the speedups are relative to the slow JVET reference software, not to a production encoder. Perceptual tuning (XPSNR-based QPA) is available.
caveats: First-party wiki numbers; compiler, flags and thread pinning are not stated and no timing harness is published, so not reproducible-tier. The measured code does different work from the baselines: VVenC runs 8 threads while VTM and HM are single-threaded, and every preset except slower gives up compression relative to VTM (faster loses roughly 28 BD-rate points against VTM), so the 2400x headline compares a fast, lower-quality multi-threaded VVC encode with the single-threaded JVET reference encoder. VTM and HM are research reference encoders, not production encoders; the category baselines x264/x265 are a different codec generation and VVenC is not shown to be faster than them in wall-clock time: the x265 3.5 comparison exists only as figures (CRF rate control versus constant QP for VVenC; the reference [14] links the x265 Release_3.4 tree while the text says v3.5), and third-party search snippets (forasoft.com, dev.to; not opened, blocked) describe vvenc medium as far slower than x265 medium on wall clock. The page prose disagrees with its own Table III (e.g. slower 'more than 20x' versus 19x HD4K in the table). Peer-reviewed first-party papers (ICMEW 2021: snippet only, single-threaded VVenC at 46% of VTM runtime and fastest configuration over 140x faster than VTM for an early version) were not opened. License is the Clear BSD License (BSD-3-Clause-Clear), which is FSF-libre but not OSI-approved per the SPDX license list 3.29.0, and it explicitly grants no patent rights; H.266/VVC itself is covered by patent pools. Page last edited 2026-03-30.

name: zita-resampler
baseline: libsamplerate (Secret Rabbit Code), named in the library docs as the comparison
workload: No benchmark workload behind the libsamplerate claim. The repo's test/speedtest.cc only times zita-resampler itself (44100 -> 48000 Hz, given channel count and hlen, input frames per second) with no baseline and no published results.
claimed_speedup: Directional only: 'Even at the highest quality setting libzita-resampler will be faster than most similar libraries providing the same quality, e.g. libsamplerate.' No numbers. Separately, the docs say the 1.8.0 SSE2 build 'will reduce CPU load by a factor of at least 2'; that factor is against the library's own scalar build, not against libsamplerate. The quality/CPU trade-off spans 'approximately 1:6' (CPU load roughly proportional to hlen).
stars_or_usage: 35 stars, 5 forks (digital-stage GitHub copy). Upstream is packaged in nixpkgs (1.11.2), an older 2012 version is vendored in Ardour (libs/zita-resampler), and it is the resampler behind zita-ajbridge (named in the SampleRateTap comparison table).
tradeoffs: GPL, so copyleft for linked code. Single-precision float only, interleaved multichannel, fixed-ratio Resampler plus variable-ratio VResampler class. Quality/CPU trade-off range of about 1:6.
caveats: Tier D: a first-party directional claim with no numbers. The repo is digital-stage's 2021 import (8 commits, 2021-02-16 to 2021-03-10, no releases, not a GitHub fork) of upstream release 1.8.0 by Fons Adriaensen; its sources, docs and README match 1.8.0 (version macros 1.8, copyright 2006-2020, AUTHORS Fons Adriaensen) with a CMake build added. The canonical upstream is https://kokkinizita.linuxaudio.org/linuxaudio/ (unreachable from this environment), which has moved on to at least 1.11.2 (nixpkgs bumped to it on 2025-06-04), so this copy is behind upstream and abandoned; upstream's own activity date could not be checked. The copy's CMakeLists.txt sets non-standard variables (CMAKE_CXXFLAGS_FLAGS, CMAKE_CPPFLAGS_FLAGS) that CMake ignores and never defines ENABLE_SSE2, so a CMake build of this copy gets the scalar path without -O2 unless the user adds flags; the 'factor of at least 2' SSE2 gain applies to the upstream Makefile build, which enables SSE2 by default. GPL-3.0-or-later copyleft (file headers say 'version 3 ... or any later version'; nixpkgs labels upstream 1.11.2 gpl3Only, not checked at source). The SampleRateTap comparison (now async/docs/COMPARISON.md) lists 'zita-resampler + zita-ajbridge' with 'no published CI-verified figures' and measures only libsamplerate, soxr and r8brain-free-src.
